--- LOVE AND VISION. My love is more than life to me. And you look on and wonder In what can that enchantment be You think I labour under. Yet you, too, have you never gone Some wet and yellow even Where rivbet moors reach on and on Beneath a windy heaven?— Brown moors which at the western edge A. watery sunset brushes With misty rays yon sullen ledge Of cloud casts down on the rushes. You see no more; but shade your ayes,

Forget the showery weather, Forget the wet, tempestuous skies And look upon the heather. Oh, fairyland, fairyland! It sparkles, lives, and dances; By every gust swayed down and fanned, And every rain-drop glances. Never in jewel or wine the light Burned like the purple heather; And some is the palest pink, some white, Swaying and dancing together. Every stem is sharp and clear, Every bell is ringing, No doubt, some tune we do not hear For the thrushes' sleepy singing. Over all, like the bloom on a grape, The lilac seeding•grasses Have made a ha4e, vague, without shape, For the wind to change as it passes. Under all is the budding ling Grey-green with scarlet notches, Bossed with many a mossy thing,
And gold with lionen-blotchei: Here and there slim rushes stand
Aslant like carried lances. I saw it and called it fairyland; You never saw it, the chance is.
Brown moors and stormy skies that kiss At eve in rainy weather— Pronounce on that—what the heather is 1. know, for I saw the heather. —From the At hen crum. A. MARY F. Ronlx3oN.

div.p: Varietal.

Sympathy comes near and speaks low. Such as every one is inwardly, so he judgeth outwardly. He rises the highest in the Christian life who bends the lowest. David's pen never wrote more sweetly than when dipped In the ink of affliction. It is surprising how many people there are who do not like to work between meals. The strongest man is rarely strong enough to hold his tongue at the right time. Life does not count by years. Some suffer a lifetime in a day, and so grow old between the rising and the setting of the sun. "My nephew is not content with a gig," says Mrs. Rams- botham," but he gets two horses, pats one before the other, and drives about the country in a tantrum." An old bachelor says—" It is all nonsense to pretend that love is blind. I never yet knew a man in love that did not see ten times as much in his sweetheart as I could."

"A lawyer once jeeringly asked a Q laker if he could tell the difference between also and likewise. "Oh, yes," said the Quaker. "Erskine is a great lawyer; his talents are admitted by almost every one. You are a lawyer also, but not likewise." A French gentleman, who supposed he had mastered the English language, was sadly puzzled one day when a friend looked at him and said, " How do you do?" "Do vot ? " "I mean, how do you find yourself ?" "Sair, I never loses myself." "But how do you feel ?" " Smooth ; you just feel me." A Scotch lady gave her servant very particular instruc- tions regarding visitors, explaining that they were to be shown into the drawing-room, and no doubt used the Scotti- cism, "Carry any ladies that call upstairs." On the arrival of the first visitors, Donald was eager to show his strict attention to his mistress's orders, _ Two ladies came _ _

together, and Donald, seizing one in his arms, said to the other, "Bide ye there till I come for ye," and in spite of her struggles and remonstrances, ushered the terrified visi- tor into his mistress's presence in this unwonted fashion. " Bulls " are not all of Irish origin. It was the mayor of a Portuguese city who once enumerated, among the marks by which the body of a drowned man might be identified, "a marked impediment in his speech." The American General Taylor was made ridiculous for a time by the sen- tence which occurred near the beginning of his message sent to the Thirty-first Congress, December, 1849, as fol. lows :—" We are at peace with all the world, and seek to maintain our cherished relations of amity with the rest of mankind." Bat Mr. Buchanan almost matched it in speech which he made at the South, in which he said—" I do believe, gentlemen, that mankind, as well as the people of the United States, am o interested in the preservation of this Union." FORBEAIZA.NCE.-It is in our daily association with other

people whether in society, in buAiness, or at home, that we are in the deepest need of forbearance. We are irritated at countless things, and seem goaded on to utter bitter words, or spiteful allusioDs, or stinging repartees. Tao following whimsical circumstance happened some time ago in Kilkenny :—A tailor, who was married to a very sickly woman, grew enamoured of a young girl who lived in his neighbourhood, and on certain conditions he agreed to give her a promise in writing to marry her imme- diately on the demise of his wife; in consequence of which I'4 r. Snip passed the following curious note of band :—" In two days after the demise of my prosent wife, I promise to marry :Jigs Moran, or order, value received, under £5O sterling. Given under my hand this 16th day of May, &c. —J. Sullivan." Shortly after Mary received the above note she died, leaving it endorsed to a female friend, who also chanced to take a fever, and died before the tailor's wife ; however, on her sick bed, she also endorsed the note and gave it to a cousin, whom the tailor absolutely married, agreeably to the endorsement, in two days after the death of his wife.

HOW we POISON THE AIR WE BREA:PHIL—The Sir which we draw into our lungs with every breath contains 21. per cent. of oxygen, but when we expire it again it only contains 13 parts. We have, in fact. abstracted 8 per cent. of oxygen and given back in its place a poisonous uracture of carbonic acid, organic matter, and watery vap•Jur. We breathe out this poisonous mixture at the rate of one gallon each minute, but (even apart from the organic matter) it is so impure, owing to the amount of carbonic acid which it contains, that each gallon would require to be diluted with 100 gallons of pure air before being again fitted for respiration. In a city such as London then, the air is being polfated even by the carbonic acid which we exhale at the rate of nearly six hundred million of gallons per minute, to each art extent as to render it unfit to be breathed again. Surely this should make us welcome every strong gale as an angel sent from heaven, bearing healing on its wing?. But it is in dwellings, and especially in the dwellings of the poor, that the polluting effects of respiration are greatest, for in these it is too often the case that man places every possible obstacle in the way of nature's methods of ventilation. Moreover, in apart- ments that are crowded it is practically impossible to maintain the air in a state of purity. and thus they become hot-beds of disease. The very interesting experiments made by Dr. Angus Smith upon himself in an air-tight leaden chamber, led him to the conclusion that, in air con- taining an Increased amount of carbonic acid, this gas alone, even without the other hurtful ingredients, such as or- ganic matter, rapidly produces poisonous effects—indicated by feebleness of the circulation, extreme slowness of the heart's action, and great rapidity of the breathing—and that when men are exposed to it they are really gasping for breath, without being aware of the cause.—" Poison in Common Things," by Professor Simpson, in " Good Words" for October. DEATH IN THZ DRAINS —This has been sufficiently es- tablished, that when diseases do come amongst us they take root with most effect in those places where decomposing matter is found, and that the germs of these diseases find in the organic element of sewer gas a congenial soil in which they can increase and multiply indefinitely, and by which they can be carried from the dead to the living. That typhoid fever depends to a great extent, upon the polluted air of sewers, ceserpoOls, and of the soil is proved by very strong evidence. In some cases the disease ha a been con- fined to a particular part of the house, especially exposed to the effiavia from badly trapped drains, where there could be no doubt as to the source of the infection. The sewer air, laden with the specific poison, may be inappreciable to the senses, but its hurtful effects make themselves felt none the less, and, as recent events have shown, may sometimes exhibit themselves in the most exalted stations of life. Nay more, it would seem that persons of the upper and middle ranks in towns are more liable to be attacked by typhoid fever than the poor classes; the reason being that the houses of the former are more generally connected with sewers, and either from structure or situation are of higher eleva- tion, so that the light sewer gases, obeying natural laws, are more apt to accumulate in the drains of such houses, and failing efficient trapping and ventilation of the drains, to effect an entrance into the houses themselves. There is good ground for the belief that cholera, diphtheria, scarlet fever, as well as many other diseases, are occasionally spread by means of the air of sewers and cesspools; but whether these diseases originate spontaneously in this way, or whe- ther the sewer gas only serves as a carrier of the disease- germs, is a question, as.in the case of typhoid fever, as yet unsettled.—lbid. How SMELLING-BOTTLES ARE PILLED.—The most usual composition consists of equal parts of hydrochlorate of am- monia (sal ammoniac) crashed to a coarse powder, and car- ! bonate of potash (pearlash), mixed together, and scented' with any essential oil, such as lavender, lemon, rosemary, I &c., or a combination of them all. When exposed to the atmosphere, by the stopper being removed, the composition attracts moisture, and decomposition commences. The hydrochloric acid unites with the potash. while carbonate of ammonia is liberated. This action is increased by the application of a gentle degree of heat, such as holding the bottle in a warm hand. Occasionally the ordinary seequicarbona.te of ammonia (snelling salts) is employed for this purpose, either alone or scented. Sometimes concen- trated acetic acid is used instead of the salts of ammonia. In this case, the bottle is previously filled with crystals of sulphate of potash, or pieces of sponge, which are after- wards moistened with the acid, previously scented with lavender. rosemary, or any other scent that way be preferred. Household Guide. CHAIM—Chalk, a very abundant form of carbonate of calcium. It is white, soft, opaque, and without the least appearance of polish in its fracture. It will not dissolve in pure water. but is readily soluble in dilute mariatic acid. When purified, chalk is called whiting; when burnt, it is changed into lime. It is extensively used in agriculture, as an addition to sods which are deficient in lime. On micro- scopic examination, chalk is found to contain a large num- ber of fcseil foraminifera and other lower organisms; and, combining this with the results of deep-sea dredgings, there is little doubt that the chalk has been formed from the cal- careous remains of these low organisms, just as the cal- careous mud is being formed at the bottom of the deep sea at the present day. In systematic geology the chalk forms the most itepprtant division of the cretaceous series of rocks, and in some parts of England is more than 1,000 feet thick, It is also found in many parts of the world, and is remark- ably uniform in its general character. Many parts of the chalk contain a large number of fossil mollusca, crinoids, sponges, and echinoderms (see urchins), many of the latter being characteristic of this formation. Remains of eaurians and other reptiles are also found, the most notable being the pterodactyle, an enormous winged liz ad. Nodules of flint are also very common in the chalk. The name chalk is also occasionally applied to other minerals; thus black chalk is k a peculiar kind of elite, also called drawing slate, which ,produces a black shining streak on paper, and is used in crayon drawing. Red chalk is a clay coloured by oxide of iron.—Cassell's Concise Cyclopedia. Tam MILL FIRE AT BOLTON.—People not familiar with the interior of a cotton mill will probably be amazed at the rapidity with which such an extensive establishment cm be destroyed, and many lives be endangered, in spite of the best precautions that have or can be adopted, but not so those who are acquainted with them. In spite of the pre- sence of numerous buckets of water and three " extincteurs" in each room, hose-piping on each landing, and a stationary engine in the yard, capable of supplying twelve jets, not the slightest success appears to have attended any effort, if any were made, to even check the fire so as to permit of the im- prisoned workpeople having a chance to escape. This, of course, is to be attributed chiefly to the loss of all presence of mind on the part of those who ought to have worked the extinguishing appliances. Evidently, there was a lamentable want of organisation for the purpose, and of familiarity with the use of these appliances, of a highly culpable character. It is quite useless making extensive and costly provision for extinguishing fires, unless a corps of men are drilled to their use and kept thoroughly familiar with them, as the machinery will never operate of its own accord. The manager, we see, blames the panic amongst the " winders," but as these were women, nothing else, in the circumstances, could have been expected. The only thing for women to !do in such a case is to get out of harm's way as speedily as possible, fcr which they should be provided with every facility. This brings into strong prominence another defect in the internal arrange- ments of this mill, which largely contributed, in our opinion, to the magnitude of the disaster—the want of a sec and staircase. Mills of this dimension, or we would prefer to say all mills, ought to have a second staircase, thus giving ingress and egress at each extremity; and this should be in constant use, so that in a case of necessity one or the other would be always available for retreat, and quite familiar to those who would have to use them. This extra staircase would afford the best means of fighting the fire that could be devised, as it could be attacked from both sides without any, or, at least, with greatly diminished risk of the de- moralisation that has occurred in this case. No one can reasonably be expected to be brave in the case of fire when he is liable to be surrounded; but if he knows that there is always a way open, he may stand his ground, and put forth efforts that in many cases would be an effectual check to the flames, and prevent the loss of life and property such as has occurred in this instance.—Textile Manufacturer. THE Booetor MvsEum.—Miss A. B. Edwards writes to the Academy :—While Egyptologists of every nationality are congratulating themselves and each other upon the safety of the Boolak Museum, it will not be amiss to note that a priceless addition had been made to the treasures of that famous collection shortly before the breaking out of the late rebellion. Several of the royal mummies discovered last year at Dayr-el-Banaree were, it will be remembered, . found garlanded with flowers, those flowers being for the most part in as perfect preservation as the specimen plants in a" Hortus Silents." M. Arthur Rhone, in a recent letter to Le Temps, hAs described the extremely carious way in which these garlands are woven. They consist of the petals and sepals of various flowers, detached from their stems, and enclosed each in a folded leaf of either the Egyptian willow (Satix salsaf) or the Mimusops Kummel Bruce. The floral ornaments thus devised were then arranged in rows (the points being all set one way) and connected by means of a thread of date-leaf fibre woven in a kind of chain stitch. The whole resembles a coarse "edging" of vegetable lacevsork. Among the flowers thus preserved are the bright blue blos- soms of the De7phinium orientalis, or larkspur; the blue lotus, or Xympkoea coerulea ; the white, or Tymphoea lotus, with pink-tipped sepals; the blossoms of the Sesbania Aegyptiaca ; ard the orange-hued flower of the Carthamus tinetcrions, or safflower, so largely employed as a dye by the ancient inhabitants of the Nile valley. The dried fruit, as well as the dried yellow blossom, of the Acacia Nilotica is likewise present; and mention is also made of the blossom of a species of water melon now extinct. The foregoing are all interwoven in the garlands in which the mummy of Amenhotep I. was elaborately swathed. With others of the Royal mummies were found fine detached specimens of both kinds of lotus, the blue and the white, witb stems, blossoms, and seed pods complete. Still more interesting is it to learn that upon the mummy of the priest Nebsooni, maternal grandfather of King Pinotem 11. (XXlst Dynasty), there was found a specimen of the lichen known to botanists as the Parmelia furfuracca.. This plant is indigenous to the Islands of the Greek Archipelago, whence it must have been brought to Egypt at, or before, the period of the Her-Hor Dynasty Os c. 1100 or 11 c. 1200). Under the Arabic name of "Kheba," it is sold by the native druggists in Cairo to this day. These frail relics of many a vanished spring have been arranged for the Boolak Museum with exiuisite skill by that eminent traveller and botanist, Dr. Schweinfurth. Classified, mounted, and, so to say, illustrated by modern examples of the same flowers and plants, they fill eleven cases—a collection absolutely unique, and likely ever to re- main so. The hues of these old-world flowers are said to be as brilliant as those of their modern prototypes; and, but for the labels which show them to be three thousand years apart, no ordinary observer +mid distinguish between those which were buried with the Pharaohs and those which were gathered and dried only a few months ago. Tatum CH&NoES.—Let Us take a most important trade, the business of supplying East India cotton to the manufac- turers of the Continent. I will give the history of East India cotton intended for the supply of an Austrian manu- facturer some 40 years ago and at the present time. At that time cotton came down from the interior of India in bul- lock carts, each cart carrying four bales. A native merchant, generally a Parsee, collected and assorted the cotton, and shipped it under advances from an English merchant in Bombay, who charged 2i per cent, for so doing. It was car- ried by an English wooden sailing ship to England, con- signed to an English merchant in Liverpool or London, who stored it in an English warehouse, insured it with an Eng- lish assurance company, and sold it, with a commission of 24 per cent. to another Liverpool or London merchant. The latter purchased it under orders for an Austrian manufac- turer, to whom he charged a farther commission of 2 per cent. for his trouble. Each of those merchants received thus a handsome commission, and the English warehouse owner, assurance company, and labourer were in turn paid for their services. Then the cotton was shipped on an English sail. lug ship or steam vessel for Trieste, whence it was finally forwarded for the manufacturers' use. Now, all these opera- tions, profitable to English merchants, shipowners, labourers, and others, have in most cases ceased, and the Austrian manufacturer can and does contract with a Bombay house Bomb choatyt otno, Ti tr ii se sttreu oe f, IT set rileql cuai rr re ide db ablye saonf Ec ontgt loins h. through its European agent for the shipment direct from shSiopm,ebuotf this for a much shorter distance, and for a small fraction of the freight formerly charged. I need not add that even for this fragment of the old traffic the energetic Mediterranean shiPowner competes severely with the shipowner of our own country. For the Mediterranean shipowner has the advantage of being present in person at one end of the voyage to watch with a master's eye the disbursements, the condition of his vessels, and the conduct and manegements of his captains and his crews. What has '-pen sliit or our Austrian competitor holds no less true of all our other cam. i

THE SALVATIONISTS AT BOMBAY.—The three Salvationists who were arrested at Bombay have been convicted of being members of an unlawful assembly, and as they have re- fused to pay fines have been sent to prison, the major for a fortnight, and the other two for a week each. The stipendiary magistrate, in giving judgment, entered at length into a comparison of the conditions under which the Salvationists work in England, where people are of one religion, and those under whick they work in India, where there are many re- ligions; and insisted upon the absolute necessity of avoiding noisy and peculiar demonstrations, which were sure to pro- voke angry feelings and counter demonstrations. He further stated that the vagaries of the Salvationists had created a stir in the Mahommedan community which might easily develop into a disturbance of the peace, and reli- gious outbreaks are too dangerous in India to be provoked with impunity. The sort of service which the Salvationists have been holding is described as "knee drill and free and easy," by which is meant prayer interspersed with hymns and addresses.

The business of the Church Congress was commenced at Derby, on Tuesday. The Archbishop of York, preaching to a crowded congregation in All Saints' Church (where the offertory was devoted to the foundation of the new Bishopric of Southwell) pointed out the present wants of the Church—namely, a more thoughtful clergy, greater cohesion, a spirit of order, and less feeling of caste among the clergy—above all, more devoted zeal on the part of those who profess to work for the Church. The President, the Bishop of Lichfield, delivered his inaugural address' and papers were afterwards read " On the unity of belief in relation to diversity of thought," followed by discussion. The Church Congress at Derby was engaged, on Wednes- day, in the discussion of a variety of subjects, chief among which was that of "The Church and modern thought." This subject was dealt with in its various phases by the Rev. J. L. Roberts, Professor Stokes, and the Rev. Stanley Leathes. Speaking of the relations between the Church and Parliament, Mr. Stanley Leighton M.P., said that these relations were fast becoming intolerable. The position of Churchmen in the Lower House at, all events was most un- satisfactory, because the Church did not feel that it had that amount of outside popular support which was necessary for successful action. He asked Churchmen not to rely upon either of the two great political parties, but to press her claims upon both. Mr. Cecil Raikes, M.P., also spoke. At night there was a large workingmen's meeting, addressed by the Archbishop of York and others. At a meeting, promoted by the Church of England Workingmen's Society, a letter was read from the Rev. S. F. Green, against whose continued imprisonment the meeting emphatically protested, such im- prisonment being "an act of 'unnecessary cruelty, and a scandal to the cause of religion." The importance of demanding Mr. Green's immediate release was urged upon the rulers of the Church.

The sittings of the Church Congress were resumed on Thursday at Derby, under the presidency of the Bishop of Lichfield. The chief subject of discussion at the morning meeting had reference to the position of the Church towards other communions, which was introduced by the Bishop of Lincoln. At the conclusion of the meeting the president an- nounced that the Bishop of Manchester had taken steps to release the Rev. Mr Green from prison. The afternoon meet- ing was rather stormy. The discussion was upon the sub- ject of Liturgical improvements, and was introduced by Mr. Beresford Hope, who advocated ornate ceremonies. The Hon. C. Wood, president of the English Church Union, de- clared that the Church, from neglecting her own principles, had practically fallen between two stools. In the course of the discussion it was urged that the Prayer-book should be revised from time to time; and Canon Gregory regretted that the subject had been taken up with warmth, for what the Church wanted waz pace.

BILLS or SALE AND FAILUEES.—In the week endin; Sep- tember 30th, 1882, there were 734 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 231 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 176, a decrease of four. The totals for portion of year te Sep- tember 30th, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and \Vales, 35,478, a decrease of 2,227; the failures gazntted number 7,950, a decrease of 757.—Stabbs' Mercan- tile Gazette.

ADVANCED IRON PRICES IN STAFFORDSHIRE.—On Tues- day, the customers of some of the rolled-bar firms in South Staffordshire received citculars notifying a rise in makers' prices of ss. per ton, and customers who bought some time ago were offered a rebate of 53. a ton to reduce the quantity one half. The makers of best thin sheets for stamping and working-up purposes were contemplating a rise of 20s, per ton. The committee appointed by the galvanised braziery firms have issued an advanced price-list, and rooing-sheet makers decline to quote. THE WEATHER AND THE COTCR TRADE.—The Mark-lane Express says:—' During the p tst week the weather has been showery and unsettled, but on the whole milder. The month of September has been rather favourable for tillage operations, and so far nothing has yet occurred to prevent the sowing of the 1883 wheat crop under favourable circum- stances. With regard to th.:: trade for English wheat both in London and tne provinces the tendency has been con- tinually downwards. Towards the close of the week there appeared to be something of the nature of steadiness observable in several important exchanges, but the variable quality and almost invariably poor condition of native offerings places English wheat at a great disadvantage as compared with foreign. Flour is now freely offered, and values continue to droop. The demand for matting barleys is not active, but values are maintained; grinding sorts, however, are continually cheaper to buy. For other des- cription of native produce there has been no material change in values. The trade for foreign wheats ciff stands in Lon- don has passed through another week of extreme depression, and at the end of the week Monday's rates could not be obtained. In Liverpool prices declined 2d. per cental, trade closing with a better demand at the decline. Foreign flour at Mark-lane has been cheaper to buy." The Farmer says —" Fine weather makes the market disappointingly weak, and below the moderate expectations formed last Friday Wheat is neglected at the very low prices asked. Foreign sorts are Is. clftaper from last Monday. Flour if also neg- lected. Barley is relatively steady in price, and oats remain as last week. Beans keep at quotations. Peas from scarcity are is. advanced. London is overweighted with supplies, and the outlook of the w'aeat trade is still dis- couraging." THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE: MANCHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—The iron market here continues to be charac- terised by great firmness. The chief factor at present con- tributing to the strength of this market is the large amount of iron going away for shipment and the activity in other iron-making centres. A considerable portion of the local business stirring has passed into the hinds of Lancashire makers of pig iron, whose prises are comparatively low, and fairly large sales of local pig iron have been made during the past week or so. Lancashire makers have not advanced their rates, but they are now very firm at 465., less 21-, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, district brands of pig iron average fully 2s. to 3s. per ton above this figure. The temporary withdrawal by the miners throughout the district of the notices for an advance of wages, and the fact that considering the recent pressure of the demand the actual upward movement in values has been comparatively limited in extent, has tended somewhat to relieve the anxiety of buyers, and since the commence- ment of the month there has been rather a falling off in the number of new orders coming in. The advance in orices with the commencement of the month has varied in different districts. The principal Manchester firms, as intimated last week, have not gone beyond an advance of 10d. per ton on the wharf and delivery rates for house-fire coals, and sd. per ton all round on engine fuel. In the Bolton district house coal has been advanced 10d. and engine fuel sd. per ton, but in some of the outside districts all round coals have been advanced is. and burgy and slack 5d., whilst at the Oldham and Ashton collieries prices generally are without material alteration. In the West Lancashire districts, where prices were put up pretty generally about 61. per ton upon round coal during September, there has been a further advance of from 6d. to is. per ton, with bu-gy and slack generally slightly dearer; and for coal going on to the Cheshire side notices have been sent out from some of the Wigan and St. Helens collieries of an advance of Is. 81. per ton.

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
A new Nordenfeldt torpedo has been submitted to the inspection of the Sultin, its special characteristic being that it is peculiarly adapted to defend the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus.
The other day a mob assembled in the Jewish quarter of Pressburg, and broke the windows of several of the houses. The military restored order after forty of the rioters hal been arrested.

The Marquis of Lorne, in opening the Agricultural Exhi- bition at Victoria, Vancouver Island, advised the people to accept any offers of labour in order to secure the speedy completion of the Pacific Railway. There has been a political fight in South Carolina. At a meeting at Lancaster the blacks and whites tried conclu- sions with pistols, the result being that one white man was , wounded, four blacks were killed, and many wounded. The insurrectionary movement in the Herzegovina appears to be spreading. There have been serious disturbances at Niksic, where the Mmatenegrin Government has had to resort to military force in quelling the rioters. One insurgent leader has been shot and another captured. The Porte haying made over to the foreign bondholders the revenues proposed to be raised by a system of trade licenses for foreigners in Turkey, the Dragomans of the dif- • ferent Embassies met on Saturday to discuss the scheme, , and declared themselves opposed to it. I The riots in Hungary, in which many unfortunate Jews • have suffered severely, both in person and property, have been strongly denounced by M. Tisza, the President of the • Ministry. He calls upon the local authorities to repress s such outbreaks by the employment of the military, and de- • dares that no "half-hearted "proceedings will ba tolerated. I The accounts from the distributed districts show that urgent s necessity exists for the prompt and effectual interposition of s the authorities between the "Jew baiters" and their victims. A REMARKABLE CRIMINAL.—A remarkable criminal has t just been dealt with at Bemen and Strasburg. This was a man by name Theophile Mary, a hairdresser, born at Barr, • whose vicious tendency took the form of inflicting slight stabs with a dagger on young women. At Strasburg he att icked no fewer than 18, nearly all of whom he struck on the breast. He made his first appearance two years ago, when for a month he spread terror among the inhabitants, s all efforts to capture him failing. He then vanished from Alsace, and some time afterwards appeared at Bremen, s where he again distinguished himself by attacks on a young woman. Here, however, he was soon arrested,- sentenced to seven years' imprisonment, and handed over to the Stras- burg authorities to be dealt with there. The 18 young women whom the prisoner had wounded appeared as wit- nesses against him. An expert declared him to be in posses- sion of his senses, ascribing his acts to a morbid \rarity, and the court sentenced him to one year's impaisonment, to be added to the seven years give him at Bremen. The man is 31 years of age. TORPEDO EXPLOSION ON A RUSSIAN IRONCLAD: Loss OF THIRTY LIVES.—A terrible accident occurred last Friday on board the Russian ship Poporfka. It had just returned to Sebastopol from a cruise, and there landed all its combus- tibles, when suddenly the torpedo magazine blew up, killing Lieutenant Zoozen, an engineer, and nearly thirty of the sixty seamen then on board. div.head: BAPTIST UNION.
div.p: THE BAPTIST UNION.

The Baptist Union commenced its work on Tuesday, at Liverpool, with a missionary sermon to young men at half- past seven in the morning, by the Rev. R. Glover, of Bristol ; and at half-past twelve o'clock Dr. Stanford, of London, preached to a crowded congregation at Myrtle- street Chapel. Meanwhile a public missionary breakfast had taken place in Hope Hall, at which the progress of mission work in Central Africa was discussed. In the even- ing a very successful meeting was held in the Philharmonic Hall, under the presidency of the Mayor, who in the course of an address gave some interesting information as to the work of the Baptist Missionary Society. On Wednesday morning the session of the Union was opened at Myrtle-street Chapel, where the president delivered his address, and in the afternoon Mr. Spurgeon preached a forcible sermon to an immense gathering in Hengler's Circus. The presidential address of the Rev. J. J. Brown did not aim at any high flights of rhetoric, the exposition of profound mysteries, or the solution of perplexities. It dwelt upon the simplicity of the principles and discipline of the Baptist ' Church, its freedom from pomp, and the little importance it attaches to culture and social refinement. The purity, activity, and usefulness of churches was, Mr. Brown de- clared, the pressing question of the day, and he admitted that, while to doubt is one of the signs of being in the front rank of modern thinkers, there are mines of spiritual s ealth as yet almost entirely unworked. In the evening a tem- perance meeting was held, at which Mr. W. S. Caine pre- sided, and Sir W. Lawson was also present. Papers on "The duties and responsibilities of church members," and "Evangelistic work in large towns," were read at the closing sitting of the Baptist Union, on Thurs- day morning, Mr. Spurgeon taking part in the discussion. A resolution was passed condemning grocers' licenses, and in favour of Sunday closing. On the motion of Mr. Spurgeon, thanks were voted for the hospitality which had been ex- tended to the delegates. The fund for assisting rural churches was increased to £l,OOO. A total abstinence con- ference was held in the afternoon, and a communion service, tract society meeting, and working men's meeting at night. The Mayor of Liverpool held a reception at the Town Hall in the afternoon, invitations to which were extended to the delegates attending the meetings of the Union.

div.head: TITE STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: TITE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Synan, M.P., has informed his tenants who are in arrear and unable to pay their rents that in order to save them costs he will jAn with them in any applications they may make under the Arrears Act.

Tuesday was the anniversary of the signing of the treaty of Limerick, which took place in 1691. The town was in- vested in August, 1690, by the English and Dutch, and afterwards surrendered on honourable terms. Mr. Dillon has consented to defer for a time his retire- ment from the representation- of Tipperary. The formal announcement of the fact is made on the authority of Dr. Croke, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Cashel. Ireland seems to have suffered most by the severe gale on Sunday. From all Darts of that country come reports of serious damage to property, and it is feared th it the loss to farmers through their cereal crops being scattered by the storm will be grievous. A farmer named Brown was on Tuesday found shot dead in a field near Castleisland. A Cork correspondent says there is no doubt that an agrarian crime has been cemmittjd. Another murder is reported from county Roscommon, but it is not so certain that it is a result of the agitated state of the country.

The Dtrkin Express publishes a letter from Lady Flor- ence Dixie detnanding that a statement of the Land League funds should be made by an eminent firm of public account- ants to be appointed. Commenting upon this letter the Express says it is estimated that altogether £200,000 has been raised, and asks, where is this enormous sum, only the smallest fraction of which has been accounted for?

Replying to a resolution of the Liverpool branch of the Land and Labour League urging him to reconsider his deci- sion to retire from political life, Mr. John Dillon, M.P., writes :—" I feel grateful for the kind feeling dis- played in the resolution. I shall give the matter my most earneßt consideration. Kindly assure my friends that noth- ing tut ill-health would have caused me to leave Irish poli- tical life at this time."

THE MURDER OF LORD ARDILAUN'S BAILIFFS.—The constabulary have made an important arrest in connection with the murder of the two Huddys, Lord Ardilaun's bailiffs, who were found drowned in Lough Mask. The prisoner's name is Patrick Higgins, and his house is situated near the path or border which leads to Kerrigan's house, where it is supposed the Huddys were murdered. Prisoner was conveyed to Cong under heavy escort. The Recorder of Dublin, in charging the Grand Jury, on Monday, spoke with regret of the criminal state of the city, and repl.,ing to a plea that Dublin was no worse than Manchester and Salford, which hold an eminent position in the statistics of crime, he said that "a very large contin- gent of the criminals of these places were recruited from the Emerard Isle." This is plain speaking, but the Recorder appears to think the truth needs to be told; people apolo- gising for criminals, he said, did a good deal more harm than they thought of. THE LETTERPRACK MURDER —The trial of Michael Walsh for the murder of Constable Kavanagh at Lttter- frack, county Galway, resulted at the Dublin Special Corn- miLsion in a verdict of guilty, with a recommendation to in-e7cy on the ground of youth and the existence of a doubt as to whether the prisoner fired the fatal shot. These were several persons concerned in the assassination of Kavanagh, and the finding of the jury is equivalent to a conviction as an accessory before the fact. A painful scene occurred when sentence was pronounced, the convict wildly protesting his innocence and denouncing the witnesses, whilst his mother was carried shrieking out of the court. THREATENED DESTRUCTION OF ENNISKILLEN CASTLE.— A fire broke out on Sunday evening at the Castle Barracks, Enniskillen. Fanned by the high wind, the flames speedily obtained a complete hold of the wing of the building in which it originated. The 2nd battalion Royal Enniskillen Fusileers now occupy the barracks, and they at once turned out so as to extinguish the fire. It is believed the fire originated in the cook house. A correspondent, at a late hour on Monday night, states that the fire had been put out owing to the plentiful supply of water. The flames were confined to one building, a party of pioneers cutting away the roof and walls intervening between the castle and the burning buildings. The castle stores and magazine were saved. No casualties.

STARTLING REVELATIONS.—At the trial of ten persons, at Armagh, for treason-felony, some extraordinary details were given of the working of an Irish Assassination Society, which called itself the Patr;otic Brotherhood. Originally it wag a Ribbon Society; but on the appearance of a man from America, it became a Patriotic Society. Its members were sworn to obey orders, and to keep secret the motive of the society from the police and the clergy. Its organisation covered both town and country; and, amongst other matters of business, it decreed the death of Mr. Brooks of Castle- blaney, and nominated four men to shoot him. Another feature of its operations was the burning of Mr. John M'Cullagh's mill at Carnally. The revelations made at the trial are startling and revolting, though they only confirm suspicions that have been widely entertained. It is a healthy sign to find the proceedings of such a society ex- posed in a court of law ; when once that begins to take place, the power of secret societies begins to be broken.

A proposal to confer the freedom of the borough of Drog- heda upon Sir Garnet Wolseley led to an ill-tempered dis- cussion in the Town Council on Monday. Something was perhaps due to the manner of the mover of the proposal, who made an amusing speech, in which he enthusiasticaily apostrophised the British commander in Egypt. " Well done, Sir Garnet, well done, thou soldier of Christ," he cried ; and the mover of a direct negative asked what sort of Christianity was it that was introduced into Egypt by fire and sword, to which the mercurial alderman who had brought the question forward made the somewhat irrelevant reply that as a Roman Catholic he asserted that there was as much freedom of religion in Ireland as there was in Rome or in Catholic France. A councillor bearing the name of Greene.said no country should sympathise so much with Egypt as Ireland should, whereupon the Mayor informed Mr. Greene that Ireland was not a pagan country. The voting was equal, and the Mayor gave his casting vote on the side of Sir Garnet.

RELEASE OF Mn. G. D. GRAY, M.P.—Tn Dublin, on Saturday morning, Mr. Justice Lawson made an order that the unexpired portion of the term of imprisonment to which he sentenced Mr. Gray, M.P., six weeks ago should be remitted, and that the hon gentleman should ba discharged on payment of the fine of £5OO which was imposed upon him at the same time. His Lordship made a statement justifying his action in punishing Mr. Gray for his con- tempt of court, and said that since he committed him to prison the attacks on the proceedings of the court had ceased, and a change for the better had taken place in the tone of the Freeman's Journai. The learned Judge also removed the obligation laid en Mr. Gray to find security for his future behaviour, doing this "for the sake of terminating an unpleasant state of things ; " but he gave the warning that "in case of further transgression hereafter they had an Executive armed with full powers to d.z,al with it, and pos- sessing the firmness to put such powers into operation where nc•cess try." Mr. Gray left Ric.l):nord pt is3n tli3 after-

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY' [Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblelchite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] THE HYDERS.
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY' [Published by Mr. E. J. Kibblelchite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission.] THE HYDERS.

lam beginning to feel at home at last. So far as one can judge of race by location, I apprehend that my ancestors— British, Saxon, and Danish—were in England long before the Norman. Still, as these were all conquered races—mere Afghans and Zulus, who, by the divine right of triumphant scoundrelism, calling itself superior civilisation, had to put their necks beneath the yoke—l ought to feel the vast superiority of those whose fathers came over with the Con- queror. But when I reach the Ryders I begin to feel at home. The British aristocracy is not altogether an exclusive caste. The great-great-grandfather of the Earl of Harrowby kept a shop in Smithfield; I had a great-grandfather who kept a shop in Fetter-lane, not five minutes distant. Among our Lares and Penates we still kept a pair of broken images which once figured in the shop window of our ancestor; I wonder whether Lord Harrowby still keeps among his house- hold gods the identical yard-stick with which his ancestor measured silks and calico. Lord Harrowby is too good a man to be offended at being reminded that his forfathers rose from the ranks. I might also remind Lord Sandon when, like a consistent Conservative, he votes against the Burials Bill, he votes to perpetuate one of the odious badges of inferiority under which those from whom he sprang once suffered. The term "Liberal-Conservative " is not so often heard now as it was five-and-twenty years ago, but it still repre- sents a mental temperament which must exist as long as the Conservative party itself.. However loyal Conservatives may be to their party, there are divers shades of Conserva- tive feeling. Culture, travel, religion' philanthropy, each in their own several way, temper ,the Conservative instinct. Take, for example, the Conservatism of the Earl of Beacons field, the Marquis of Salisbury, and Mr. Cross Every thoughtful Liberal, as soon as he gets away from specific questions' will at once recognise that they are of a different species. The first we despise, the second we hate, the third we reason with. In the adignturer we know that success is the only morality, in the latTdlord that class-privilege is the criterion of politics, in the Liberal-Conservative that reason and sentiment have considerable weight. Family traditions are frequently an important element in the political life of great houses, and it wJuld be easy to point out several arislocratic families of an essentially Liberal-Conservative type. Of these the Ryders will form a very fair example. There has always been a strong dash of Puritanism in the Ryders, which may, perhaps, be attributed to the fact that their earliest ancestor, of whom anything positive is known, was a Nonconformist minister. The Rev. Dudley Rider (they spell the name with a "y" now) was Rector of Bed- worth, in Warwickshire, then a good living worth .C2OO, and now of the value of £562 annually. This he renounced for conscience sake when the Act of Uniformity was passed in 1662. It is stated, too, that he also sacrificed a good estate, for his uncle, who had made him his heir, refused afterwards to have anything to do with a man who had incurred the odium of Nonconformity. After his ejection from Bed- worth, Mr. Rider removed to Weddington, from whence he was driven by the iniquitoas Five Mile Act, passed by the Tories of those days. After preaching at King's Lynn and elsewhere, he retired into private life, and diid in 16*83. The eldest son of the Bev. Dudley Rider became a trades- man of Nuneaton ; his son went into the Church and became Archbishop of Armagh. The second son came to London, and opened a mercer's shop in Smithfield. He appears to have been faithful to the Nonconformity of his father, for his children were sent to a Dissenting academy at Hackney. His second son,who appears to have been originally intended

for a Dissenting minister' studied at Edinburgh and at Ley- den, and, haying entered himself as a student in the Temple, threw off the Nonconformity which was then an insuperable bar to his professional advancement. Whi!e at the Univer- sity, he seems to have suffered from straitened means, but he had a happy faculty of pushing his way in the world, and was fortunate enough to be the friend and fellow-stulent of Lord King, by whom he was recommended to Walpole. In 1733 he was appointed Solicitor-General, and four years after Attorney-General. His time of office was unmarked by any exciting event save the Jacobite Rebellion of 1745, Sir Dudley Ryder appearing for the prosecution at the trial of the chief of the Rebellion. Once he had the misfortune,

by order of the House of Commons, to prosecute an auda- cious printer for a libel on that august assembly; but though he tried to bully the jury into a verdict of guilty, they acquitted the prisoner; and Sir Dudley had the addi- tional mortification, on returning borne, to be compelled to treat a mob to drink the health of the jury. In 1754 he was made Lord Chief Justice; but Lord Hardwicke obsti- nately objected to his elevation to the peerage. Two years afterwards, the Duke of Newcastle needing votes in the House of Lords, it was intimated to him that he would be created a peer, but before the patent of peerage was made out he suddenly expired, and the Government was shabby enough to withhold the title from his son. The son, how- ever, having sat for Tiverton nearly twenty years, zealously supporting Lord North's Ministry, was at length raised to the peerage by the title of Lord Harrowby. Harrowby, by the way, is a small place in Lincolnshire, not far from Grantham. He adopted as his family motto, Servata fides cineri—' The promise made to my ancestor's ashes is now kept"—very appropriate under the circumstances. The first Lord Harrowby had three sons. The first sat in his father's lifetime for Tiverton, as did also the second, who held at different times several lucrative offices. The third went into the Church, and became Bishop of Lichfield; one of his sons had a canonry in Lichfield Cathedral. The second Lord Harrowby, a staunch supporter of Pitt, and that statesman's second in the Tierney duel, filled a number of offices in his lifetime. He was successively Under- Secretary of State, Comptroller of the Household, Treasurer of the Navy, Paymaster of the forces' Ambassador to Berlin, President of the Board of Control, and President of the Council. In 1809 he was advanced to an earldom. He appears to have been a moderate Conservative, for whom the stiff Toryism of the Wellington Administration was too strong. Although a staunch supporter of Catholic emancipa- tion, he was a prominent member of the Evangelical party and took a warm interest in their religious and philanthropic societies.

His eldest son, the present Earl, who is now over eighty years of age, originally sat for what was once the family borough of Tiverton. Before the passing of the first Reform Bill the election of members was vested in the Corporation of that borough, and it deserves to be recorded in Lord Harrowby's honour that, having declared himself in favour of Reform, the Corporation of Tiverton, in 1830, refused to re-elect him. In the following year, however, he was elected for Liverpool, and his name appears in the Division List as voting in favour of the second reading of the Reform Bill of 1832. Faithful to the Liberal-Conservative tradition, he also voted for the Abolition of the Corn Laws. He con- tinued to sit for Liverpool till 1847, when his father's death removed him to the Upper House. Faithful also to the Puritan traditions of the family, Lord Harrowby has always been a warm supporter of the institutions of the Evangelical party. He has been Secretary to the Board of Control, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, and Lord Privy Seal. As he was first elected for Tiverton in 1819, his legislatorial career has extended over sixty years. Probably no living legislator can boast of so long a period of active service. The Earl of Harrowby owns in— Staffordshire 4,940 acres. Lincoln Gloucester 3,207 „ Warwick

T0ta1...12,625 „ with a rent-roll of £22,696. All of this has doubtless been acquired in a perfectly legiti- mate manner. Sandon Hall, near Stone, in Staffordshire, was purchased by the first Lord Harrowby, in 1776, of Lord Archibald Hamilton, the Dukes of Hamilton having pre- viously acquired the estate by marriage. Lord Sandon, the eldest son of the present Earl, is better known to the world now than his father. I once had to transact a little business with him, and his urbanity con- trasted very favourably with the manner of some men with whom I had previously been brought into contact on the front Opposition bench. He seems to have inherited the family traditions. According to Dod, h formerly ranked as a Liberal, and even now his Conservatism has not the flippancy of Mr. Cavendish Bentinck or the pugnacity of Lord Cranbrook. Of all the members of the late Govern- ment, not even excepting the ever suave and courteous Chancellor of the Exchequer, he seems the last man to create political enemies. He sat for Lichfield for three years, but since 1868 he has sat, as his father did before him for Liverpool. It will be remembered that he was one of the members of the first London School Board. . _
_ The Ryders have certainly had their share of good things in both Church and State, but not to such an extent as to give them a reputation for greediness, or occasion anything like scandal.

"What can I do for you to induce you to go to bed now ?" asked a mamma of her five year old boy the other evening. " You can let me sit up a little longer," was the youngster's response. A quick-witted boy who was accused of going in swim- ming, the proof of which was that his shirt was on wrong side out, told his mother that the shirt must have got turned while he was climbing over a fence. The reason why so many are unable to take Cocosvis that tha varieties commonly sold are mixed with starch, under the plee of rendering them soluble ; while really making them thick, heavy, and indigestible. This may be easily detected, for if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. Cadbury's Cocoa Essence is genuine; it is therefore three times the strength mf these Cocras, ar d a rcfreshirg bevcge Iho !s, or cottee.—.eldvt.

div.head: SIR STAFFORD NORTHOOTE AT GLASGOW.
div.p: SIR STAFFORD NORTHOOTE AT GLASGOW.

Sir Stafford Northcote visited Glasgow on Wednesday, and spoke in the afternoon at a meeting of the National Union of Conservative Associations of Scotland. The right hon. gentleman admitted that at the last election the Con- servatives were placed in a decided minority, owing partly to Use better organisation of their opponents, partly to the Midlothian speeches, and partly also to the operation of the Birmingham Caucus. He commended the establish- ment of the Union, which he regarded as a correct means of diffusing correct information and of dissipating political fallacies. The Government, he said, by their recent action had gained considerable popularity, but he doubted whether it would last long, and anticipated a reaction when the whole of the Egyptian question came to be discussed. At night Sir Stafford Northcote addressed a crowded meeting of the Conservatives of Glasgow and the West of Scotland in the St. Andrew's Hall. Referring to Egypt, he paid a generous tribute to the bravery of our troops, but threw upon the Government the responsibility of having brought about a war which he believed was unnecessary, and, being unnecessary, could not be said to have been justifiable. It was the supine- ness of the Government in the early stages of the Egyptian difficulty which rendered the employment of military force in the end nec.ssary.

Sir Stafford Northcote was on Thursday presented with the freedom of the city of Glasgow, in the presence of a large gathering in the City Hall. In accepting the burgess ticket the right hon. baronet thanked the Town Council for having admitted him to the privileges of citizenship, an honour which he greatly valued. He spoke of the rapid growth of Glasgow as a mercantile community, and of the material improvements which had been effected in the city in recent years. He was glad to think that, although differ- ing from many of them in politics, after so many years of public life, during which he had been always more or less a party man and obliged to engage in party battles, the relations in which they stood to each other were such as to make it possible for that great honour to be conferred upon him.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO REV. A. DIGNUIL
div.p: PRESENTATION TO REV. A. DIGNUIL

On Sunday afternoon last the Rev. A. Dignum, prior to his departure for India as a missionary of the London Missionary Society, delivered a farewell address to the teachers and scholars of the Wycliffe Sunday School, at which school Mr. Dignum was formerly a scholar. Mr. Dignum, at the commencement of his address, spoke in eulogistic terms of the Rev. G. S. Reaney; the former pastor of Wycliffe Church, to whom he was indebted for having infiataiced him in deciding to give his life to missionary work, and for whom he should ever cherish the watmest affection. In a most excellent address he spoke of the mission he was about to undertake, namely, Gooty, Madras. Its population was larger than most of our English coun- ties. Its position was very favourable to missionary work, and the climate was healthy. The present condition of the mission was encouraging, although the work done was hardly appreciable, the workers being so few as to be prac- tically lost in so vast a district. In concluding, Mr. Dig- num eat nestly appealed for help. Funds were needed to extend the work undertaken, Wycliffe had done nobly in the past, and he earnestly hoped that the same spirit would , animate them in the future.

At the conclusion of the address Mr, Wm. WALLINGTON, superintendent of the school, addressing Mr. Digmun, said: —"I have a very pleasant and agreeable duty to perform, a duty which I can assure you I shall discharge with all the ability and earnestness I can command. The business before us is to present to you on behalf of the teachers, officials, and scholars of this school this little memento of their regard for you upon your removal to India as a missionary. It is not of much value, perhaps, pecuniary, but this, in my opinion, is not the p: oper test of its value. It is the spirit in which it is given; this gift represents so many loving hearts, who have spontaneously determined that you shall not leave this country without tiking with you sme token ,)f their esteem, for one who, after being a boy in our midst, has decided, with Divine assistance, to give up home and early associations to preach in distant lands the glorious Gospel of Jesus Christ: and this s,acrifice on your part is the very thing that makes us feel proud of you. Allow me, then, to present to you this small token of our respest for you on behalf of Wycliffe Sunday School teachers and scholars, and may God's blessing go with you into your dis- tant home; may you feel happy in your work; may you be able to gain the esteem and good will of the people among whom you are going to labour; and may the whole of India be wan for Jesus Christ."

Mr. WILLIAM Rol;Enrs said he had much pleasure in reading the inscription upon the present, which was as follows:—" Presented to the Rev. A. A. Dignum, by the teachers and scholars of Wycliffe Sunday School, upon his going out to India, with earnest expressions of esteem and good will. Warrington, October Ist, 1882." He could assure Mr. Divnum that the little gift did not represent the full measure of their regard for and interest in him. When he had gone from them they would still remember him in the work he had undertaken and which was of the noblest character, and worthy the ambition of any man. They earnestly hoped that he would long be spared in health aml strength, and that his missionary life might be eminently useful. They would think of him when far away, and rejoice with him in his success. Mr. 3. S. GARLAND said: I should like to say a very few words to you on this moat interesting occasion. We have all listened with mush pleasure to the address given to us by Mr. Dignutn. I am sure he has touched your hearts by what he has said to you. Your sympathy on behalf of the London Missionary Society, under whose auspices he is going out, will be much increased. For several years he has been quietly pursuing his studies at the Lancashire College, obtaining the knowledge and experience necessary for the great work to which he has devoted his life. I am sure he will not forget Wycliffe Sunday School, and pray that God may prosper the work done here. Then let each one of us sustain -him in his work by our united prayers that God would be with him and prosper him, and abundantly own and bless his labours.

Several-of the teachers having spoken, Mr. DIGNInf, in acknowledging the gift, thanked them for their kind expressions towards him, and also for their beautiful present. Every time he wrote a letter he would be reminded of them. He felt greatly encouraged by their good wishes, and would earnestly strive to do good work for his Master. He should write 1.0 them from time to time giving them some account of his labours. He con- cluded by wishing them all an affectionate good-bye. Prayer having been offered by Mr. F. R. Roberts the pro- ceedings terminated. We should state that the present consisted of an elaborate writing case with gilt trimmings and inscription plate, and was supplied by Mr. Garland, Bridge-street.

div.head: NEWTON ADJOURNED LICENSING
div.p: NEWTON ADJOURNED LICENSING
SESSIONS.

The adjourned sessions for the consideration of objections by Superintendent Weir against the renewal of certain licenses were held at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday forenoon last, the magistrates on the Bench being Messrs. J. Pearson, T. J. Gillespie, and R. Houghton, Esqs. The first case called on was that of John Caunce, of Gol- borne.—Mr. Moore, solicitor, of Warrington, said that he appeared for Caunce, and applied for the renewal of his license. Superintendent Weir had given notice of an objec- tion to it, and he would first hear what Mr. Weir had to say —Superintendent Weir stated that he objected to the rsnewal of Caunce's license upon the ground that he had been fined in a penalty of 203. and costs for opening his house at eleven o'clock on Sunday morning. He was convicted at that court on the 2Gth of August, and was fined the amount stated.— The Clerk: Is that the only conviction ?—Superintendent Weir replied that it was the only conviction.—Speaking on behalf of Caunce, Mr. Moore contended that the law had been unintentionally broken on that occasion. It was really a question as to the distance, and as to whether the persons resided three miles away.—The Chairman said the magis- trates were disposed to renew the license, but very great cue must be taken in future. He hoped the ohjection would act as a warning. Superintendent Weir said he also objected to the renewal of the license held by James Foster, of Golborne. He stated that Foster was a grocer in High-street, and his license was to sell beer off the premises. On the 12th of August last he was brought up at that court and fined 40s. and costs for opening his house at 11-30 on the Sunday. If the magistrates thought necessary they had the power to withhold the license in that case.—ln reply to the clerk and chairman, he added that that was the only conviction recorded against Foster. There were a great many com- plaints about the house, however. There had been a system of carrying the beer out by a woman with a false pocket, and she could not be detected carrying it.—The applicant stated that he had held a license for five years.—The Chair- man : The Bench are unanimously of opinion in this case that the license should not be removed.

div.head: RENEWAL OF A PROVISIONAL LICENSE.
div.p: RENEWAL OF A PROVISIONAL LICENSE.

Mr. Fearn, of the firm of Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., of Warrington, applied on behalf of Messrs. Greenall and Co., brewers, Warrington, for the renewal of a provisional license which had been granted about that time last year for the Pear Tree Inn, Burtonwood, situated near to Collins Green station. The new house would not be proceeded with until the railway company had compieted the alterations they were at present carrying out. Messrs. Greenall had arranged to build the house, and there had been no trifling with the undertaking. When the company's alterations were completed Messrs. Greenall would be able to commence building the new premises—As there was no objection to the renewal, the application was granted.—This concluded the busiuess

div.p: Avery serious difficulty has arisen between the Burnley Tramway Company and the Corporation, which threatens to prevent the use of steam on the line. At two points in par- ticular the streets are very narrow. The Corporation are willing to widen these streets, but they think the Tramways Company should contribute something towards the cost. They have asked the Company for £l,OOO, but the latter positively decline.

a:111E110'S CATHEDRAL.—Considering the poverty of the eq°cese of Truro and the general prevalence of Noncon- ?rarity, Bishop Benson has been exceedingly fortunate with t„lle funds for this cathedral. £40,000 was the sum which "as to be expended on the work, and about that amount or little more was promised. The Fertescue memorial has nted to the work to be undertaken, and now Lord Robartes, 7,n0 for years represented the eastern division of the elinty, has offered to build the northern transept' at a cost hfa £lO,OOO, in memory of his parents, whose death was stened by the burning of their historic mansion. The Z„c'cr.ks at Truro are being pushed on, and although the faun- lon stone was only laid in May, 1880, the arches of the Ch. thoetr are now fast approaching completion. The part of b Parish church of Truro to be iqcorporated in Mr. I,eareon's new work has turned out after all to be little more tgan the shafts and base of about five or six columns, the :otainder, in spite of the protests of old inhabitants and elltiquarians, being deemed to be incompatible with the pile m°W in course of erection. It Ae ACCIDENT AT SOUTIIPORT.—An accident oc- i:,ltred on Montlay on the Lane islaire and Yorkshire Rail- at Southport. As the train which is due in Southport tern Liverpool at twenty minutes past eleven in the fore- Was proceeding round a curve about 300 yards from ie Station, the engine suddenly gave a jump and swerved }lt across the hires, at the same time breaLing the couplings. tjte end of the guard's van caught the end of the tender, and cue front of the foimer was knocked in. There were six tjages attached to the engine, and these were thrown off (51in°, but were not overturned. The passengers escaped Wlth a'shaking, none being otherwise hurt. As soon as the ti!rd felt the shock he applied the patent vacuum brake, Doulch has not long been adopted on the Liverpool and South- TOSystem, and thus the train was immediately stopped. a stoker is the only person injured, one of his arms being "everely hurt. The letter relates to a contribution by Pro- Geddes to Homeric study. Mr. Gladstone says (V. is true that I have been long persuaded that the plot of foilacl,' as it stands, has a consistent structure, such as to ural a strong argument for the unity of the poem. rgretting to ob,erve the difference of opinion between us, I klaN'e, nevertheless, a subject of satisfaction in my first tervey of your book, partial as it is, which outweighs that apet. It is that I find you pursuing that method of close et'd• Minute investigation of the text in its numberless ottlirecteristic points, which I have always held to be the 0,,1Y Way to truth and reasonable certainty in the Homeric te.Stion. I had far rather see my own conclusions, for tusg'eli I would first do battle, overthrown by the effective El of that method than established by any other." 1,01? —D .OREEHROOIKE ON THE EGYPTIAN POLICY OF THE lia?ftNllENT.—The following letter from Lord Sherbrooke 14' been sent to us for publication :—" Sherbrooke, Cater- kettle September 2d, 1882.—Dear Sir,—l think the Govern- were quite, right in putting down the military revolt bei,spPt. Egypt is really more European than African, ottig4P, united to the one by the sea and separated from the eby burning deserts. We ought to keep a sufficient Isa force there to keep the peace. The government b_a_uld be ostensibly in the Khedive, but it should be made `,Tatieeirstood that nothing should be clone contrary to the will at%te,„ English General on whose support the existence of thar." uePends. We ought to be able to manage this better huli"danY one, for we have been practicing it in India for a • disc red years. Everything will turn on his prudence and aMtion. We never can allow our troops to be made the tlieinnr,B Of enforcing injustice or oppression. Above all Ilowte I would avoid a joint occupation with a European • 'r• It hampers us in time of peace, and is very likely, ltS preBe a recent instance, to desert us in time of war. In the 'With rlB, state of Europe I think our policy should be—Friends I% ail, alliance oe joint enterprise with none. Our object llot to teloe, conquer or annex, but to foster and control.—Your "tent servant, SHERBROOKE."
