div.p: The Act passed practically abolishing imprisonment for debt in Scotland came into operation on Sunday. Serious defalcations have been discovered in the Swan- sea borough treasury, and two sanitary-rate collectors are

in custody. The failure is announced of the well-known firm of Paul Ta'mbaci and Son, shipping merchants, Sic., of Manchester. The liabilities are estimated at £159,000. It is annonnced that in consequence of continued indis- position Sir C. Hall has resigned the Vice Chancellorship to which he was appointed by Mr. Gladstone upon the deatb of Sir John Wickens in 173. Two Mormon missionaries attempted on Sunday to con- duct a Mormon service on Clerkenwell-green, London, but were set upon by a violent mob, and compelled to take flight after being considerably maltreated. A fisherman named Gowin Strong has caught in the sea, about a mile from Watchet, a large conger eel about 20Ibs. in weight. The fisherman found in the fish's throat a purse containing half a sovereign, neither the worse for the curious position in which they were found. Thomas Pickard, a quarryman, who on the 23rd of last month, at Markfield Quarry, near Leicaster, killed another labourer, named Thomas Brooks, by striking him on the head with a pickaxe, was on Monday committed for trial on a charge of a wilful murder." Sr. Thomas' COLLEGE, RllYL.—After an examination, held OR the 261 h, and the two following days, of last month, the third entrance scholarship has been awarded to Arnold James Thomson, son of Dr. Thomson, Kingswinford, near Dudley. There were 14 candidates. , A movement has been inaugurated in Blackpool with the object of making arrangements to bring a branch of the Cheshire Lines system to that town. It is stated that the Town Council will at once move in the matter, there being a strongly favourable opinion amongst the inhabitants. Professor Blackie and others interested in the Highlands are about to commence a fresh land agitation quite unconnected with the Land League party. Meetings are to be held in different centres, and petitions will be sent to Parliament setting forth the distress that exists in the Highlands. The first notable gift of pictures for the future Corpora- tion Art Gallery of Manchester was received on Tuesday at the Town Hall from Sir Joseph Whitworth. The present consists of four fine works of Etty, and will make a valu- able addition to the examples of the Great English colourist already in the Royal Manchester Institution. The mast important of the works presented by Sir Joseph Whitworth is the grand picture of "The Last Judgment," which was exhibited at the Art Treasures Exhibition in 1857. StrocKnap MURDERS BY A FARMER.—A shocking double murder was perpetrated the other day at the village of Beckington, three miles from Frome. A farmer named Samuel Phippen, aged 30, of White Row Farm, first shot Christopher Hill, a labourer in his employ, then attacked a boy named George Greenland, aged 13, and shot him through the arm, and afterwards walked across two fields to where his carter, Charles Shepperd, aged 60, was ploughing and shot him dead. Hill died from his injuries. The boy's arm will have to be amputated. Phippen, who is in cue-

tody, was addicted to drinking. SINGULAR DEATH—A man named Feder Mackaskie, who lived in Norris-street, Liverpool, has met with his death under very regrettable circumstances. Some lads,were amus- ing themselves by setting off fireworks, and they annoyed Mackaskie by pushing some under his front door. Mrs. Mackaskie went out and the lads ran away, but, hearing them returning, the man got a poker and threw it into the street. Then he took off his belt and hit a boy named Ross with it, and Ross, seizing the poker, dealt Mackaskie a blow on the skull which killed him. Ross, who is only fourteen years old, has been committed on a charge of man-

slaughter. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—There was a collision on Saturday morning on the Great Eastern Railway between Lowestoft and Beccles, occasioned by a goods train running into a ballast train, both proceeding in the same direction. So great was the shock that the engine of the goods train and several of the trucks were hurled off the rails, and the permanent way was completely blocked. The engine was considerably damaged, and some of the trucks greatly shattered. The rails, too, for some distance were torn up and bent, and traffic was rendered impossible. The driver, the stoker, and the guard of one of the trains were

injured. THE STAMFORD HILL BURGLARY.—John Saunders, burglar, was on Wednesday committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court on the double charge of burglary and attempted murder in the house of Mrs. Reynolds, at Stamford Hill. The prisoner, being detected in the act of burglary, attempted to secure his escape by shooting a groom named Howe, and aiming at other persons, whom, fortu- nately, he did not succeed in wounding. Howe was suffi- ciently recovered on Wednesday to give evidence against his assailant, who will in all probability, as a warning to other armed burglars, be sentenced to penal servitude for life. Mr. Vincent, the director of criminal investigations in connection with the metropolitan police force, has issued a caution to the public concerning the numerous so-called private inquiry offices which are springing up, and whose agents have in several instances been found to be imperson- ating detective police. Mr. Vincent states that all legiti- mate inquiries, in furtherance of the operation of the are readily made on application to the police, and in the case of domestic inquiries which the police cannot undertake, Mr. Vincent is always ready to give the name and address of some retired dicer, whose pension affords a guarantee of integrity. THE ST. LUKE'S MYSTERT.—Franz Felix Stumm and Elizabeth Stanger were charged on remand at the Worship- street police court, the former with forgery and the latter with...conspiring to aid the other defendant to defraud the executors of Urban Napoleon Stanger, husband of the second named prisoner. Mr. Poland prosecuted. Evidence of clerks in the Westminster and Shoreditch branches of the London and County Bank was to the effect that Stumm paid in a forged cheque for £7O to his own account at Shoreditch branch. It was drawn upon Stanger's account at West- minster. Evidence of the proceedings in bankruptcy against Urban Stanger followed, and both prisoners were remanded. MR. GLADSTONE ON FINANCIAL REFORM IN PARMA- MENT.—Mr. Gladstone's secretary writes to Mr. E. R. Mus- pratt, chairman of the Financial Reform Association of Liverpool :—" I am directed by Mr. Gladstone to acknow- ledge the receipt of the memorial dated the 28th ult., and signed by yourself and other members of the Financial Reform Association' in which you urge the appointment of a finance committee of the House of Commons for the purpose of examining the estimates annually laid before Parlia- ment, and I am to state that Mr. Gladstone is not without hope that the plan of the Government with regard to pro- cedure, when fully stated, will be in the direction of your wishes." FATHER IGNATIUS AND LLANTHONY ABBEY—Father Ignatius, in reply to Mr. Landor's complaint as to his pro- ceedings at Llanthony Abbey, says I have never attempted to collect Money to restore Llanthony Abbey, for the simple reason that until I built the present abbey there was no such building in existence as Llanthony Abbey. Neither am I collecting, or have I collected, funds for build- ing Llanthony Abbey. The funds have all been provided by three members of our own order. The only Llauthony Abbey that ever existed belongs to me, and not to Mr. Landor. I have built it on land, the title deeds of which are in the bands of my lawyer. I have not attempted to no anything for the old priory which Mr. Landor temporarily possesses, except to pray to God for its restoration to His ; service i a His own time and in His own way."

PLOT FOR A GENERAL ESCAPE OF CONVICTS FROM DA.RTMOOR.—A plot among the convicts at Dartmoor to make a general escape has just been disclosed. A discovery has been made of skeleton keys constructed of the bones which the convicts have found in their meat at meal times and secreted. Recently two convicts were found together in a closet after having unlocked and escaped from their cells' their evident intention being to secret themselves there until the opportunity presented itselflfor getting away. It is believed that many cf the convicts have possessed themselves of these bone "keys," and it is even stated that not long ago a convict actually made an offer to one of the officers to unlock any door in the prison, while another is said to have informed the authorities that a plan had been formed for breaking out of the prison. It was intended to make keys , of bones, to unlock the cells in one pert of the prison, seize the warder in charge at night, and, when the night watch- man, who carries a pistol and some of the keys, went his rounds, overpower him and throw open the cells of the other pvieoners. REMARKABLE BICYCLE RIDE.—The 24 hours' road com- petition promoted by the manufacturers of the "Facile ' safety bicycle, took place on Saturday last. The event has' attracted great interest among bicyclists and others, and the start was made from Anderton's hotel at 12 mid-day on Friday, in the presence of an immense gathering of specta- tors. There were 26 starters and the result of the race was as follows :-Ist prize, value £lO 10s., won by Walter Snook; distance ridden in the 24 hours, 2141 miles. 2nd prize, value £6 Os., won by W. F. Sutton; distance ridden, 198 miles. 3rd prize, value £4 48., won by C. H. Cole; distance ridden, 189 miles. Besides the above, 14 riders are entitled to the gold medal, value £3 35., having accom- plished 150 miles, and two to the silver medal, value £1 is. (123 miles). All the competitors rode "Facile " bicycles, varying in size from 36in. to 44in., and taken altogether the performance of the winner may be considered the most remarkable that has yet been accomplished upon the "silent steed." The whole arrangements for checking the race were in the hands of Mr. G. P. Coleman, official timekeeper to the Bicycle Union. LORD DERBY AND MR. MATTHEW ARNOLD.—It the open- ing meeting of the session 1882-3 of the Liverpool Univer- sity College on Saturday afternoon, Mr. Matthew Arnold delivered an address to the students. Beginning with a half-playful allusion to the familiar phrases "sweetness and light" and "seeing things as they really are," Mr. Arnold said he feared that not in his lifetime would these phrases cease to sum up crying needs for the nation. He then dilated at length on what some people would have catled his "one nostrum for practical application," viz., the provision of public schools for the middle flosses. He eulogized the efforts made in Liverpool to meet the necessities of the case. One product of the teaching of the Liverpool University , College would, be predicted, be "lucidity "—a quality which he contended Britons wanted, just as Frenchmen I wanted morality, and Germans civil courage. Without giv- ing a precise definition of "lucidity," he explained that "negative lucidity " was the perception of want of truth i and validness in notions long current. Lord Derby, who presided, did not dissent from Mr. Arnold's conclusions, but he hinted that what some people might regard as want of "lucidity," others might look upon as a form of intellectual modesty or even disguised scepticism which made people refrain from positive and perhaps new conclusions until they found the conclusions capable of verification.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882. THE BRLT ISLI IN EGYPT.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882. THE BRLT ISLI IN EGYPT.

At Guildhall Police Court, London, George William Bard well, clerk, and Charles Gold, were committed for trial on a charge of stealing foreign bonds, value £12,000, from Desborough and Sons, solicitors. The funeral has taken place at Upleatham, Yorkshire, of John Parken, who, as servant to Admiral Dundas, served during the famous Peninsular campaign, and in that capacity was present at the death of Sir John Moore. Parken was in his 98th year, and up to the moment of his death enjoyed a pension from the Dandas family. A signalman, named John Hunt, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, was found drowned in a pit, near Timperley Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. The deceased left home on Sunday after- noon, and was then apparently in his usual health and spirits. Since her admission to the Southampton Workhouse the Claimant's wife has written to him asking his approval of the step she has taken. The Claimant has replied that inasmuch as he has placed all his affairs in the hands of his friends with the view of obtaining a divorce, he can hold no further communication with her. Intelligence received from Lloyd's on Thursday morning states that the barque Orenoque, 300 tons register, has fcundered in the North Atlantic Ocean, and all her crew,ten in number, have been drowned. The vessel at the tints of her loss was on a voyage from Glasgow to Trinidad with a full cargo of merchandise. Two passenger trains collided at Hutchinson, Kansas, on Sunday night, through a misplaced switch. The engines crashed together, wrecking the forward cars of both trains. The wreck caught fire, and both drivers and both stokers were killed and their corpses burned. Six passengers were killed and several wounded.

A Central News telegram says that two arrests were made on Wednesday night, near Cork, in connection with the murder of . Lord Mountmorres. The prisoners are man and wife named Flanigan. It was to their house that the bady was refused admittance when first discovered. It is be. lieved they wilt turn approvers. On Thursday afternoon a destructive fire broke out at Clough Mills, Shaw, near Oldham, belonging to Messrs. Cheetham and Sons. It was confined to the old portion, containing 20,000 spindles. It is supposed to have origi- nated through friction, and was confined to two spinning rooms. The damage by fire and water is over £2,000, but it is covered by insurance. Henry Bentley, a cabman, in the employ of Wm. Butler, cab proprietor, was, on Thursday morning, at Hanley, charged with embezzling money, the property of his employer. Amongst the items he embezzled were a fare, Br,, paid to him by a borough magistrate, and 4s. by the chief constable, for the use of the cab on police service. He was fined £3 and costs; in default, one month's hard labour. The Bury Town eouncil, at a- meeting on Thursday, resolved to oppose the application of six electric light com- panies who had given notice to apply for provisional orders to light the district, as the Corporation are applying for special powers under the local Act next session. At the same meeting a new rate of twopence in the pound on owners was laid to make up the losses or. the waterworks. Lord O'Hagan, speaking at a prize distribution at Burnley Grammar School, on Thursday, said education was now the main key to wealth and honour in this country, and the monoply of places of public trust by the privileged classes was a thing of the past. Comparing the educational ad- vantages of this country with those of Ireland, he remarked that Until very recently the middle classes of Ireland had only an indifferent education. ATTEMPTED MATRICIDE.—The Press Association North- ampton correspondent reports the attempt by a young men named Thomas Luck to murder his mother. The brother of the delinquent on returning home on Thursday found a sharp-pointed coalpicic partly buried in his mother's neck. Thomas had disappeared, and it was supposed he had com- mitted suicide. The woman lies in a precarious condition. The missing man was of a peculiar temperament, and the theory of temporary insanity is entertained. 'Mille a heavy Caledonian goods train was proceeding, on Thursday, between Perth and Dundee it broke down near Errol. The axle of one of the wagons snapped, and before the train could be stopped 21 trucks had left the metals— tearing up the line' and doing considerable damage. The, contents of several wagons were scattered over the track. The passenger traffic is being worked on a single line. Gangs of workmen have left to clear the block and repair the way. No personal injuries are reported. At the Preaton Police Court, on Thursday morning, John Thompson, a labourer, was charged with violently as- saulting Thomas Leonard on Sunday evening. Late at night prisoner went to the prosecutor's house and broke open the door, and attacked him. Prisoner was removed, but the prosecutor happened to venture out of doors after- wards, when he was again attacked by the prisoner, hurled to the ground, and kicked violently about the head. The Bench committed the prisoner to two months' hard labour. A point of some importance has been decided by the Re- vising Barrister for Middlesex. The Conservatives objected to the validity of the Liberal objections on the ground that they did not bear the date of the day on which they were signed, the date exhibited being the 18th August, whereas the notices bore the postmark of the 17th August. The Barrister held that it was unimportant whether the dating and the signature corresponded so long as they were both within the prescribed time. SERIOUS COACH ACCIDENT. The Press Association's Aberdeen correspondent telegraphs that a four-in-hand coach plying between Ballater and Braemar overturned on Thurs- day forenoon, near Invercauld Bridge, in consequence of a wheel caming off. Fifteen passengers were thrown violently to the ground. The Rev. A. Whyte, Edinburgh, and the Rev. A. Orrock Johnstone, Glasgow, were amongst the seriously injured. The sufferers were inquired for by Her Majesty, who passed the spot afterwards. DETERMINED ATTEMPT AT WIPE MURDER AND SHOCK- ING SUICIDE.—A determined attempt at murder and suicide was made at Portsmouth, on Thursday, by a labourer named Thomas Cull, who pointed a pistol at his wife's head, but in trying to fire it the cap snapped without discharging the bullet. Apparently thinking he had accomplished his purpose, Cull swallowed a packet of phosphorous, and then ran to tee railway, where he lay down before an evening train, and was cut to pieces. His wife was uninjured. THE SEIZURES FOR NON-PAYMENT OF TITHES.—Three auction sales under distraint to recover tithes on hop and fruit ground were held on Thursday at Swanlev, Kent. The first sale was announced to take place at Bower Farm, Eyns- ford, by the authority of the dean and chaplain of Rochester. Here, however, it was found that the landlord, Sir W. Hart- Dyke, had a bailiff in possession. The auctioneer, never- theless, proceeded with the formalities of the sale, but, failing to get a bid, gave notice of a sale by private treaty. The other sales at Heath Wood and New Barn-passed al amid signs of hostility from the attending farmers, who afterwards held an indignation meeting. • A deplorable story was told on Thursday in the course the Board of Trade inquiry in Liverpool as to the loss of the barque Arethusa. It was shown that the master, mate, and several of the crew were under the influence of drink when the vessel sailed from the Mersey, and for two days it was drifting helplessly about the Channel. At last one or two able seamen took the navigation of the vessel on them- selves, but both master and mate continued to indulge in drink, and were unable to give proper directions, in conse- quence of which the Arethusa was wrecked* Off Blackpool. The certificates of the master and mate were cancelled, the Court atating that it was as gross a case as ever formed the subject of enquiry. At a meeting of the London Common Council, on Thurs- day, Mr. Stevenson moved that the freedom of tile city be presented to Admiral Sir Beauchamp Seymour in a gold casket, together with a sword, and that an address be also presented to Sir Garnet Wolseley, he having already received a sword from the city, and that the thanks of the court be presented not only to the officers, but also to the rank and file of the army in Egypt. Alderman Dakin seconded the motion, declaring that he was gratified to find that the rank and file were recognised in the proposition before the court. It was then proposed that the presentation should take place in the Guildhall, and that the expense should not exceed £5OO. A proposal to increase the amount to £2,000 fell through. THE INCOME OE THE WESLEYAN METHODIST MISSIONARY SOCIETY.—The Rev. J. Kilner has issued from the Wesleyan Mission Home an appeal for an increase of income. The statement shows that the total deficiency on December 31st, 1881, was £33,308 Os. 6d. This was met by (1) grants from the Thanksgiving Fund: Amount paid up co date, £5,037 Bs. ' • amount to be paid, £5,037 85.—X10,074 16s. (2) Special donations for debt : amount paid up to date, £13,271 18s.•, amount promised, yet to be received,£B,937 Bs. 6d.—£17,209 6s. 61. (3) Balance met by a transfer from lapsed annuities' account, £6,023 18s.; total, £33,308 Os. Cd. It is stated that the present rate of expenditure. even after all the retrenchments contemplated halse been made, is about £5,000 in excess of last year's income. It is therefore plain that unless the income for 1882 be increased by this amount the Committee will have to show a new debt to thyxtent of that disparity. The Committee think that an increase of 5 per cent. on last year's income might be easily raised. EXTRAORDINARY CASE.—At Marylebone, on Thursday, Alexander Mitchell, butcher, Brixton, George Jos. Mitchell, butcher, Snow-hill, and Rebecca Mitchell, were charged with being concerned together in assalting John Davy, of Earl's Court-square, South Kensington, and Laura Davy, his wife, at the Edgware-road Station of the Metropolitan Railway. Mr. Griffiths, for the prosecution, stated that prosecutor's wife, who was deaf and dumb, was left a considerable sum by her father, and by the will £l,OOO was to pass to her husband on marriage. Her mother was averse to the mar- riage, and seemed to have conceived the idea of possessing herself of the girl's money. She invited the young people to her house at Gunnersburv, on. the 15th August. Mrs. Davy went on first, and when prosecutor reached the house his wife had disappeared, and he could not find her where- abouts for a month. It would be shown that the unfortunate lady was taken to Joseph Mitchell's house, where she was shamefully treated. Prosecutor got his wife from the house by a ruse, and the Mitchells followed them and assaulted them at Edgware-road Station. The case proceeded until late in the evening, when the prisoners were all remanded. Bernard Garrity, was charged at ',the St. Helens Police Court, on F riday, with having stolen two dresses the property of Mr. Lanagban, landlord of a beerhouse in Watery-lane, Sutton, on the 28th ult. It appeared from the evidence that the defendant had gone to the complainant's house begging, and after having received some alms, he stayed a short time, and then went away. On the same day Mrs. Lanaghan missed the stolen articles, and informa- tion was given to the police. P.C. Carter spoke of finding the defendant in the Bridge Inn trying to sell the stolen articles for 6d. and a glass of beer. He asked prisoner what he was doing with the dresses, and he replied that he bad brought them from home. He was, however, appre- hended, and taken to the police office.—Prisoner made no defence, and was committed to the sessions for trial.

REVIEW OF THE TROOPS. The great military demonstration at Cairo took place on Saturday with perfect success. A correspondent gives the following description of the review :—On taaturday, 17,000 troops—the flower of the British army—for an hour and a half filed past the Khedive. Viewing the long lines of magnificent troops, the Egyptian Nationalists might well find consolation for their defeat. The square presented a brilliant appearance. Upon one side was a long wooden pavilion gaily decorated. In the centre was the dais of the Khedive. The Sultan's flag flew overhead. The Royal Standard of England was on the right; the Egyptian flag on the left. The pavilion was filled with Europeans and Egyptian officials, very few unofficial natives having a place there. Opposite with a space between for the march of the troops, was die General's staff, with a body-guard of Marines, in bright red coats and white trousers. General Wolseley took up his place in front of the,Khedive's raised dais. At four o'clock the march-past began. At the head of the cavalry division rode General Drury-Lowe, with his staff, whose handling of his troops daring -the war places him on the roll of distinguished cavalry leaders. Borrowdale's Battery of Horse Artillery had the place of honour. After the Horse Artillery came the stately Household Cavalry, with drawn swords. Scarcely inferior in size of men or horses were the 4th and 7th Dragoon Guards. Following these came the 19th Hussars, perhaps the most smartly turned out body of cavalry upon the ground. Following the Hussars came the Mounted Infantry, rifles at rest. The Indian cavalry next filed past—a splendid and picturesque body—the curved swords of the 2nd and 6th Bengal Cavalry flashing in the sun, and the pennons of the 13th Lancers making a gay show. After the cavalry, 30 guns of the Horse Artillery— no finer could be seen in the world—rumbled through the square, their quiet business-like look being all the more effective after the gay show of the Indian horsemen. The bands, which had hitherto been playing a lively trot, now changed the tune, and a march heralded the approach of the Blue-jacket contingent—that from Ismailia under Cap- tain Fitzroy, that from Alexandria, chiefly the men who had done good service in the armour-clad train, under Commander Henderson. Then came the Garrison ad Marine Artillery, under Colonel Towson. The appearance of the Duke of Connaught with his Steil now indicated the approach of the Brigade of Guards. With ranks closely locked they passed in solid columns to the "British Grenadiers" March. The leading company of the Scots Fusiliers attracted special admiration, the men averaging six feet two inches in height—certainly the highest average in the British army—and the whole brigade is a remarkably fine- one. After the Guards, the steady stream of British infantry flowed past in unbroken order, the regiments deploying into column as they entered the square, forming column of front at the double as they emerged from the narrow streets with perfect and unvarying discipline. After the Guards came the 18th Royal Irish, the 50th West Kent, 84th York and Lancaster, and the 87th Irish Fusiliers—four strong regiments—the first two dressed in the new gray fighting uniform, only issued when the campaign was over. The battalion of Royal Marines fol- lowed, in new red tunics and brilliantly white helmets, quite eclipsing in appearance all which had passed before, and presented a splendid spectacle. The Marines have throughout the war fully maintained the high reputation which the corps has always borne. They completed the line of the First Division. General Willis, whose wound has quite healed now, left the side of the Commander-in-Chief and followed his divisien, and General Hamley and his staff approached. The drums and bagpipes now heralded the coming of General Allison's Highland Brigade. The Black Watch went past to the tune of "The Highland Laddie," and the Cameronians to "The Pibroch of Donald Dhu." The Gordon Highlanders and the 74th; equal in physique and appearance to the leading regi- ments, completed the brigade. Then came the Third Brigade from Alexandria, led by General Sir E. Wood, .upon whose breast glittered three lines of medals. The 60th Rifles, a divisional regiment, completed the march past of the Second Division. The Indian Contingent, under Generals Mac- pherson and Tanner, finished the display. The 72nd, the Seaforth Highlanders, headed the division' nearly every man wearing the Afghan medal and Candahar Cross. The 20th Punjaubees, almost entirely Sikhs and Afghans, and the 2nd Belooches well represented the Imperial Indian Army. But little sign of feeling was manifested by the crowds in the streets, who watched the display in gloomy silence. REVIEW OF THE INDIAN CONTINGENT. The review of the Indian contingent is thus described by a correspondent of the Daily News :—"The Duke of Con- naught inspected the Indian contingent this (Monday) morning at Abbassieh. His Royal Highness arrived at 10 minutes past seven, attended by Colonel Lane and his staff, Baron Hageman also accompanying him. The Indian regiments of cavalry on the right, the infantry in the centre, and the artillery on left, were drawn up in line on the large open space betweeen the Abbassieh Barracks and the Mokat- tam Hills. General Macpherson rode up with kis staff five minutes after the Duke's arrival. After the band had played the National Anthem the inspection began. Several officers, with the Duke, passed down tne front of the cavalry which was arranged from left to right, as follows :-13th Lancers, Colonel Macnaghten ; 6th Bengal Cavalry, Colonel Upper- ton; 2nd Bengal Cavalry, Colonel Campbell. The infantry came in this order :—The Belooches, Colonel Galloway; the Punjaub Infantry, Colonel Roberts; the 7th Bengal, Colonel Wolseley; and the 72nd Highlanders, Colonel Stockwell. At twenty minutes to eight the march past began, the 2nd Bengal Cavalry leading the way. The first movement con- sisted in bringing round the three regiments by the south and west and drawing them up in front of the barracks. This effected the march past the saluting flag, at which the Duke was stationed, began. General Macpherson was at the head of the troops. After General Macpherson came General Wilkinson, com- manding the cavalry. The three regiments seemed the beau ideal of light cavalry, and rode past with admirable steadi- ness, each regiment in columns of squadrons. The infantry were in double companies. H 1 Royal Artillery followed, after which came the mule battery under Major Free. The corps was the pictare of smartness and neatness. In the rear of the battery came the Madras suppers and miners, one of the most efficient corps in the Indian service. The in- fantry division then passed, General Tanner at the head. The Highlanders marched past as splendidly as on the re- view day. The 7th Bengal Infantry was in full strength. The effect was rather spoiled by the men being dressed in kakn uniform, the parade uniforms havaig been left at Suez. In this respect the Belooches in their Zouave dress have the advantage over them. The review was a complete suc- cess. After the review the Duke expressed a desire to see the mountain battery at drill. His Royal Highness was greatly pleased with the celerity of the operations. Within forty seconds after the word of command each gun, carried in pieces on six mules, was put together and got ready for action. In somewhat less than thirty seconds the guns were again limbered." A NATIVE ACCOUNT OF THE BATTLE OF TEL-EL-KEBIR. A native officer present at the battle of Tel-el-Kebir makes the following statement :—" On the 12th we were informed that a general attack would be made that night. We were all under arms and at our posts shortly after sun- set. During the night scouts were sent out with orders to fire in the air as a signal if any body of troops was approach- ng. They three times reported all quiet. We had given up all expectation of attack; we were tired. and the officers were beginning to lie down, when three scouts were sent out as a last reconnaissance. We had expected that the attack would begin at about 2,000 yards. Our guns were sighted for this range. Arabi exhorted his officers to wait ten minutes for the result of this last reconnaissance; but hardly had they left the camp when they fired the signal. Instead of 2,000 yards, they must have been 200 off. We fired, but most of our shots must have gone over their heads. Almost at the same moment, it seemed so quick, they were scram- bling over us, first over our right, and then rolling over all down the line like a wave. We never expected war like this. Our soldiers stood fire at a distance very well. On the sth of August many were killed, and they were not afraid of shells -,but these men came close up to us, and the only way to save life was to run away. The native soldier has never exercised this close way of fighting. No soldiers but the English could fight like that. THE REORGANISATION OF THE ARMY. Baker Pasha was on Monday officially presented to the Khedive by Sir E. Malet. The task which Baker Pasha has undertaken is one of the most arduous and certainly the most urgent, of those connected with the general reorgani- sation of the country, and it is satisfactory to know that it is committed to such able and energetic bands. A special correspondent in Cairo telegraphs that Baker Pasha is strongly in favour of recruit- ing the gendarmerie in Egypt from the Albanians, who, he says, would gladly enter the service if no political obstacles were put in the way. He describes them as brave, loyal, and amenable:to strict discipline. Baker Pasha is also strongly of opinion that the army reorganisation question should be taken up without delay. He thinks that municipal govern- ments should be established in all the important towns, and that the European inhabitants, who at present contribute nothing, should pay their share of the local taxes. THE POLITICAL SITUATION. With regard to the political situation, a Vienna despatch in the Times says the negotiations have not within the last few days advanced even by a single step. "The Cabinet of St. James's has not yet shown any disposition to make com- munications of any kind whatever to the Powers relative to its plans, and the Powers have wisely abstained from asking any questions of the English Government concerning its intentions. In short, matters are, diplomatically considered, still in exactly the same position as they were on the day of the battle of Tel-el-Kebir." THE PROCESSION OF THE "CARPET." The procession of the "Holy Carpet" took place on Thursday, with all the usual gorgeous surroundings. The Khedive drove early from the palace to the Kiosk in state, being received on arrival by a brilliant assemblage of pachas, and also by Sir G. Wolseley, the Duke of Connaught, and other leading British officers. Our troops presented arms as the Viceroy drove up. A camel bearing the carpet was led threetimes around the place, and then a grand proces- sion was formed to the railway station, the Khedive, Sir Garnet, and the Duke of Connaught following. MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. Among the prisoners who have been removed from Cairo to Alexandria for trial is Arabi's European adviser, the Swiss Ninet. A telegram fume Sir Garnet Wolseley, received at the War Office, gives a list of the casualties which occurred at the recent explosion and fire at the railway station in Cairo.

The formal trial of Arabi and Ton Pa.shas does not seem to have ben begun yet. Lord Granville has tele• graphed permission to Mr. Broadley, who is to appear for the defence of Arabi, to go at once to the scene of the trial. The Brood Arrow states that in addition to the patent of nobility General Wolseley and Admiral Seymour will each be granted a sum of £50,000, which will represent an annuity of £2,000 per annum. It is announced in the Timestliat it has been resolved to keep a force of 12,000 men in Egypt for the present, "in 'order to carry on and consolidate the work for which the suppression of Arabi does little more than clear the way." On Saturday the Khedive conferred upon Admiral Sey- mour the Grand Cordon of the Order of the Osmanieh. People are returning to Alexandria in such numbers that rents have been greatly increased. Only 175 artillerymen remain at Ramleh for its defence. Already two batteries of Artillery have left Cairo for Alexandria, on their way to Europe, and it is expected that by the end of the month the British force, excepting the troops required for the occupation, will have left Egypt. • Arrangements for the return of the troops who will not form part of the army of occupation are being rapidly matured. Sir John Adye returns at once, in order to give the Government the benefit of his advice on the question of the occupation, but Sir Garnet Wolseley will not embxik until about three weeks hence. _ _ _ _ _ _

With reference to the disaster at Cairo, it is stated that the damage done by fire to the railway station and rolling stock is not less than £25.000. The total extent of loss caused by the conflagration and explosions will amount to several hundred thousand pounds, At last the Turkish labourers returning from British ser- vice in Egypt have been set at liberty. They were obliged to give security for their good behaviour, but this is said to be a mere formality. The liberation of the men, it seems, was only granted after the receipt of a very energetic Note from Lord Dufferin.

Several wounded officers and 167 sick and wounded soldiers returned in the troopship Orontes, which arrived at Portsmouth on Monday. Only one death had taken place on the voyage, and, with fear exceptions, the wounded men are doing well. The most not Able fact in connection with the Egyptian question is the universally-pronounced opinion of the Berlin newspapers that on the whole problem an understanding has been arrived at between the two great Saxm Powers, Germany and England, without, however, necessarily im- plying any hostile action towards France. A Correspondent at Alexandria telegraphs that in spite of cooler weather the health of the army in Egypt is far from satisfactory. Since Alexandria has again been the base of operations nearly 800 sick have passed through, and 200 more are expected. Every care is taken by the authorities to make the sick comfortable on board ship, but the dis- couraging part is the number who are being invalided. It has been determined to give a war m!dal to all who took a military part in the recent Egyptian campaigns, and pains have been taken to secure its distribution immediately on P4e return of the first troops from the war. The design on the reversa will be a Sphinx, with the word "Egypt," and the date 1882. On the other side will be the Queen's head, the same as that OA the Ashantee medal. The colour of the riband and number of clasps to accompany the medal have not yet been decided upon.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS. The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Town Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. Dr. Steele (the chairman) presided, and there were also present :—Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Norman, J. Dobson, W. Fisher, G. S. Hazlehurst, Lake, Lightburn Robert Shaw, Briscoe, P. Speakman J. J. Speakman, Meahowcroft, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), Dr. Mouritz (medical officer), W. Brookes (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

_ TYE HEALTH or THE TOWN. Dr. Mouurrz, the medical officer, presented his monthly report, which stated that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 41, represent- ug a death-rate of 32 per 1,000 per annum. Of the above deaths 11 were due to pulmonary diseases, nine were due to diarrhosa, four to measles, three to cardiac diseases, three to abdominal diseases, two to cancer, two to dropsy, two to phthisis, two to debility. Scarlatina, disease of brain, and premature birth accounted for one each. Of the above deaths 21 were children of four years and under, and of these 15 were below one year. One inquest was held. Total deaths 42. The past month had certainly been a sickly and fatal one. In the corresponding month last year there were 11 deaths and two inquests.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that the medical officer had told him that the health of the town was somewhat better—Dr. Mouurrz said in addition to watering the streets with carbolic acid, Mr. Barker commenced that morning to wash the hack entries in the different streets in Newtown, Dukesfield, and else- where, to see if they could not stamp out the disease now ' existing.

div.head: -RECENT ACTION AGAINST THE GLYCERINE WORKS,
div.p: THE -RECENT ACTION AGAINST THE GLYCERINE WORKS,

The CHAIRMAN referred to the action against M. Clolus, and said he understood there was an impression in the town that the minute in reference to the establishment of the works had been tampered with in the minute book. He thought the public should be assured this was not the case. Of course, Mr. Fletcher did not mean to insinuate anything against the Commissioners, but a false impression had been given. The reporters would perhaps put the matter right. —Dr. MCDOUGALL said it had I.lQen stated that the resolu- tion passed :..at the Board was not an exact copy of that printed in the newspapers. The resolution in the minute book seemed to be qualified, whilst the resolution published seemed to have been unqualified. This involved an impor- tant point, and he moved that a committee, consisting of Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst, Mr. Lake, the Chairman, and himself, should be appointed to inquire into the matter. It would be the duty of the Board to do so, as the allegation was a very serious one, and affected the existence and honour of the Board. It was therefore very desirable that the point should be cleared up.—Mr. LIGIITBURN inquired if there was sufficient data upon which a committee could sit.—The CLERK: Oh, yes, quite sufficient.—The CHAIRMAN said his impression certainly was that the resolution stated that per- mission in the meantime be given. The works were already at work, and he thought it was the opinion of the Board it would be unfair to say to M. Clolus "You must stop." He was quite astonished that the papers had reported that permission had been given. However, in future he would not accept any motion unless he had it given him in writing.:He hardly saw the necessity of appointing the committee proposed.— The CLERK said the question was: " Has the mistake been made by the Board or the reporters?"—Mr. NORMAN thought the point ought to be closed up, and seconded Dr. McDou- gall's proposition.—The LAW CLERK said The Examiner re- port was only an epitome. It was only about ten lines in length.—The consideration of the matter was then deferred .until the conclusion of the other business —At that time Mr. P. SPEAKMAN said he was of opinion that nothing would come from a reconsideration of the question but bad feeling. —Dr. McDouGALL hoped there would be no opposition to his proposition. It was for the honour of the Board that the committee should sit, for either the minutes were " cooked " or they were no'.- —Dr. McDougall then gave a written reso- lution, xvhich stated the committee were to inquire whether the resolution passed at a meeting held on the 3rd January, with reference to the applica- tion of M. Victor Clolus was a correct record of the proceedings of the Board.—The resolution was passed. HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE: THE FOUNTAIN WATER.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee stated Mr. Norman had been appointed chairman of the committee. It was resolved that the surveyor write to the brine works contractor with reference to the damage to the road on the common by the heavy carting to and from the reservoir, and requiring them to put the road in repair. Instructions were given to the surveyor to examine and report on the best and most feasible means of ascertaining the source of the pollution of the Sprinch !eater and of remedying the same, and on the cost of sink- ing shafts on both sides of the glycerine works. It was recommended that a slab boarding be erected at the bottom of the garden at Waterloo-road. At a meeting held on the 28th Feptember it was recommended that instructions be given to the surveyor to sink a shaft near to the site of the I old lime kilns, with a 'view to ascertaining the source of the pollution of the Sprinch water, on obtaining permission of the Bridgewater trustees. The communications from the Library Committee, which have been previously published, were considered, and it was recommended that a reply be sent stating that the Board would allow them the use of the Board-room on Thursday evenings as requested, and that they had no power to rent the building to the committee. It was resolved that Mr. Joseph Jackson and his wife be allowed to live in Waterloo House as caretakers, rent free. A sub-committee was appointed consisting of Messrs. Nor- man, McDougall, Fisher, Lake, J. J. Speakman, Briscoe, Shaw, and P. Speakman, to consider the advisability of rearranging the duties and salaries of the officials of the Board, and of appointing a successor to the late inspector of nuisances. Plan of a house in Greenway-road, for Mr. Jas. Ditchfield ; of six cottages in Collier-street, for Mr. H. White; alterations and additions to cottage in the Runcorn cemetery; alterations to property in Fryer-street and Alcock- street, for Mr. W. Hankinson ; were approved.—Mr. NORMAN moved, and Mr. BRISCOIt seconded, the confirmation of the minutes—Mr. P. SPEARMA.N objected to any further expen- diture being incurred with regard to the Sprinch water. The Board had nothing to gain by doing so, because there seemed to be an understanding that they would agree with the Water Company to have a water tap fixed in the fountain so that anybody could drink of pure water. He proposed that that portion of the minute referring to the sinking of a shaft near the old lime kiln be struck out.—Mr. LaGian9unien could not see any practical result to be derived from sinking the shaft, and therefore he seconded the resolution.— Dr. McDouciALL pointed out that it was the wish i of the ratepayers that the water should be purified, and said f the Board did not make an effort to fulfil their wishes, it was incompetent to do its duty.—Mr. SHAW: I beg to differ front the doctor.—Dr. MeDonotaa. ; It is not the first time, Mr. Shaw. (Laughter).—Mr. SHAW: No. He com- mented upon the way in which the committee passed reso- lutions without making an investigation into the matter at issue, as in this case, and said he should vote for the amend- ment.—Dr. McDouoiLL asked if the magistrates had power to compel the local authority to remove the impurity which was in the water.—The CLEuIC. said the magistrates would no doubt have power to compel whoever was responsible.— Er. MRADOWCROFT thought the petition from the ratepayers ought not to be dismissed without the Board taking ordinary means to ascertain what was the cause of the pollution.— Mr. LIGHTSURN asked if the water was polluted before the establishment of the Glycerine Works.—No reply was vouchsafed.—The CIiiIIIMOT remarked that the proposed

Ishaft could not be sunk under a cost of 10 or £2O, and he did not think they were justi- fied in incurring any more expense.—Mr. 'NORMAN , remarked that Mr. Shaw was always either ' the sanitary or some other committee, but if he would at- tend the committee meetings, and give his advica there, it would be much better than taking up the titne of the Board. —The amendment was then put and lost.—Mr. P. SPEAK- MAN said that at the committee meeting he protested agahast the resolution to proceed against M. Victor Clolus, but his protest was not recorded.—The CH AMMAN said it was not usual, but in future the names of members who voted for and against resolutions would be taken. (Hear, hear.)— The minutes were then passed. I

ELECTRIC LIGHTING. The CLERK said the Gulcher Electric Lighting Company, and the Brush Electric Light Company, bad given notice of their intention to apply to.the Board of Trade for a provisional order to supply the electric light for public and private purboses under the provisions of the Electric Lighting Act. It seemed to be the general opinion that it would be premature to give permission at the present time, and the notices were laid on the table.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY QUESTION: A GENEROUS OFFER.
div.p: THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION: A GENEROUS OFFER.

The following letter was read : Runcorn. October 3rl, 1812.—T0 the Chairman of the Run- corn Improvement Comtnissioners.—Dear Sir,—l desire to lay before you the following al‘ernative propositions. First, to take the Commissioners' rooms on my own responsibility at an annual rent of £2O, in order that, a reiding room may bo. open daily. I will also give a guarantee to the Library Comtnitteo that for the space of three years no financial difficulty shall arise therefrom. Second, to take the Commissioners' rooms on lease for three years at an annual rent of £2O. This offer is not made from a foolish desire to get my own way on a C Infested question; whether I get that or not is a matter of no moment to anybody; but the public position of the Free Library is of great importance, and I have only one motive in laying the proposals before you. Permit me to ask the favour of a decision at this meeting instead of referring the matter again to a com- mittee —Believe me, dear sir, faithfully yours, GEORGE S. HAZLEEIIIRST.—If the Comm'ssioners do not think £2O per annum sufficient, I am willing to increase the amount. The communisation was referred to the Highway Com- mittee. COMMITTEES.

The Canal Boats Committee, at their meeting on the 27th ult., appointed Mr. Fisher chairman. They recommended that notice be sent to the Ellesmere Trustees to terminate the tenancy of the Hospital premises at the Ferry Pier on the let February, 1883. The General Purposes Committee appointed Mr. Briscoe chairman; while the Finance Corn- tnittee conferred that honour upon Mr. J. J. Speakman.— The receipts for Septeniber were £279 6s 61, and accounts amounting to £245 us 103 were recommended for pay- ment. • This was all the business.

TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SITOW AT RUNCORN. The annual show of the Tarporley Agricultural Society was held in Mr. Peacock's field, Greenway-road, Runcorn, on Thursday. The society was established in 1863, and it is the first time during its history that the show has been brought to Runcorn. Formerly it has confined its operations within a very narrow area round Tarporley, but perceiving the benefits which the society would re- ceive, and the benefits which would be imparted to the districts visited, the committee decided, for this year at any rate, to widen their borders. Mr. Steward (a former secretary), Mr. Cooke, and Mr. Lockwood were therefore deputated to wait upon the Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, Runcorn being the place selected as favourable, to ascertain how far the inhabitants of the town would be disposed to aid them. Several meetings between the Board and the deputation were held, and eventually it was decided to hold the show in Runcorn. A local com- mittee, with Dr. Steele as chairman, and Mr. O'Leak as secretary, was appointed to make the requisite arrange- ments and collect their subscriptions. The committee succeeded in raising about £lOO. The president of the society is Mr. Charles Wigg, of Halton Lodge, Runcorn, and the patrons are the following :—The Earl of Hadding- ton Ardvine Hall; Lord Tollemache, of Helmingham, Peckforton Castle; Sir Philip Da B. G. Egerton, Bart., Otilton Park; and George Wilbraham, Esq., Delamere House. Mr. A. C. Lockwood, of Cheshire, is the secre- tary, and his indefatigable exertions in promoting the success of the arrangements are worthy of recognition. Considering that only six weeks have intervened between the holding of the show and the settlement of the place at which it was to be held, the show may fairly be considered a good one. The entries were not so numerous as last year, but no two opinions were held as to the improvement ob- servable in the quality of the exhibits. In cheese there were 11 entries, butter 17, cattle 40, pigs 15, sheep is, horses 76, poultry 105, vegetables 24, dogs 108, implements 8. In a district in Cheshire so noted for its cheese as Tar- porley, one would have expected the entries for that class of exhibits to have been more numerous. What, however, was lacking in quantity was compensated for by the ex- cellency of the specimens of cheese-making exhibited, and the same remark applies to the butter. The vegetables were a very good show. The carrots and potatoes were excellent. Some really fine animals were shown in the cattle classes. Two bulls, with extremely massive forms, attracted much attention. Mr. S. B. Chadwick exhibited a dairy cow, which succeeded in carrying off the first prize. Sheep and pigs were a good class. The poultry was scarcely above the average; the ducks, however, being very fine birds. With his Rouen ducks, which have obtained quite a reputation, Mr. Thomes Wakefield, of Golborne, took the first and se- cond prizes. Dogs were fairly represented, Mr. W. M. Pothecary, of Lymm, exhibited his St. Bernard dog "Pilgrim," which he valued at £5OO, and he was awarded the first prize. It was certainly a noble animal, possessed a head worthy to be transferred to canvas, and was viewed with general admiration. Horses were divided into about 15 different classes, in which of course animals suitable for agricultural purposes preponderated. The animfls were perhaps not a very showy, but certainly a very useful lot. The horses in the jumping class were the finest ever seen in the district. Their symetrical form, and high action, attracted much attention. There was also a good show of turn-outs. Among the implements we may notice the col- lection of Messrs. Richard Lea and Son, of High-street, Runcorn. The display was a very interesting one. A steam engine and a collection of steam pnmps were at work, and there was exhibited a number of hydraulic engines for organ blowing, &c. With the prevailing uncertainty as to the future of gas for lighting purposes, a patent gas engine in operation, and several gas stoves, could not fail to attract much attention, as a probable solution of the question. They certainly appeared very useful and highly desirable articles. Mr. Richard Spann, of Warrington, exhibited some of his handicraft as a wheelwright in the shape of lorries, &c.; and Mr. H. Cesar, of Knutsford, had on the ground several picturesque rustic summer houses. Fortunately the show during the day was favoured withl charming weather. The discomfort of a rather cold wind was minimised by the genial rays of the sun, and the attractions of an agricultural show to the ordinary quiet in- habitants of Runcorn proved irresistable under such cir- cumstances. The attendance on the ground in the morning was large, but in the afternoon the people, we think, might have been counted by thousands. The ring where the parade of prize cattle and horses, the exhibition of turnouts, and the jumping over hurdles and water, were to take place, was surrounded by an eager and expec- tant crowd. The sight was well worth witnessing, the jumping being a splendid performance. One of the riders was thrown off his horse as it leaped over the hurdle, but he happily alighted on horse, back, and sustained no injury, for be immediately remounted the animal, and successfully cleared the obstruction. The judges of the various classes were :—Cheese: Mr. Barrett, Manchester. Butter: Mr. Wilkinson, Liverpool. Horned stock : Mr. Roberts, Saltney ; Mr. Wm. Williams, Chester. Sheep: Mr. John Cheers, Barrow, near Chester ; Colonel Talbot. Pigs: Mr. Gamon, Chester. Heavy horses: Mr. J. P. Edwards, Chester; Mr. James Lloyd, Trafford. At half-past one a public luncheon was provided in a large tent on the ground. The repast was served in Mr. A. C. Doe's usual good style. Mr. Charles Wigg, the presi- dent, occupied the chair, and he was supported by Dr. 'Steele, chairman of Commissioners; Rev. S. Hague vicar of Kingsley; Rev. Mr. Brooke, Shra.wardine Rectory, ; Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., Mess-s W. Fisher, Henry Rey- nolds, J.P., John Ashton, Henry Lin deer, of Frodslam ; W. H. Linaker, W. Whitlow, U. Cook, L. Boutb, J. J. Steward, J. Stokes, and 0. Leak. The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a short address, remarked that it was somewhat extraordinary that an alkali manufac- turer should be called upon to preside over an agricultural meeting. He thought it was a proof of that good feeling which ought to exist among all classes of the community. In carrying out their daily avocations chemical manufac- turers did a certain amount of damage to vegetation in the neighbourhool in which their works were placed. But he thought they were not an unmitigated evil. They brought almost to the doors of the farmers a large population ready to consume their produce, thus saving them the expense and trouble of sending it to a distant market, where, he had no doubt, they would not realise so much profit. The other day at an agricultural meeting Lord Wilton said the farmers for the last few years had worn out their waistcoat pockets in looking for the money which was not there. He (the chair- man) bad no doubt that was the case. Farmers had suffered from a series of bad harvests; but with the present good harvest, and others to follow he hoped that farmers would wear out their pockets with the money which they had realised by their produce. (Applause.) He had not th. gloomy opinion of farming which many people had. He drew a parallel between manufacturing and farming, and said if farmers were to succeed in their'basiness they must adopt the scientific improvements of the age. Two yea: g ago at the Farnworth Show Mr. F. H. Gossage read a paper in which he showed tbc value of alkali waste as a manure, and since that time many farmers had tried it, but it had not met with that mErit which it deserved, considering that it could be obtained free. After exposure to the air it lost its dileterions properties, and became a fertilizer, being rich . in those elements which were required for the soil. He should be glad to supply any further information to any gentleman who wished to ask for it. As far as agriculture was at present cencerned they could not expect England to be a corn growing country, and it was his opinion that farmers would have to pay more attention to dairy farming and the rearing of cattle. In the production of milk and butter the English' farmer need fear no foreign competitor, and as fresh meat would always sell esell in competition with imported meat, there was also nothing to fear in That direction. There was still a profitable business to be made in farming. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN then proposed the usual loyal toasts, which were honoured. He then proposed 'The bishop and clergy of the diocese, and ministers of all denominations ; and the Rev. Mr. BnooK responded. In proposing " SUCCeSS to Tarporley Agricultural Society," the CHAIRMAN said he had no doubt the society had done a great deal of good in the districts which it had visited by inciting a spirit of emulation amongst the farmers. -Mr. GEO. COOKE, who responded, said the shows of the society were not excelled by the county society's. The committee were pleased that the show was being held in Runcorn that day, and he had no doubt from what he could gather but that the show would be a success. The CHAIRMAN gave " The judges," which was responded to by Mr.. GREEN and Mr. GrAMON. Mr. STEWARD preposed the health of the president, who, be remarked, had liberally subscribed to the society, and had done everything he possibly could to make the show a success. The toast was drunk with musical honours, the audience singing "For he is a jolly good fellow."- Mr. STEWARD then coupled with the toast the name of Dr. Steele, of whom he spoke in eulogistic terms. . The CHAIRMAN remarked, in reply, that the compliment paid to him was undeserved. Dr. Steele was much more deserving than he was, having paid much attention to the arrangements for the show, and he was glad that his (Dr. Steele's) name was coupled with the toast. Dr. STEELE said when he heard the society was desirous of visiting Runcorn, he was willing to help it forward all he could. He had great pleasure in proposing the health of the secretary. Considering that it was only six weeks since it was decided to hold the show, Mr. Lockwood must have had a hard task in completing the arrangements for a suc- cessful show. Mr. Lockwood and Mr. O'Leak were called upon to respond, and the proceedings concluded.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882.

- Stafford Northcote, the leader of Her Majesty's rkei, tr4,l "on in the House of Commons, has this week kgria: a descent upon Scotland in the hope, we pre- tllei„' of awakening the people to a knowledge of PoliticAl darkness. We confess we sympathise With Sir Stafford in the task he has under- wo have very seriot. 4 misgivings as to the of his efforts. There ..ierns to be no lack of N41,461481'1 at every turn which the Baronet takes, eika 'e have grave doubts as to whether that enthu- Z 4 4rises from sympathy with the cause which Sir °td advocates, or whether it is due rather to kti(lll°.veltY of a Tory being found across the Tweed. tht certainly Tories are very rare iu Scotland. Of ket:tb°Y ra:-.lnbers which Scotland sends to Parlia- the -h,"here ape only about half-a-dozen Tories, and hv which these are returned are in e.LPvt'r" - f , Melina. With only one exception, too, these

members represent county constituencies, where, of coarse, the voting power is possessed only by the few; but once the franchise has been extended to the counties, we doubt not that Scotland will be repre- sented exclusively by Liberals, as Ireland promises ere long to be by Home Rulers. Under such cireum • stances it is not likely that the impression, if any, Sir Stafford may make upon the " eannie Scot" will be a lasting one; and for all the good he is likely to do his party in Scotland, the worthy Baronet may as well be at the Pynes enjoying the quietude of his own home. Throughout the length and breadth of the "land o' cakes" a Tory is generally looked upon with the very greatest suspicion,. no matter in what guise he presents himself, and though the Scotch- mantis ear may be for a moment tickled by Sir Staf- ford's plausibilities, the Scotchman's understanding • will remain invulnerable. Sir Stafford is necessarily discursive in his observations, and on Wednesday he travelled over a very wide field. In the afternoon he attended a meeting of the Scottish National Union of Conservative Associations, an association which is only in its embryo stage, and if we may venture to take a leaf out of Sir Stafford's book and to prophesy, it would be that as this is the first of the meetings of that Association so it is likely to be the last. However, no more fitting gathering could be found for Sir Stafford to hold forth upon the bene- fits to be derived from organisation, and also to re- count the disasters of the last election. Singular enough it is now two-years-and-a-half since Sir Stafford and his colleagues were dismissed from power, yet they are still on the look-out for an explanation of their defeat. Sir Stafford attributes it to three causes, via., the great Midlothian speeches of Mr. Gladstone, the action of what is known as the Birmingh am caucus, and also the energy of the late Sir William Adam, the whip of the Liberal party. We admit that the activity of the late whip contributed in a very great degree to the success of the Liberals at the last election; we cheerfully grant that the mueh derided Birmingham caucus—which, by the way, Sir Stafford seems now anxious to approve rather than condemn— also materially aided the Liberal victory; and it would be idle to dispute that Mr. Gladstone's Mid- lothian speeches went a very great way towards creat- ing a healthy Liberal sentiment; but Sir Stafford should not forget that what more than anything else led to the return of a Liberal Government to power was the absolute incapacity of a Conservative Government—even with a mechanical majority at its back—to govern the affairs of the nation satis- factorily. The three important factors which Sir Stafford mentions as contributing to the Liberal success would, collectively and individually, have been of no avail, but for the important fact that a Tory Administration had been weighed in the balance and found wanting in everything which could tend to good government. In the evening Sir Stafford Northcote attended a great meeting in St. Andrew's Hall, and delivered anpther address, chiefly ,on the Egyptian question, though Irish matters also re- ceived a fair amount of attention. It is some satisfaction to hear Sir Stafford admits that the Government, by its brilliant conclusion of the Egyptian campaign, has materially improved its position in the country, though we deny its position has ever been on the wane, or that the Government has in tally degree lost the coufidence of the people ; but it is rather ungenerous, after mak, jag thie frank Omissi on, for Sir Stefford straight- Viely to proceed to predict that in the final settle- r ment of this difficulty there is trouble in store. It leads one to suspect that he, at least, instead of loyally supporting the Government and assisting it, as he ought to do, is more likely to throw obstacles in its path. Sir Stafford complains that the Government did not show sufficient determina- tion at the outset of the Egyptian question, and that if it had war would have been averted. But he conveniently forgets hove :or Weeks and months we were hampered bri Prance, and that not until she parted coilapany with us could we act with promptitude. And who is responsible for our alliance with France in this matte i ? Is it not Sir Stafford and his colleagues? They established the Joint Control, which has been at the very root of our troubles in Egypt, and on them, therefore, must rest the responsibility which they would fain wriggle out of. In dealing with Irish affairs Sir Stafford showed his predilection for a policy of coercion rather than one of conciliation as a remedy for Irish grievances, and it is to behoped this will be noted by Irish electors. Perhaps the worthy Baronet is about the only man who would be bold enough to assert that there is not an improvement in the condition of Ireland, and that that improvement is to be attributed to the working of the Land and the Arrears Acts. Sir Stafford, how- ever, will not admit that there is an improvement, and says in effect that if there is it is due to the adminis- tration of the Coercion Act and not to the remedial ' measures. These remedial measures, however, passed the House of Commons by great majorities. The House of Peers did not dare to throw them out, though they could have done so; and notwithstanding all Sir Stafford may say, it is a singular coincidence that the improvement in the state of Ireland dates exactly from the passing of these measures. We should have been better pleased had the leader of Her Majesty's Opposition, instead of dealing in stale platitudes, indi- cated the policy the Conservatives would carry out were they returned to power; and until he has done that he is not likely to make much headway anywhere, and certainly not in Scotland. "Facts are (shiers that winna ding." This Seotchmen know, and what are facts to Sir Stafford are to the majority of Seotchmen only fallacies.

div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

The Liberal demonstration in the Volunteer Hall, on Monday evening, showed that the party in Widnes still re- tained its pristine vigour, but the result of the revision court on Thursday was still stronger evidence of that fact. The nett gains of the Liberals at that revision were 118, exclusive of a very large number of re-claims—about 64— which of course are not counted. So judiciously had Mr. H. B. Shores, the secretary to the Liberal Association, chosen his grounds for objecting to the Tory claims, that he was successful in sustaining no less a number than 114, and he was only called upon to ply costs amounting to 15s. Tories came from Southport, Liverpool, Manchester, Warrington, and Preston Brook to sustain their claim, to be placed on the register, but through the judicious discrimina- tion above referred to, had the melancholy satisfaction of paying their own expenses—not even their fares being allowed. If elections are fought in the revision court, the Liberals have fought theirs extremely well, and are deserving of all praise for it. The glorious uncertainty of the law needs , no illustration from me, but asslhowing the differences of ' opinion which exist among revising barristers, I may state that the one who presided at the Widnes Court, allowed no ' vote to any claimant who did not pay 7s. per week in rent, while Mr. Foulkes, who presided at Runcorn Revision Court, allowed about 30 claims to householders who did not pay ss. per week in rent. Of course no Liberal will quarrel with the latter (decisions, but it is nevertheless a curious fact.

There is a good deal of soreness felt in teetotal circles in consequence of some rather sever e remarks made by the Rev. S. Mees, in a sermon in St. Paul's chapel, on Sunday morning. It appears that Mr. Mces has met with people whose only virtue was their abstinence from alcohol, and who could not see any good in other people, however pious they may be, who partook, even moderately, of the intoxica- ing• cup. This uncharitable way of treating those who differed from them was denounced in strong terms. The warmth displayed led not a f,ter to suspect that what he had called "the holy cause of temperance" was suffering in his hands; while others approved, and thought it was time that the intemperate language of temperance people was checked. lam of opinion that Mr. Mees would have shown greater wisdom if he had let the matter alone. The pulpit is not the place for discussions ; as one warm-hearted teetotaller said "if he had not been ten feet above con- tradiction we might have had a lively time of it." Those who look to the revenue returns as an index of the state of trade throughout the country will, I think, after perusing the figures for the quarter ended on Saturday, be somewhat disappointed. Yet it is an undoubted fact that trade daring the past two or three years has been decidedly LJVLca,4II it was tor several years previously. Notwith- standing this, the reyenue for the quarter just ended corn.

pared with that for the corresponding quarter of last year shows an increase of only £226,200, for the half-year there is an increase of £443,988, and an increase on the year of £063,987. Land tax and house duty are as productive as ever, the increased revenue under these heads being £15,000; and the post-office and telegraph services, the two chief trading departments of the Government, show an increase of no less than £65,000 during the quarter, which augurs well for the future; while the yield of miscel- laneous items has increased during the same period by £401,116. This large increase is accounted for to a great extent by the fact that the receipts from fees have recently been transferred from the heading of stamps to that of miscellaneous. For this reason the receipts from stamps glows a decrease during the quarter compared with that of the previous year of £39,488. The interest on ad- vances is less by £6,428, and on property and income tax £115,000. To me, however, the most gratifying feature in the whole return is the decrease in the drink duties, which during the quarter amounts to £4,500 on customs and £90,000 on excise. The decrease in these duties is a matter to which Mr. Gladstone referred in introducing his last budget, it has been going on now since 1874, and I think it may be fairly concluded it is in a great measure, if not entirely, due to the increased habits of temperance and thrift among the working classes engendered mainly by the spread of education. F.LRNWJRTH PARISH SITNDLY SCHOOL9.—Mrs. Bond, wife .of the Rev. G. Bond, the vicar, presented the prizes to the scholars attending these schools on Friday week. An enjoyable entertainment, presided over 'ay the Vicar, was held. Miss Bond presided at the harmonium. THE ALLEGED ROPE ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.—James Williams, a boatman, was brought up on remand at Run- corn Police Court, on Wednesday, on a charge of stealing 51lbs. of rope, value 255., the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. The evidence has been published in The Examiner.—The prisoner was committed for trial. WEsLEYAN METHODISM AT WIDNES.—At the Victoria. road Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday, the Rev. R. Harper delivered a sermon in the morning, on "Ruth, the beautiful gleaner;" and in the evening on, "Noah and the deluge." Collections were made on behalf of the Kingswood and Woodhouse Grove schools.

POLICE INSPECTION AT RUNCORN.—Lieutenant-Colonel Hamersley, the Chief Constable of Cheshire, made an inspec- tion of the officers and constables of the Runcorn division of the Cheshire constabulary, on Saturday afternoon. Under the command of Mr. Superintendent Williamson and Inspec- tor Hollingworth, the men were drawn up on parade in the court-room, and put through a series of exercises. The total number on parade was 24. The Chief Constable com- plimented the men upon their smart appearance, and intimated that his inspection was highly satisfactory. The Inoks and accoutrements of the men were also found in a satisfactory state. THE CORONER AND A: RUNCORN JURYMAN.--At an inquest held at Itunco.o. uki',llwsdny, by Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coron,r. a juryman named Mr. T. D. Liv,s-y failed to pot in an appearance when the inquiry Was 01 0(1. Another juryman was ob'ained in his ptace, and ,u',=“inmtly Mr. Livesey arrived, too late to act. At the conclo-,ion of the inquest he was called tiro the room, and the Coroner addressing him, said he was vary sorry to have to c.oApiain, but he wished to say that when people were summoned upon a jury they ought to attend. It was a warrant from tho Quee*, and it was a warrant that had to be attended to. Coroners had power to inflict a fine upon jurymen who did not attend, but he should not do so in this case, because he hoped that what he said would be sufficient. But he must really impress upon him that when an officer issued to him a warrant to attend an inquest, it meant that he must be there. If he cou!d not be there from some cause, he must tell the officer that fact at the time, so that he would not put down his name. When his name was pat down he must certainly attend.—Mr. Livesey said he thought the time of the inquest was eleven o'clock.—The Coroner: The other eleven were here to time.

MR. PIERPOINT'S ANNUAL GRAND CONCERT at Runcorn will take place on the 13th of November next. The bril- liancy which has charactised Mr. Pierpoint's former con- certs may be taken as a guarantee that his prospective one will be of exceptional merit. Full particulars will be announced in due course.

SAD CASE OF DnOW3ING.— he other day, the inhabitants of Penketh were thrown into a state of excite- ment when the report was circulated that Mr. Joseph Griffiths, captain of the flat Harmony, had met with his death by drowning. It seems that when his flat was lying at anchor off Dingle Point, she was run into by the tug Toiler, and by the collision the ,deceased was thrown over- board and drowned. The other hands of the flat beached her at Dingle Point, where she now lies, half full of water. The deceased was the owner of the fiat, and his loss will be greatly felt: He was a quiet, inoffensive man, and enjoyed the good-will of all his neighbours.

ST. AMBROSE BRANCH OF THE C.E.T.S., WIDNES.— The first of a series of public tneetinzs in connection with this branch was held in St. Ambrose mission-room, Widnes, on Tuesday evening. The society, which was only recently formed, has a membership of about 50, but with the vigour which the organisers are infusing into their wolk 1011 soon be largely augmented. The Rev. G. Bond occupied the chair. There were also present the Rev. T. Storey Bates (secretary to the Liverpool branch of the C.E.T.S.), the Rev. S. A. Spooner, and Mr. W. E. Windle. Addresses on the temperance movement were delivered by the gentlemen named; and during the evening the children sang a number of glees in c tpital style. The Rev. S. A. Spooner presided at the harmonium.

LECTURE ON THE HOLY LAND AT RUNCORN. —A large audience gathered in Bethesda school-room, on Tues- day evening, to listen to a lecture on "A visit to Jacob's well," by Mr. James Rose, who has been engaged in the Prntestant schools of Mount Lebanon. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided. The lecturer gave a very lengthy, but interesting and instructive outline of the results of the ex- plorations which had been conducted by the committee since the formation of the fund in 1865. Incidentally, he stated that he once heard one of the inhabitants soy to another, as explaining the meaning of the excavations, that the English were going to put down the Turk, and were searching for the title deeds. Palestine under the Turk was Palestine cursed. What with a corrupt Government, oppres- sive pashas, and judges whose hands were full of bribes, the people would not live beyond hand to mouth because of the exactions of the tax collectors, and all energy and phy- sical power was reduced to a minimum, and the poor people sat down in despair, and groaned and sighed and died. When he was coming away one of the chief men of the place (a Mahommedan) said, "Tell the English people, if you please, to come and sa.ve us from the grinding and oppres- sive hand of the Turk." He was very thankful that this Egyptian war was over, not only for the sake of Egypt, but for the sake of Syria, which had been in a state of ferment during the war. No doubt interesting archeelogicil dis- coveries would be made east of the Jordan as soon as the officers got right into the work. The people were so favourable to the British that if ever Queen Victoria should want 25,000 fighting men to follow her to any part of the world, she would find them amoug the Druses of Lebanon. They were a bold and fearless set of mountaineers, and be hoped that nothing would arise which would alienate their affetqinn from us.—The meeting concluded in the customary manner.

HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN.—The members and friends of this association commenced their ninth session on Monlay night with a tea party aud entertaiutneut. Trinity schoolroom, whets the gathering took place, was tastefully decorated. Along each side tanks were arrantied holding plants and flowers and laden with tempting viands and fruit. Tea was not partaken of in the usual style of tea parties, but was served out by young ladies and then handed to the visitors by gentlemen waiters, the company being broken up in groups. Mr. George Rhodes lent a fine microscope, and the Rev. W. Preston a graphoscope and views, which afforded much pleasure. During the evening a musical entertainment was given by the following :—Miss Wright, Messrs. C. and J. Pownall, and Mr. Sutton. Mr. R. Pierpoint gave two solos on the cornet, which elicited encores. Miss B. Hankinson gave a pianoforte solo with much taste and ability. The Rev. Canon Burbidge, of Liverpool, gave an address on Christian works. He re- marked that working with and for God VMS the great test of true religion ; idleness and Christianity being op- posite terms. Christians must of necessity be like the angels in Jacob's vision, none of whom were standing still. It was possible for everyone to do some work, however few his talents. Votes of thanks closed the proceedings.
