MIMES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY —Tnis society, which has made extraordinary progress during the past few months, held its second demonstra- tion on Saturd ty afterd4ou. Meeting in the Waterloo-road schoolroom at four o'clock, the members of all sections of the society—juvenile and adult—numbering about 100 C, paraded the principal streets of the town, afterwards return- ing to the Parish Church. where a sermon was preached by the vicar, the Rev. J The edifice was packed. Subsequently a tea party took place in Waterloo- road school, followed by a public meeting in the Volunteer Hall. The Vicar presided, and there was a large audience. Mr. Chadwick, joint secretary to the society, read a report which stated the society was established on the 28th April, 1881, and though the original number of members was not large the increase was very gratifying, for twelve months after the formation the total number of members of all classes was 350. Since that time the progress made by the society bad been much more rapid. The increase in mem- bers during the last five months had been so very large, and the secretaries had been so much occupied that it was almost impossible to give the exact figures as to member- ship. Six months ago the numbers were :—Total abstainers 134, general 32, juveniles 184. Since then thrre had been initiated 487 total abstainers, 5 general, total 492. A senior boys and girls branch had also recently been formed at the Widnes road end of the parish, and now numbered 254 mem- bers. The total number of members in the society was 1,203. The Tontine Society in connection with the branch continued to make fair progress, the number of members having increased to 65, and the funds, if they accumulated at the same rate as at present, would provide for a bonus return at the end of the year of £1 5s 6d for each full member, this being in addition to the benefits derived from the society by those who required melical aid.—The Rev. W. H. Duggan con- Kratulated the society on the satisfactory report, and the Chairman complimented Mr. Chadwick on the efficient manner in which he had performed his secretarial func- tions. He called a'tention to the fact that the adult mem- bers of the society now numbered about 509, whereas only five months ago the number was 140.—Mr. Kilcross said the committee of the Widnes Branch of the Church of Eig- land Temperance Society had thought it their duty to mark their recognition of the services rendered them by their president, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, from the day of their first commencement, by a token more substantial awl marked than an ordinary vote of thanks. They had commis- sioned to ask their president to accept a gold badge and case as a mark of their esteem and respect.—The Chairman received the badge, which he fastened to his coat amid loud applause.—The Vicar then replied.—An entertainment con- sisting of songs and recitations followed. Messrs. Thomas, W. Hunt, Roberts, Strine, awl Powell took part; and the Star of Temperance band played selections of music. ROBBING THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION COMPANY AT Rurecoart.—At the •Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, before Mr. William Bankes, James Williams, George Hemm- ing, and Joseph Stephenton were charged with having on the 26th ult. feloniously stolen 3 cwt. of hay, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. They were also charged with having received the hay knowing it to have been stolen.—Mr. Lake appeared for Williams and Mr. 0. Leak represented Hemming.—Gilbert McWharrell said he was the agent of the Bridgewater Navigation Company at Preston Brook. The prisoner Hemming was employed by the Company as captain of the narrow canal boat "Cloud," and Stephenton was a hand on ;the same boat. Witness purchased for the Company four stacks of hay from Colonel Talbot's estate, Ashton Grange. Being in want of hay on the 25th September he sent the boat " Cloud" for the hay that was left, and they returned to Preston Brook on the 27th September. They had a cargo of hay weighing 1 ton 17 cwt. and 241 b., made up in trusses. The hay produced .was similar to the sample from the estate. Hemming and Stephenton had no authority to sell the hay.—Frederick Edwards, farm bailiff, Acton Bridge, deposed to the loading of the hay, which was similar to that produced, and James West, foreman porter, Preston Brook, corroborated the first witness' statement.—James Weedall, constable for the Navigation Company at Runcorn, deposed to seeing the "Cloud " and the prisoner Williams' boat fastened together in such a way as to arouse his suspicions that something was wrong, and he informed P.S. Whal- ley, who deposed to searching the prisoner Williams' boat about one o'clock on the 27th ult. He found on the boat five trusses and a part of one. The greater portion of the hay was tied with bands. Subsequently he again visited the boat, and the bands had then been removed. One of the five trusses was a different sample of hay to those pro- duced, and was tied up with strings. He charged Williams with stealing the hay, and he replied "I bought it on the road," adding that he purchased one truss at Middlewich. Questioned as to the other trusses, he said he knew nothing about them. On Sunday last he (witness) apprehended the prisoners Hemming and Stephenton at Preston Brook, and brought them to Runcorn police station, and charged all the prisoners together. Williams then stated Stephenton was the man from whom he purchased four trusses of hay, for which he paid 63. to Hemming. Stephen. t9n stated he received the money for the hay, and acknowledged that he sold the hay. Hemming said he knevi nothing about the transaction as he was not present.— Cross-exarnined by Mr. Superintendent Williamson, P.S. Whalley said he had been used to farm work. There would be on the brat about 6 cwt. of hay, which would be worth about 15s. or 165.; 63. was not a reasonable price.— Mr. Leak addressed the Bench on behalf of Hemming, and said that when a boat entered the lock at Runcorn it was the custom of a man to take away the horse. It was done in this ease by Hemming, who was away from the boat about 20 minutes, probably half an hour. When he came back the boat, which was then in charge of Stephenton, had passed through the locks, and he met it at the bottom locks. There was nothing whatever to connect Hemming with the theft, if such there had been.—Hemming was then discharged.—Mr. Lake submitted that there was no case againat Williams, but tiro Beuch committed tae latter and Stephenton to Kautsford Sessions for trial.

WIDNES CIIORLL SOCIETY: ANNUAL SOIEDE.—The members of the Widnes Choral Society inaugurated their winter's labours by a soirée, which was held in Lacey-street school, on Thursday evening. About 120 persons sat down to an excellent repast. The ladies who presided at the tables were—Mesdatnes Bond, Carey (senior), B. White, J. W. Davies, Pritchard, W H. Kershaw, Lord, and Hunter. We noticed amongst those present the Revs. G. Bond, S. Allen, S. A. Spooner' and W. H. Duggan; Messrs. Eustace I Carey, S. Kidd, and W. E. Windle ; Miss Bond, Miss Ida Bond, and Miss Haddock. At the subsequent entertainmen,t Mr. H. Brunner presided, and addressed a few words to the audience. The musical part of the programme was a very enjoyable one. The Misses Bond sang with their accus- tomed taste the duet, "I would that my love."- The humor- ous song "Tit for tat" was rendered with appropriate ex- pression by Miss Bond ; while Miss Ida Bond sang with her accustomed sweetness " A bunch of cowslips." Mrs. Lea, who favoured the audience with the song "Looking back," has lost none of the power of her fine contralto voice. In conjunction with Mrs. Maho she also sang the " Elphin call," and the excellencies of the interpretation were recognised by the audience according them an irresist- able encore. Miss Haydock executed the pianoforte solo "Moonlight sonata" with much skill; and Mr. J. R. Lea received the plaudits of the audience for his rendition of a song. Mr. Scott was successful in the comical song" Peter Piper ;" and no less so were the Misses Purver in their vocalisation of a pleasing duet. Mrs. Mahon rendered in a praiseworthy manner the beautiful song " Sweet spirit hear my prayer." Mr. Hunter and Mr. Williamson gave read- ings. The programme concluded with the glee "Lovely night," which was sung in good style. On the proposal of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Hunter, a vote of thanks was accorded to the vocalists; and a similar compliment was paid to Mr. Farrant, who had lent the flowers with which the tea tables were adorned, and to Mr. Haigh, who had kindly lent a piano. A vote of thanks to the chairman, on the motion of the Rev. G. Bond, c.mcl tried the proceed- ings.

SA.D DROWNING CASE AT ROSCOE. Nr. J. E Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Rail- way Hotel, Runcora, on Wednesday morning, on the body of Walter Jackson, 12 years of age, stepson of Jesse Bibby, a flatman, residing in Holloway-road, Runcorn.—George A. Relding, 10 years of age, son of Henry Relding, painter, Holloway, said about a quarter to six on Sunday night the deceased and himself started from home to go for some corn to a flat lying in the Francis dock. They went up towards Weston soapery, and crossed the locks. When they got to the slate wharf they saw the flat they were in search of, but apparently there was another intervening between it and the side. With the intention of crossing over, they took bold of each others hands and jumped as they thought upon the fiat. It, however, was only a shadow' and they fell into the canal. The deceased went down and only arose to the surface once. Witness was held up by his clothes, and he screamed out to a woman who was on a flat. She heared him, and called to a man on another fiat that a boy was in the water. 'Get him out then," was the heartless reply. The woman then called her husband and another man, who got witness out of the water. They took him into the cabin and took all means to restore him to consciousness. When he became conscious he told his rescuers that the deceased was in the water, from which they pulled him out with the boat hook. He was dead.--A juryman remarked that'it was scarcely a fit time to send a boy like the deceased across the locks.—Jessie Bibby deposed to sending his step-son for the corn.—James Johnson, flat:llan for the Bridgewater trustees, of Green-lane, Patricroft, stated that whilst lying in the cabin he heard some one shout "Ob." He went on deck and saw some one struggling in the water. He placed the head of a mop within his reach, and Skelding grasped it. He (witness) held him there and called for aid, and a man com- ing they pulled him out. Had he known the deceased was in the water he would have got him out.—The Coroner: We think you behaved very well in getting Skelding out. If if had not been for you he would certainly have been drowned—in summing up the Coroner said Johnson had cleverly managed the rescue, and complimented the boy Skelding upon the intelligent manner in which he had des- cribed the occurrence. Re:nuking upon the fact of sending such a young boy as the deceased across in the twilight, the Coroner said the boy had been accustomed to go about flats, and his step-father, on doubt, thought he was perfectly able to take care of himself. He di.i not think there was any I blame attaching to the step•father.—The jury returned a ' veadict of " Accidental deatla."
THE EXAMINER SATURDAY OCTOBER 7,1882.

ROBBERY OF IRON PIPING AT WIDNES.—TWO boys named James Dugan and Thomas Ellis, both of Widnes, were charged before Messrs. H. S. Hall and Holbrook Gas- kell, janr., at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, with stealing a quantity of iron piping, value 3d, from a house in Oxford-street, the property of the Warrington Per- manent Bencfit Building Society, on Tuesday. Mr. E. Wood, agent for the property, stated that he saw the pri- soners pull the iron from a spout, and they were each sen- tenced to receive three strokes of the birch rod. A WIDNES MILK SELLER IN TROUBLE.—On Saturday, at the Northwich County Court, before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, Henry Porter, milk seller, Widnes, was sued by John Gerrard. farmer, Acton. for .£25 12s. 101. balance ot an account alleged to be due for milk supplied.— Mr. Cooke appeared for the plaintiff.—From the evidence it appeared that the plaintiff had been in the habit of sending milk to the defendant, and enclosing a bill in the milk tankard every fortnight —The defendant denied the debt; but his Honour decided against him giving a verdict for the plaintiff for the full amount claimed. RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTLIORITY.—TIIO fort- nightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, when there were present:—Messrs. Mclntyre (in the chair), Rev. J. Lockwood, T. Andrews, J. Darbyshire, W. Whitlow, E. A. Wallington, J. Knowles, J. Smith, C. Rigby, John Davies, John Ashton, P. Hall, W. Jackson, W. Pickering, James Weir, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (inspector).—A. communication was read from the Local Government Board confirming the appointment of Dr. J. G. Bride as medical officer.—There ws no other business of public interest. ASSAULT ON A RurreonN BUTCHER. —At the Run- corn Police Court' on Tuesday, before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. John Brundrit, Thomas Frodsham, a butcher's assistant, was brought up in custody charged with stisaling two ropes, belonging lo Jacob Hedley, butcher, Church-street, Runcorn. He was further charged with assaulting Hedley. The rope, it appeared, had been used to tie Hedley's cattle to the rail- way trucks. The prisoner took the cattle to Savage's-yard, and the ropes were afterwards discovered in his pocket. Hedley accused him of stealing them, whereupon the pri- smer struck him a violent blow in the face with his fist. When arrested by P.C. Noden, the prisoner, whilst acknowledging that he struck Hedley, stated he believed the ropes belonged to Mr. Sivage.—The Bench dismissed the charge of felony, and fined the prisoner 2s 6,1 and 63 8d costs for the assault.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST HARVEST FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN. —Harvest thanksgiv7ng services were con lucted at Green- way-road Chapel, on Sunday. The sacred edifice lad been artiAically cl,corated with flowers, cerials, and fruit. Tee communion table was covered with rich fruit and bright blooming plants. Running round the front or the gallery was the sentence, "The earth is the Lord's," and on the pulpit the words, "The Lord of Harvest praise." The letters were formed in white on a blue ground, and bordered with a fringe of oats. For the choice decorations thanks are doe to Mrs. Samuel White, Mrs. Booth, Mrs. Collier, Mrs. Billingsley, Mrs. Fleet, Miss Joynson, Mrs. It)wland, Mrs. Faulkner, Mrs. Horton, and Miss Gittens. The trustees wee indebted to many members of the congregation for large contributions of fruit and flowers. The Rey. D. Schofield preached the morning sermon, and the Rev. J. Pickwell occupied the pulpit in the evening. The choir sang two authians at eacb t•ri.,l(..'e in good style, WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.—A. special meeting of this Board was held in the Board-room, on Tuesday morning, for the purpose of appointing a gas and water engineer, at a salary of £2OO per annum, to till the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Roberts. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were also present Messrs. Kershaw, Shuttleworth, Handley, Johnson, Sadler, Webster, Midwood, Forster, Carey, Pankburst, and Allen (clerk). Mr. Pankhurst remarked that they had received 75 applications for the appointment. He had gone through the whole of the appli- cation., and had selected six candidates, who the committee recommended should be written to. The six gentlemen who had been selected were the following, all of whom were present :—Mr. Philip Edenger, aged 35, Preston ; Mr. T. 0. Moorland, 28, Gloucester ; Mr. T. A. Bullough, 31, Widnes; Mr. Thomas Holgate, 26, Burnley; Mr. J. F. Bell, 27, Birkenhead; and Mr. J. Carr, 27, South Shields. The appli- cants were each called before the Board and interrogated, and on the vote being. taken Mr. J. Carr was appointed.— This was di the htffiiiEgg. A FATAL FALL IT WIDNES.—Mt. Coroner Dciffi.9ld held an inquiry at the Angel Inn, Mersey-road, Widnes, on Monday, touching the death of Sarah Reading, who died on Friday from injuries received by falling down the stairs at her home, 59, James-street.—Wm. Reading said the de- ceased was his wife. He had been married to her between 11 and 13 years. For some years she had been much ad- dicted to drink. She was not a strong woman. and she suffered from many complaints, brought on he thought by drink. On the 21st ult. his little boy Henry saw his mother the worse for drink. She went upstairs to make the beds, an,..1 on coming down she somehow slipped, and fell, rolling to the bottom. Her arm and head were slightly bruised, but she went about her household duties as usual until Friday, when she.died.—A woman named Mrs. Edwards deposed to having seen the deceased during her illness.— The Coroner, in summing up, said the evidence pointed to the fact that deceased had died from apoplexy, brought on perhaps by excessive drinking.—The jury returned a verdict to that effect.

CRt7ELTV TO I HORSE AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesiey, before Messrs. H. S. Hall and Ho!b:ook Gaskell, junr., John Sbncick and F. T. Simc )cic were charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it in an unfit condition.—F.C. Strickland stated that on the 22nd September he was on duty in Ann-street West, when be saw a horse driven by the defendant F. T. Simc3ck, dragging a cut which c erried a load of boxes. He atoppel the horse and examined it, when he found there was a large wound on the back. He then saw a wouni on its back about the size of a five-shilling piece. The wound was emitting a great quantity of matter. He also found two other wounds on the shoulders. The horse appeared to be in a very poor cenlition, and as it walked relel to and fro like a drunken man. The defend ints told him that they had had the horse at Liverpool that day, but previously it had not been out for a fortnight.—The Chairmen remarked that he considered the case a very bad one, and imposed a fine of 15s. and costs on F. T. SimcJek. but John Simcock was discharged.

HARVEST FESTIVAL AT RUNCORN PARISH CAURCIL—Last evening a thanksgiving service for the ingathering of the fruits of the earth, was held in the Runcorn Parish Church. The handsome church was bright with floral decorations of a remarkably pretty and artistic nature. Immediately on entering the south door, the visitor was impressed with the striking beauties of the font, which was decorated with sheaf:lets of corn, evergreens and flowers. In various pro- minent positions in the sacred edifice, were displayed artistically designed shields quartered according to the rules of heraldry, and they reflected the highest credit upon the members of the congregation who had made them. Amongst them we may notice the" mitres," the arms of Chester, worked in wheaten straw on a crimson ground; sickle and the sheaf, cross and anchor (the emblem of faith and patience) on a mauve ground and numerous others. The pulpit was adorned with a fringe of oats, the panels being filled with various de- signs in wheat and flowers, on a blue ground, and it had a pretty appearance. The communion had been elaborately decorated. On the table was pladed a cross of flowers of a most charming and beautiful description, the offering of Mrs. Charles Hazlehurst. On each side was a Gothic arcade, constructed of oats, the desivls of the pinels being formed of wheat and flowers. In the centre of the front of the table was a star of barley, with a centre piece formed of lilies, a magnificent bunch of grapes being placed on either side. The grapes were the gift of Mr. Thomas Bankes, of Weston. Over the table were the words, worked in wheaten straw, on a blue ground, "I am the true vine," " I am the living bread." Over the door at the west end of the church was a scroll containing the words "The earth is filled with the fruit of Thy work," having on each side a crimson shield with a sheaf of oats in the centre. Over the north door was the motto "Sing, heavens," and over the south door "Rejoice, 0 Earth." The following are the tames of the ladies and gentlemen who carried out the decorations :—Miss Barclay, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. John Brundrit, Miss Cox, Miss Crosby, Misses Edwards, Miss Howard, Miss Hughes, Miss liaison. Miss A. Imison, Miss A. Jones, Mrs. Jowle, Miss Malcolm, Miss A. Mouritz, Mrs. Steele, Miss Ward, Mrs. Lloyd Wig, and the Misses Wigg ; Messrs. John Davies, Rev. R. Ed- wards, Jowle, A. Lightburne, —Sutton. There was a , crowded conaregation present at the service, and the sermon heis taeaeued by Lire Rev. GL.11.6 Liy:tva SLovaLI.,I,LA., Precenter of Cheater Cathedral.
Sr. AMBROSE CHURCE, WIDNES.-With the object of building a boundary wall round this church, a movement is on foot to raise a fund.
STAR or WIDNES LODGE, I.O.G.T.—The Hope of Run- corn Lodgei on Wednesday, gave an entertainment before the members of the above lodge. Bro. Hufton, W.C.T., of the Star Lodge, presided.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHOIR were a few evenings ago entertained to a dinner at Wilson's Hotel through the generosity of Miss Barclay. The health of Miss Bircfay and the Rey. Canon Barclay were heartily drunk.

ROBBING A. RABBIT COTE.—John Duffy and Thomas Rourke were charged at the Widnes Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday, before Messrs. H. S. Hall and Holbrook Gaskell, jun., with stealing two tame rabbits, the property of Mary Murphy, grocer, Widnes Green; and Margaret Fallon was charged with receiving the rabbits, knowing them to be stolen.—Mr. Husband represented the fema'e prisoner.—The prosecutrix stated that she saw the two prisoners, when she was in her room upstairs on the 20th ult., enter the yard and take the rabbits out of the cote where they were kept.— A constable, from information he had received, went to Mrs. Fallon's house, and enquired if she knew either of the prisoners. She denied all knowledge of them, and pretended to know nothing about the theft. Fubsequently, however, he saw her coming out of her back yard, and being suspici- ous he went up to her and found that she had a rabbit con- cealed under her apron.—Mr. Husband, for the defence, contended that there was no evidence to show that Fallen received the rabbit knowing it to be sto'..en, and the Bench dismissed the case against her.—Several witnesses were called who stated that the prisoner Rourke could net possi- bly have entered Mrs. Murphy's yard at the time in ques- tion, and he was also discharged; but Duffy was fined 2s 6] and costs.

WIDNES REVISION COURT.—Mr. W. H. Butter, the re- vising barrister, commenced the revision of the parliamen- tary voters' lists for the townships of Bold, Cronton, Cuerd- ley, Ditton, and Widnes, on Thursday. The Liberals were represented by Mr. Powell (solicitor) and Messrs. H. B. Shores, and H. Major (agents); and the Conservatives were represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift (solicitor) and Messrs. T. A. Bullough and W. Woodworth (agents).—The Conservatives claimed a vote for Mr. W. W. Patten, who is the agent of the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company, and resides in a house attached to the company's premises. Mr. Patten WAS objected to by the Liberals on the ground that he paid no rent for the house.—Mr. Patten said he paid 63. Bd. per week.—Mr. Powell : Do you pay 6d. a week rent P—Ap- lieant : No I don't ; arid I never have done.—Mr. Powell: This is the London and North-Western Railway Company's property ?—AprOicant : No it is not ; it is the Sheffield and Lincolnshire Company's. lam gools agent for them. —Mr. Powell : The rates are paid by the co:np any. ' He is obliged to live there.—The Barrister : Are you obliged to live there P—Applicant : No, sir, I am not.—The Barrister : Who would live there if you did not P—Applicant : Very probably a signalman.—The Barrister : You say the Rail- way Company deduct Cs. 83. per week from your wages because you occupy this house P—App!icant : Yes. —The Barrister allowed the claim. Na other important case came up for hearing.

CREDITORS' MEETING AT WARRING rON.-011 Wednes- day, a meeting of the creditors of Mr. Timothy Ashcroft, coal merchant, Latchford, was held at the offic!s of Messrs. Moore and Son, Bank-street. The statement of accounts showed liabilities amounting to £336 is. 2d., and the assets were set down at £204 7s. Liquidation was resolved upon, and Messrs. Moore and Son were entrusted with the regis- tration of the resolutions.

ROYAL LANCASHIRE AGRICITLETTRAL SOCIETY.—TE e statement of accounts of the Preston Committee of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society shows that after paving the cost of the local prizes (nearly £710), a donation of £250 towards the expenses of the society's visit and working expenses, there is a balance of £270, which, excepting £7O, has been handed to the society. The total received by the Preston Committee was £1,300. The society by their show at Preston made a gaiu of ulnut £5OO.

ST. JOrlti TIES BAPTL9T CHURCH, EAILLESIOWN. Two special sermons were preached in this place of worship on Sunday last by the Rev. J. P. Kirkman, M.A., F.R.S , rector of Croft, and collections were made in aid of the orgln fund. In the evening Mr. Kirkman drew attention to the object for which the services were being held, re- marking that the organ was one of beauty and power, and impressed upon his hearers the necessity there was for pay- ing off the debt at present resting upon it. At the same service (when the edifice was crowded) the solos in the anthem " I know that my Redeemer liveth," from the " Messiah," were sung by Madame St. Clement, whose dis- tinct and clear voice resounded through the edifice, im- pressing the congregation with its sweetness. As the chorus, the words of the 405th hymn, "Jesus loves," were sung by the choir. The collections amounted to about £9.

GOOD TEMPLARS' MEETING.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown Lochze of Good Templars held their usual week'y session in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, on Monday evening. There was only a moderate attendance Sister M. Allison presided in the abeence of 'the W.C.T. through illness. After the routine business had been gone through, one candidate was initated, and Bro. John War- burton, lodge deputy, read a communication from the secre- tary ef the Morning Star Lodge at St. Helens announcing their intention of paying a fraternal visit. It was resolved that they should be entertained to coffee and other refresh- ments previous to leaving for home. The pro eramme of the evening was then proceeded with, and a variety of articles were presented to the lodge and sold to the highest bidder, the sale creating much amusement, fruit, biscuits, &c., being handed round to the members by those who purchased them. A very pleasant and enjoyable evening was spent, as well as a nice sum realised by the sale. The lodge closed , in the usual form at 9-45. THE EARLESTOWS TRACT SOCrETY : PIISLIC MEEnt*. —A public meeting to adroc ite the claims of the Religious Tract Society was held in the Congregational School, Crow- lane, on Wednesday evening. There was only a small attendance. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. Allatt, who was supported by Mr. Richard Butcher, the association secretary for the Lancashire and Yorkshire district. Among others present were Mr. B. B. Glover and Mr. P. M. Camp- , bell. After the meeting had been opened with singing and prayer, the Chairman remarked that the locd ministers and clergymen had been duly informed of the meeting, and a cordial invitation had been given to them to attend. Many of them had written, however, that prior engagements had prevented them from being present. He observed that the Religious Tract Society was not a stctarian or denomi- national society—it included within it men of all the vary- ing shades of religion. The society bad been doing a good work in connection with publications that was really amaz- ing. On the book portion of the Beligious Tract Society there was a considerable profit, which was devo•ed to good and useful purposes, and various grants were made to different objects, showing it was a truly missionary society.—Mr. Butcher observed that the society commenced its work in the year 1799. The ques- tion hsd been frequently asked how could they bring on influence for good to be exercised on men's minds, and that ,led to the formation of that society as an agency whereby the truth could be distributed from house to house, and ' tbois who would not go to hear the Gospel preached could have it presented unto them. He remarked that the British and Foreign Bible Society was the outcome of the Religious Tract Society, and they were helping every missionary society in the world, while its publications were to be found in at least 142 different languages. He pointed out that many instances could be given of the good thae,had resulted from the dissemination of tracts, as an instrument for the awakening of the ungodly, for the guiding of the enquirer, for bringing consolation to those cast down, and for teaching them the knowledge of that truth which was essential to man's eternal salvation. They were trying to supplant and counteract the evil influences arising from the circulation of many of the periodicals of to-day, and to take away the bad and put in its place that which was better. Be alluded at some length to the various magazines and periodicals issued by the society, pointing out the success that had attended them and commending them to the notice of those present. The society, he said, belonged to the Christian church, and whatever profit was made after the payment of the general expenses- was devoted to missionary, work at home or abroad. To go over the work being done in our own coun- try would take a long time, but from what he had stated they would be able to see something of the avenues into which they were able to send the precious truth. No sooner was it decided that the British troops should go to Egypt than it was arranged by the society that a vast number of religious publications should be distributed to them. The work in Which they were engaged was that which was essential to the carrying out of the Gospel in almost every country in the world. He appealed for funds on behalf of the society, remarking that as missionary lal2our extended they bad further need of their sympathy and help. He I trusted Newton would take some part in the work and thus help to bring on that period when the knowledge of the Lord should cover the earth as the waters covered the face of the deep. (Applause.)—A collection was then made ou Lehalf of the furele of the seelety, and te' cen- eluded with the singing of the Doxology.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting was held at the Workhouse yester- day, under the presidency of Mr. W. Darbyshire. There were also present Messrs. Houghton, Kilshall, Garnett, S. Sutton (assistant clerk), J. 11. Uornali (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and U. Rawlings (inspector).
ELECTRIC LIGHTING.

The ASSISTANT CLERK said he had received notic:A from two electric lighting companies stating their intention to apply to the Board of Trade for provisioaal orders to supply electricity for public or private purposes within the area of the Authority.

NOXIOUS VAPOURS. The ASSISTANT CLERK said he had received several re- plies to the circular asking for co-operation in seeking the appointment of an additional inspector under the Alkali. &c. Woi ks Regulation Act for this district. Mr. W. H Brook, Town Clerk of Warrington, wrote that the Authority'. letter had been before the Sanitary Committee, and the con- sideration of it deferred until their next meeting. The Cle:k to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners replied that the Commissioners saw no reason to more in the matter of the appointment of an additional inspector; the Clerk to the Widnes Local Board said he was instructed to inform the Authority that it was not considered advisable to join them ; and the Clerk to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority stated it had been resolved that no action be taken. The Town Clerk of St. Helens informed the Authority that the Council some time ago applied to the Local Government Board fsr an inspector to be biationed at St. Helens, and an inspector had been appointed tem- porarily. Mr. Robert Holland, secretary of the Association for Controlling the Escape of Noxious Vapours and Fluids from Manufactories (Lancashire and Cheshire), stated he was very glad to hear the Authority was asking other Boards to join in the appointment of a special inspector. He feared they would not meet with very much encourage- ment from the other sanitary authorities, but when they got all the replies he would be very glad if the clerk would let him knew the result of the Authority's appeal.—The matter was postponed for a month. THE TREASURER'S SALARY DISALLOWED.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board, stating that Mr. Haslehurst, district auditor, had reported that at his last audit of the accounts of the Guardians of the Warrington Union, acting as the Rural Sanitary Authority, he disallowed the sum of £5 in the accounts of Mr. John Dun, treasurer of the Authority. The Board requested that the Clerk would inform them whether the sum had been placed to the credit of the Authority in the treasurer's bank pass-book. The ASSISTANT CLERK said the £5 was the half-year's salary which had been paid to Mr. Dun. The auditor was not thorouzhly satis- fied as to the sanction of the Local Government Board to the terms of the appointment, and lie surcharged the amount. Mr. Dan said he was not going to be troubled in appealing to the Local Government Board, and had repaid the amount, and he had replied to that effect Mr. Dun had been treasurer since the appointment ot the Authority, an I he was appointed on the understanding that he would receive £lO a year. When the present auditor came he wanted the sanction of the Local Govern- ment Board, and they could not find it. He fancied they bad not received it.—The subject was referred to the Clerk.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

-- Mr. GORNALL reported that for the month ending Sep- tember 30:h, there 18 male and 15 female births; and 14 male and three female deaths. The excess of births civet deaths was 16; the death-rata 16.3; and the proportionate mortality from preventable diseases 23 per cent. The deaths from zymotic diseases we: e :—Two from scarlet fever, and one from whooping cough. Scarlet fever continued to be prevalent in various parts of the district. At Penketh three cases had occurred; and in the streets of the Liverpool- road several Cases had come to his knowtedge. The deaths from scarlet fever took place one at Padgate, and the other at Latchford. There had also been an outbreak of scarlet fever at the Quaker's school, Penketb, due to an introduced case on the reassembling of the scholars after the summer holidays. Some 15 cases bad occurred of a mild type. Effective steps had been taken for arresting the further pro- gresa of the disease by isolation of the patients ia hospital tents.

div.p: SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

The Sußvmat reported that during the past month in- spections had been made of houses erecting west of Lovely- lane, and of houses erecting on the Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges. Acting under the Authority's instructions, Mr. Sutton and he attended the meeting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee of the Warrington Corporation to dis- cuss terms for the proposed use of the new sewers now being laid outside the borough boundary in Latchford. The meet- ing was held on Monday evening, the 2nd inst., and, unfor- tunately, the Chairman of the Authority (Mr. Darbyshire) was not able to be present. At the meeting the proposed conditions were read, and some explanations and discus- sions were entered into. Since then he bad received a copy which he was abs to lay before the Authority, but as he understood the clerk would be absent, he suggested that a report upon the conditions be left until the next meeting.— The report was adopted.

LYMAI LOCAL BOARD. STORMY PROCEEDINGS. The monthly meeting was held on Thursday evening, Mr. Cameron presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. Dewhurst, Rogers, Taylor, Gibbon, Bailey, Forster, Callen- der, and Mallard (assistant clerk). PROPOSED REDCCTION IN THE PRICE OF GAS. • Mr. ROGERS, chairman of the Gas Committee, moved, "That the price of gas be reduced from ss. to 48. 2d. per 1,000 cubic feet from and after the 30th September, 1852." —Mr. BAILEY, in seconding the motion, said the Board de- sired to satisfy the consumers, and this, he believed, would be found to be the case—Mr. TAYLOR supported the resolu- tion with pleasure because he was in reality forwarding his own motion, of the 6th May last, for the reduction in the price of gas in Lymm. He could not help saying that Mr. Rogers would have displayed more man- liness if he had seconded his propositien then, instead of putting the gas consumers to the ex- pense of paying 10d. per 1,000 more for the past three months simply to gratify a domineering and seifish desire to appear in the eyes of the public as the one man from whom they might expect any benefit.—At this point the CHAIRMAN rose and called upon the speaker to desist frees tiersonalities, but Mr. TAYLOR, evidently determined to have his say, went on to remark that to use Mr. Rogers' own words, '"-he was running with the hare and hunting with the hounds" in face of the coming election. The finances of the gasworks were in as good a condition on the 6th May as they were at the present time, so that no thanks were due to the proposer of the present motion.—rbe CHAIRMAN: I must say that the remarks made by Mr. Taylor are very uncalled for.— Mr. ROGERS observed that with regard to the proposition made by Mr. Taylor on the 6th May last, nothing was more inopportune and no preposition to his mind was more un- reasonable. Many repairs and improvements were required to be executed at the Gas Works, notably a larger main in the yard, as the one existing was very much too small. There was a 0-inch main and a 3-inch main outside the yard, and they had only a 6-inch main from the: gasholders to supply both those main!. The demand for gas had grown so considerably that the main was not of sufficient capacity to supply the demands made upon it. They, therefore, had la larger main put down, a new governor, and new retorts were required, and another main-layer had to be engaged. When the 6th May arrived the work had all to be done. He had taken the responsibility upon himself to prepare esti- mates of the probable cost of the improvements and altera- tions. It was one thing to estimate and another thing to bring out the fact when the money was to be paid; and however careful one was it was possible to be mistaken; and therefore he maintained that it was unreasonable and most inopportune for Mr. Taylor to bring forward such a. resolution as he did until they had completed laying out what money they were obliged to expend. His meson for making the proposition was not a personal one. He scorned all such things, and he would treat the remarks with the contempt they deserved. They knew better than to reduce the price of gas to 4s. 2d., and then to find out that they could not afford to do so. The Gas Committee had been most careful, and were unani- mous in their desire to give the consumers gas at as cheap and reasonable a price as possible, but at the same time the committee were taking care to keep the works in good order, and providing for the heavy debt they had to pay. The debt on the works a very short time ago, he thought was over £7,000, but they had fortunately been able to pay about £l,lOO of that amount, and to keep the works in good order as well. They had received a notice from an electric lighting company stating that they were going to apply to the Board of Trade for a pro- visional order to supply Lymm with the electric light Suppesing that electricity was to be used there as a lighting agent, what was to become of their gas works? When they were out of debt they could set all electric lighting companies at defiance. They would have done better to have kept the gas at 55 10d until the debt was paid off rather than tell the community that they were going to re- duce the price of gas. Immediately the Gas Committee saw that they could reduce the price of gas to 4s 21 they did so. He thought it was better to leave those things in the hands of the people who have carefully gone into the matter. What Was the committee . for if they could not do a duty of that kind. Mr. Taylor rose and was about to speak, when the CIIAIR- NtAN pointed out that Mr. Taylor had no right of reply.— Mr. TAYLOR however, ignored the chairman's remarks, and said that as Mr. Rogers had replied, he likewise had a right to reply. He told the chairman to keep his place, and he would keep his. He asked him as chairman of the Board to do his duty, and not to be one-sided in a matter of that kind. There had been strong language allowed to pass which the chairman had frequently before-times taken no notice of. Ile had not used language which was not justi- fieble.—During the time Mr. Taylor was uttering these remarks the chairman repeatedly asked him to sit down, but as Mr. Taylor would not obey his ruling, he called upon the other members of the Board to assist bins in keeping older, whereupon the whole of the members rose from their seats. The chairman also left the chair, and said he would not be responsible for what Mr. Taylor said. One of the members at once left the room. The others lingered for a short time, and the meeting broke up.

A large meeting of the inhabitants of Windsor was held yesterday, at which it was decided to take steps to give a hearty wc!c.,me to the Second Life Gnards on their retam from Egypt, ad to givo a banquet to the troops.

THE WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

Sir,—lS there not sufficient Calet-ii-a both the political clubs of this town to revive the above society? These societies are agencies of good if properly conducted. I observe Manchester's first gathering is on Friday, the Gth instant, when the Speaker is to be appointed and a Govern- ment elected. Why cannot we follow suit in Warrington at an early date P I trust the friends of the old society will make an effort to do so, and that both clubs will render their assistance to the project.—Yours sincerely, Warrington, 4th Oct., 1882. BENJ. SAWDON.

div.head: " ANGLO-SCOTUS " AGAIN.
div.p: " ANGLO-SCOTUS " AGAIN.

Sir,—l have just come out of Kent into Surrey, and, there- fore, have only just seen the latest remarks of "Newtonian," so kindly permit ma to say a word or two that will ease his mind. Ido not intend to "turn my back." Bless the man! lam not hunting conies. He started something of a hybrid kind across the path, called it a coney, and when I asked him what kind of an animal it was (seeing that he prides himself in digging out the derivations of words), he replied, on the authority of a Bishop Wilkins, that it is a rabbit with short ears and a long tail. As to his charge about frittering away time and opportunity in futile fencing, I will leave readers of the Examiner to judge as to what perch that chicken will roost on when it seeks a home. lam glad to hear "Newtonian" objects to coursing, for I began to think he was introducing bees, ants, conies, dec., to de- stroy the scent, or obscure the sight. I will endeavour to begin again next week, and see if I can win anotLer pat on the back from him. Meantime, I will record in his favour the fact that the other day in the Era news- paper there was advertised for sale "a duck with four legs, of tender age, and in good condition." In the same issue some one advertised for a billsticker who could keep sober on a Monday," while another individual, residing not a hundred miles from Newton, offered a liberal salary to any manipulator of the paste brush "who would carry out a ladder and bring it back again." If such things as above advertised and inquired for exist, "Newtonian" has a per- fect right to believe that the ark contained hutch accommo- dation, and in the existence of rabbits with short ears and long tails. He: must indeed be a wag to call me a "free lance," and to suggest that Scotchmen, above all people in the world, would indulge in a "free fight." A free feed, or a free fuddle, I could understand or imagine. If he goes on manufacturing phrases in this fashion, he will land him- self in a derivation argument the premises of which it will be harder for him to reconcile and prove than the non- existence of pigeon-milk, or that Scotchmen really did in- vent the haggis.—l am, sir, &e., yours in baste, ANGLO-SCOTUS. 243, Beresford-street, 'Newington, London, S.E. P.:A.—Will " Newtonian " kindly send use the extract from the war correspondent's letter?

div.head: FEVER HOSPITAL..
div.p: THE FEVER HOSPITAL..

you kindly find space in your valuable paper for this letter, I have always thought that the Fever Hospital was open to all kinds of fever, but I have been mistaken. A case of fever has, unfortunately for me, taken place at my house. Dr. Gornall was made aware of the case, and of course he came down to see about it. Having had the case explained to him, he told my wife he was very sorry, but the patient could not be removed to the hospital, because there ;was no room for it. He said they had not a case like it there' and we should have to do the best we could with it at home. Neither did he offer us any other assistance with the case. What is the hospital for but infectious diseases ? "I claim (quoting the reply of Dr. Gornall to Dr. Carter) for myself and the other members of my family, and the public, to be protected from an infections disease." What do I pay my rates for ? part of which goes to support the hospital ; and now when I want to have the use of it, I can't have it. If there is not accommodation for all kinds of fever, then lather° be provi- sion made for cases like mine as soon as possible, for if there should be any more cases like it, I suppose parents will have to keep them at home the same as I have had to do, which is not a good way of stamping out an infectious disease. Whose door shall we lay the blame at, but at the Sanitary Committee's, whose duty it is to provide for all cases of fever. - A RATEPAYER.
THE PROPOSED SHIP CANAL. " And if a house be divided against itself it cannot stand." Sir,—l regret to see in the columns of local and othe

paper's signof what may prove weakness instead of unity - and strength, in regard to the proposed ship canal. Mr. Williams is not infallible, and the plans, etc., proposed .bY him may or may not yet prove to be the best, either as regards tunnels or steep embankments for crossing railways, or swinging bridges in the middle of the ship canal on pivots, for canal viaduct, requiring, each time a ship has to pass, the opening and shutting of four lock gates, and a loss of water during the process, and continually after each im- perfect closure. The latter part can be done with only two small valve gates and a water bridge raised from one end without any loss of water. There are, however, matters that may be dealt with better than by converting a lock canal into a tidal or semi-tidal one, after it has been found im- practical for the safety •of large vessels and prevention of floods. I have a deep interest in this matter, and on behalf of its success and the welfare of all interested, would sug- gest that these things should receive further consideration, and that all the gentlemen who have made suggestions and rendered assistance in matters of engineering and ingenuity, together with those who proposed schemes years ago for this undertaking, should be invited to help on the scheme by further suggestions that possibly neither Mr. Williams, the provisional committee, nor anyone else could reject when duly considered. If thiswere done there might appear amongst the suggestions some of Mr. Fulton's plans, and a late resi- dent engineer of Warrington, a Mr. Middlehurst, and many others might then come forward and thus prevent what has already been hinted at other schemes and companies cropp- ing up, or taking the mill to the cotton rather than the cotton to the mill. A late eminent engineer once said the River Mersey was only a ditch and oughtt to have been filled up many years ago.—Yours respectfully, C. E.
WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF SCIENCE.

DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. The Lecture Room, Museum-street, was crowded on Mon- day evening with an audience composed mainly of students' of the Warrington School of Science, who with others had assembled to witness the distribution of the prizes gained at the last May examinations in connection with the Science and Art Department, and to hear Mr. R. Betley, F.G.S., of Wigan, lecture on "The history of iron manufacture." Mr. B. Davies presided, and there were also present Mr. Betley, - the Rev. R. Pilcher, Councillor Milner, Councillor Monks, Messrs. W. Sharp, T. Morris, C. Chorley, Percy, Thurnam, J. R. Young, J. Burgess (hon. secretary), and SW. Silcock (hon. treasurer), etc. The CHAIRMAN said whatever might be thought about the latter half of the 19th century in a literary or artistic point of view, there could be no doubt whatever that it would rank in the annals of science higher, or at all events equally as high, as any half century known in the annals cf history. To support this assertion, he asked them for a moment to consider those stupendous and progressive inventions the telegraph, the telephone, and the electric light, all dis- covered and perfected in less than 50 years' a space of time which some of them at all events could over pass them- selves. Supposing for a moment that in a trial 50 years ago some eminent scientific witness had given evidence which had produced a powerful impression upon the minds of the judge and jury, and had evidently influenced them in the verdict they were about to deliver, had been examined by some clever cross-examining tormentor, anxious to shaw his peculiarity, and that his crochets were at all events as numerous as his opinions, who asked him whether he did not hold some very peculiar views upon scientific discovery, and had proceeded further to ask him whether he did not believe that in the coarse of the next 50 years a message might be sent from the antipodes and received in London between the rising and the setting of the sun; whether he did not believe that in the course of the same Period of time by a wire the Queen ' could hear the Lord Mayor's speech in the barquetting hall at the Mansion House at Windsor Castle whilst it was being delivered, and whether he did not also believe that London might possibly be lighted by another wire and a few pencils of charcoal—supposing that this eminent man had had the gift of prescience and answered in the affirmative, one could easily imagine the look veLich would have stolen over the faces of the judge, the jury, and the spectators. The im- pression would have been similar to that impression which St. Paul made on the Roman Governor, that much learning had made him mad. lie (the Chairman) took it that his evidence would have been reiected, that he would have left the box with a look of pity that his great talents should be sacrificed to such extraordittery ridiculous ideas, that he would have gained no con fdence, but lost all that his pre- Timis evidence had excited in the minds of the rest of his hearers. Well, in 50 years time all that had come to paSS and many things to which he could not allude perhaps of less apparent importance, but equally beneficial in the assistance of arts, of manufactures, and of every department of mann-

facture in this country. A hundred years ago he supposed such opinions which have consigned one to the lunatic asy- lum; and 200 or 309 years ago, to a much more cruel fate, for they must not forget that in those days the popular mind was averse to change of any kind,—actually resisted it; they did not understand it, they did not want it, and they would not have it. Novelty in religion was heresy, 1 novelty in politics was treason, novelty in science was diabolical agency; and the axe, the gibbet, and the stake were arguments that convinced everybody in those days that those visionaries really and truly were best blotted out of the world which they attempted to spoil by their new fangled notions and absurdities from its old equanimity and repose. All that had very much changed. They saw science of every kind advancing. They saw improvements made in every department around them, and he thought he might be allowed for a moment to refer in kindly terms, and he was sure to an appreciative audience to the discoveries which their respected fellow-townsman, Mr. Thomas Fletcher— (applause)—had made in furnaces, and in the different applications of heat. He was a very modest gentleman. He asked Mr. Fletcher to be present, having met him in the street. He said he was afraid he could not hear what was said, but he was sure they must all feel he had struck upon discoveries which would bear fruit in the course, perhaps, of a few years, give fresh ideas to those who were studying that subject, and he hoped add fresh glory to Warrington. (Applause.) It would be a pity if in Warrington, that War- rington of which he was a native, and of which he had been so proud all his life—(applause)—they were to advance in riches and population and to lag behind in art, i science, or learning. (Hear, hear.) It would not be agreeable to any of them, and he was extremely glad that Warrington had taken steps so as to have herself represented in science classes supported, he feared, by but a few but those however very zealous, and I supported by many students who were seeking for the means 1 of learning which he hoped he might say they were endea- voaring to put within their reach. (Applause.) He believed from the returns which his friend, Mr. Burgess, had given him, that there were 145 who entered the classes—that was a large number considering how lately the movement had begun,—(hear, hear)—and that actually 94 of those pre- sented themselves at the examinations—(hear, hear)—with very excellent results indeed on the whole. He had before him prizes for distribution, and amongst them he had the first prize for an essay on carriage building, being £5 and a silver medal—(applause)—the only one of that amount and \value which had been gained in England. (Hear, hear.) That was something for Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Then there were 18 Queen's prize men in science subjects, and three Iprizes from the City and Guilds of London In- stitute, namely, third prize for tanning leather, ,£2 and bronze medal, and third prize for iron and steel manu- facture, also amounting to £2 and bronze medal. They did not look at the amount of the prizes. There was no one in the room, and he hoped no one in Warrington, who would read the report of that meeting without feeling proud of that town in which there had. always been talent of one kind or other from the earliest day that the oldest man could recol- lect, either in learning or science, or skill in some special sphere of manufacture. They believed that Warrington might be a large place. He hoped it would add to all their happi- ness if it was, but whether large or not there was always a band of gentlemen ready, in everything he had had to do with in his life, to assist and stretch out their hands and to give their. time to push for- ward on its progress the old town. At Liverpool I they were doing also a great work. Mr. Morris had kindly I handed him an account, which told him that there were 850 I students, embracing all classes of the community. He did not think that that was, in proportion to the population, any greater than the quota Warrington bad supplied to these classes, and he was extremely proud of it. He hoped that, the coming year would see an improvement, as no donbt it would. They had only to study as earnestly as they could to do credit 1 to the town, and to do great good to themselves in futme life, for of all blessings which a man could, enjoy it was, he thought, the recollection of those hours he had spent in i acquiring knowledge which was useful either for this world I 'or for eternity. (Applause.) And yet they must have a. little support; after that excellent meeting he hoped they should; and this being proved to be a success, he hoped that many would press into it who at first were doubtful, and that their progress would be both certain and more advanced. In spite of all these advances, and in spite of what the world was doing at this moment, they were told that they were only a selected species of ape. (Laughter.) There was one gentleman at a meeting of the British Asso- ciation who undertook to point out the particular species to which they belonged. He did allow that it was a supe- rior species, and now extinct. But he must confess that I even that, kind as it was, hardly reconciled him to such an ancestry. (Laughter.) It might be that the Creator did take one type of animal life to govern Him in the forma- tion of animated beings in this world, and that some muscle or some part of them was represented in some I animal or other. That might well be; but the dignity of ' man consisted in his possessing a mind which had enabled i him to make and grasp those wonderful scientific discoveries 1 to which he had alluded; and whatever might be thought of the origin of human nature, he preferred to look upon it as improving to something even higher than they knew. He would take the view of the great poet Shakespere, when I he put into Hamlet's mouth the following words :

"What a piece of work is man! How noble in reason! How infinite in faculties! In form and moving, how express and admirable ! In action, how like an angel! In apprehension, how like a God ! " (Loud applause.) Mr. W. Saconz read the statement of accounts, which showed a balance against the school of 23 4s. 74., 'sat this amount would be cleared off by the proportion of the grant which they expected to receive in the course of a week or (Applause.) The session for 1832-3 they started with a clean page. (Applause.) The Chairman then presented the prizes, a list of which has already appeared in The Examiner. . . .

The LE&TICIRER then proceeded with his fecture. He re- marked that the manufacture of iron might be said to be of importance for three principal reasons. First of all on ac- couut of the intrinsic value of the manufacture itself, and of the employment it gave; secondly, on account of the in- fluence it exerted on other trades, notably the coal trade, and trades which supplied material used in its production; thirdly, b2canse the manufactured article entered so largely into the construction of machinery, the railroad—both the permanent way and the rolling stock—bridges, steam ships, ironclads, and munitions of war. It might lea said, in fact, to assist in all manufacturing industries, and to assist also greatly in facilitating commerce. In point of usefulness, iron took precedence over any manufactured material. The most civilised nations would be found to be those who were most familiar with the use of iron and metals. The litera- ture they had handed down to them respecting iron was very slight, although it was one of the eailiest metals men- tioned. Tubal Cain would be remembered to have been mentioned in the Bible as one of the first artificers in brass and iron, and the metal was mentioned often in the Bible as in common use for implements of war, and also for imple- plements of agriculture and manufacture. The oh! Greek and Latin writers mentioned it frequently. Although iron was so often mentioned, the quantity manufactured must I have been small, and the process by which it must have been made comparatively simple. So far as this country was concerned, it was not quite cer- tain that the ancient Britons knew of the manufacture of iron; but it was pretty certain that the Romans knew of the manufacture of iron in this country because they found in the forest of Dean, and the Weald of Sussex especially large heaps of bloomery cinder, in the 14th and 15th centuries iron was supplied from Spain and Germany, and up to the middle of the 18th century we imported the iron we used from Sweden, and a consider- able quantity was still imported for the purpose of being converted into steel. The date of the introduction of cast- iron was somewhat doubtful, but it was very likely it was introduced in the 14th century. Cannon were first recorded to have been cast in 1543. The rise of the iron manufac- ture as a staple manufacture of this country, and as adding to the national wealth, dated from the employment of coal as fuel. James I. granted a patent in 1611 for the use of sea coal or pit coal, but the process of manufacture as then carried on failed. A relative of Lord Dudley in 1620 ap- plied for and obtained a patent to use pit coal for 21 years, but when he died his process died with him. The next per- son whose name came to be honourably mentioned was Abraham Derby, who had an ironworks of Coalbrook Dale in 1701, and whose grandson erected the first iron bridge in England. :When a " change took place from the use of charcoal to coal or coke a very much more powerful blowing apparatus was required, and proper blowing cylinders were introduced in 1760. In 1740 there appeared to have been about 50 blast furnaces at work. In 1796 the use a wood and charcoal were almost given up. There were then work- ing about 121 blast furnaces, averaging 20 tons a wsek. In 1806 there were 227 blast furnaces which made a quarter of a million tons, and in 1873 there were 700 blast furnaces which made seven million tons. (Applause,) The increase in the quantity of pig iron which was proceeding at a very rapid rate about this time required improvements to be made in the apparatus for converting cast iron into wrought iron. In 1783 grooved rolls were introduced, and in 1784 the puddling process. The first puddling furnace consisted simply of an air furnace with a bed of sand. This process proved wasteful, but was carried on for something like 34 veers, when there was introduced a cast iron bottom puddling furnace with substances to fettle it, so as to keen the iron from melting the bottom of the furnace, and this process was practically that which was carried on at present. The only attempts which had been made to improve the puddling process had been in the direction of employing mechanical power instead of the hand labour which was under ordinary circumstances required by the process. He then proceeded to describe the various attempts by Walker and Warren, Tooth, Danks, Siemens, and Crompton, after which he re- ferred to the process of iron manufacture used in India, and spoke of the modern blast furnaces. He alluded to the great help iron manufacture had derived by the introduction of the steam engine, adverted to the effect the invention of the steam hammer had upon the industry, detailed the Efforts that had been made to utilize the waste gases from the furnaces, and, in conclusion, expressed the hope that im- provements would continue to go on, and that Warrington School of Science might have some:share in bringing about , similar improvements, either in the iron or any other trade ia the country. (Applause.) On the propesition of Councillor Moen's, seconded by Mr. T. Mo.Rßis, a vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer; and a similar compliment having been paid to the Chairman, on the motion of Councillor MOUSER, seconded by the Rev. It. FILCHER, the meeting terminated.
