div.p: THE EXAMINER- SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882 • WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the Council was held on Tues- day evening, at the Town Hall. Present: The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair; Aldermen Thewlis, Harrison, Kean, Webster, Davies, Burgess, and Holmes; Councillors Monks, Barker, Wallington, Dixon, Brown, Greening, Ashton, Taylor, Woolfall, Pierpoint, Mackie, Platt, Wright, Burgess Jeans, Sutton, Fairclough, Milner, Broadbent, Whittle, Collin, Francomb, and Litton; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), and J. Paterson (gas manager).

WATCII COMMITTEE. The MAYOR proposed the confirmation of the minutes of the Watch Committee, and drew attention to the recom- mendation that the Town Clerk apply to the Secretary of State for approval of the appointment of six additional con- stables for the borough. Alderman WEBSTER seconded the proposition, which was carried.

PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.-LATCHFORD DRAINAGE. Alderman KEAN moved, and Councillor WooLFILL seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Alderman ElanntsoN asked whether the ejector that they were constructing in Latchford was quite as successful as they expected. There was a rumour that there was some difficulty to be encountered that they did not dream of when they commenced the scheme._ _ _

Alderman THEWLIS called attention to the abominable state of the Latchford-road, and said it was a great pity indeed that they should have so many cobble stones to travel over. He could not conceive why they could not have pavement similar to what they had in the immediate borough of Warrington. They would very much like to have the tiles introduced.

Alderman HOLMES inquired whether the paving in Queen- street was the only paving which the committee had in con- templation during the ensuing half-year. There was a considerable amount of work to be done in other directions yet. Alderman KEAN was surprised at Alderman Harrison's question with regard to a rumour that the ejectors they were putting down in Latchford were not quite a success. At present they were only sinking the tank, and the difficulty they had had to encounter was quite anticipated. He thought it would be satisfactorily got over, at all events he was assured so by the Borough Surveyor. With regard to Alderman Iheivlis and the want of tiles in Latchford, they had known of it for a long time, but were waiting until a new scheme of sewering was laid down, which would in some measure interfere with the footpath, and afterwards they would have a footpath fit for flag Queen to walk upon. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) As to the question of Alderman Holmes, who wanted to know if all the paving they antici- pated was in Queen-street, it would be almost folly to say it was not. The minutes were then passed. THE SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. Alderman WEBSTER, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, remarked that the estimates were low, and it was gratifying to find that much valuable work was being done at a little cost. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Drxox seconded the resolution which was car- ried.
• place could be found, but he did not think the Fair Ground was a suitable site.

Councillorl3Cl;ESS said Councillor Litton was incorrect in saying that the Deputy Town Clerk advised the Committee it was absolutely necessary that the market should be re- moved. What the Deputy Town Clerk advised was that they must either put the pig market in proper repair or remove it. It was thought itwould be better if it was moved to the FairTiround, which he thought would be quite as convenient as the present site. Councillor MONKS also spoke in favour of removal, and said he would support the committee on its recommenda- tions.

Cauncillor FAincLouvar supported the Markets Committee because he thought the pig market ought to be covered, and that could not be done if the present site were retained. Alderman BROADBEN'T also supported the committee. He thought the nuisance would be less if the market were held at the Fair Ground instead of where it was now, but the question with him was whether it would not be better for the nuisance to remain where it is until they could get a much better site than even the Fair Ground, and one further removed from the heart of the town. Alderman DAVIES questioned whether at any time under any circumstances,Queen-street could be made as available for market purposes as Town Hiil, bEcause the ground was very low and not favourable for being sufficiently sewered. If the market was to be removed at all he thought it ought to be removed te a better site than the Fair Ground. Alderman BURGESS thought the Markets Committee should again reconsider the question. He pointed out that the Inspector's letter was dated the 25th July, which was a Tuesday, and maintained that on a Tuesday Town Hill could not be found in the state the Inspector described. Probably, however, the letter had been mistranscribed. He jocularly suggested that the Com- mittee should again consider the desirability of the market being removed to the vicinity of the Town Hall, for he b.ilieved such had been proposed, though one objection was that it would be too near to the Guardian Office. (Laughter.) Councillor PIERPOINT was in favour of removal, but to a better site than the Fair Ground.

Councillor PLATT suggested that the present site should be put in thorough repair. He reminded the Council that there was a probability of the Canal scheme to con- nect Manchester with Liverpool, being carried through, and if that were so, then Warrington might become a central market for almost the whole kingdom. It would then be eminently situated for that purpose. Councillor MACKIE closed the discussion. He defended the action of the Government Inspector, twitted some of the opponents of removal with their consideration for vested interests, and contended that the proper course to adopt was to remove the nuisance.

The Council then divided, with the following result : For the Amendment : His Worship the Mayor; Aldermen Holaus, Burgess, Webster, Harrison, and Kean; and Coun- cillors Sutton, Platt, Litton, Greening, Barker, Pierpoint, Jeans, Woolfall, Taylor, Brown, Francomb, Collins, Ashton, Wright, and Whittle-21. Against: Alderman Thewlis and Councillors Mackie, Burgess, Broadbent, Fairclough, Monks, Dixon, and Wallington—S. The motion was therefore lost, and the amendmmt was then carried on the substantive motion.
and that in strictness they ought to have employed a pro- fessional man. But inasmuch as Mr. Lougdin had had to do the work in his own time they recommended the gratuity._

The -MAYoR stated that since Mr. Longdin wis appointed at L2:30 a year his work had been very much increased. He knew for a fact that Mr. Longdin had done tne work in con- nection with the map in the small hours of the night, and he did not think £l5O was more than the Borough Surveyor richly deserved for the work he had done.

THE RATES. On the proposition of Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Councillor FAIRCLOUGH, the estimates for the borough rate amounting to £4,293 103. 9d. was confirmed, as were also the estimates for the improvement and sewers rates, and it was decided to make rates of is. 6d. and 2d. in the £ respectively. The Council then rose.

div.head: MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE.

Councillor GREENING moved the adoption of the minutes of this Committee, pointing out that there had been several important gifts to the Nuseum. Councillor BIIIIGNISS seconded the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor Pierpoint asked what method was adopted as to the purchase of books—whether they were got by tender or by private order? Alderman WEngrEn : We don't buy new books as a rule—we generally buy them from the catalogues. The minutes were then carried. THE CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
On the motion of Alderman THEWLIS, seconded by Coun- cillor Baowz.r, the minutes of the Cemetery Committee were passed.
THE. TOWN HALL, PARK, AND _BATHS COMMITTBR.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of this Committee, the MAYOR observed that the Council would notice that a recommendation that the sum of three guineas be given to each of the bands for playing in the Park during the sum- mer months. He thought no one in the town would grudge that small sum being given to the members of the bands for the music they had given to the ratepayers in the borough. He took that opportunity of drawing attention to a pro- posed concert in aid of the funds of the Infirmary by work- ingmen, which he thought was deserving of their support. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the motion, which was then carried. THE SUGGESTED REMOVAL OF THE PIG MARKET. _ _ _

Councillor MACKIE, in the absence of the chairman of the Markets Committee, moved the adoption of that committee's minutes. He observed that the question of the removal of the pig market had received full consideration at the hands of the committee, and they had come to the conclusion to recommend to tire Council that the market be removed to that portion of the fair ground adjoining the fire engine station, and that necessary steps for cleansing and sewering be taken. • The cost, he thought, would be some- thing like 2100, and it would be left to some future day to decide whether any special arrangements should be made to protect the pig dealers from the weather. He hoped the change would be unanimously agreed to, and thereby provide a very useful and reApectable bedy of tradesmen with a , much more healthy site for carrying on their business. I Councillor WALLINGTON seconded the motion.

Councillor SUTTON observed, amid much laughter, that the Markets Committee so often changed their opinions that it was necessary before the Council decided upon the removal of the pig market, that they should know what the committee proposed to do with the other portion of the land. They had never yet heard that the people round about .the pig market had suffered through the pigs being there; on the other hawl, they always understood that the neighbourhood of the Town Hill had been quite as healthy as any other part of Warrington. (Hear' hear.) If the market was to be removed to the Fair Ground be would like to know what provision was to be made for the fairs in future and for the potato market. He would propose as an amendment, "That the minutes be passed. with the exception of the recommendation respecting the Town Hill pig market.

—Councillor TAYLOR had much pleasure in seconding the amendment, remarking that he did not think they could have a better site for the convenience of both vendors and purchas2rs than Town Hill. A canvas of the residents in the neighbourhood had been made, and there was but one complaint among the whole of them. A great many of the dealers had expressed the determination not to go to another part of the town if the market was removed. Councillor PLATT asked if Councillor Sutton objected entirely to the removal of the market. Councilor SurTroN said as the case at present stood it was necessary to object to both recommendations of the committee until they brought out a proper scheme. Alderman lionmEs supported the amendment and said the complaint as to the unhealthiness of the district near to the present market fell to the ground. It was a serious thing to remove a market like that, and there were interests which ti.ey ought to attend to. Until the Markets Committee could show some better reason for its removal he would certainly vote against it being removed from its present site. He had in his hand a memorial signed by GO persons in the district who objected to its removal. Councillor LITTON observed that the proposal to remove the pig market did not emanate from the committee, but through the letters from the Inspector that had been pub- lished. They were advised by the Deputy Town Clerk that it was absolutely necessary the market should be removed, and it was with considerable reluctance they selected a por- tion of the Fair Ground. They were told by the Borough 'Surveyor that to put Town Hill in a suitable condition would cost as much as it would to put the fair ground in a condition for a pig market, and after serious consideration they decided that there was nothing else but to adopt it. Alderman HARRISON did not put the same interpretation upon the letter as Councillor Litton. He did not see a word in it:which justified the Markets Committee in assuming that there was compulsion about it. Councillor LITTON: We were advised so. Alderman HARRISON (resuming) said he would support the amendment, and agreed with Alderman Holmes that they should be very careful how they interfered with vested interests. There was a very strong feeling in the district against its removal, and he hoped Dr. Mackie would con- sent to allow the minutes to pass with the exception of those mentioned.

Councillor DIXON said there was not a member of the committee who personally wanted to remove the pig etarket until the letter was sent. They thought there was no other course to adopt but put Town Hill in a sanitary condition or remove the market, and the cost would be about the same for either. He knew that complaints had been made about it and about the dirt connected with it in its present posi- tion. He had no personal feeling in the matter, but after the trouble the committee had been put to he thought they would be anxious that the minutes should pass in the form presented to the Council. Councillor FRANcomn supported the amendment, as he did not think that the time had, yet cones when they ought to interfere with the pig market. It was a capital thing, no doubt, to remove a nuisance from the midst of a lot of cottages, but when they considered the central position of the present pig market and the improvements made during the last few years, he thought it would be better to wait until some future occasion before they interfered with it. He did not think that the committee had a proper scheme to lay before them at the present time. Councillor WOOLFALL was not ashamed to say that be had lived for about 20 years in the immediate vicinity of the pig market, but he never heard any complaint about it. Alderman KEAN said that whether the pig market was removed or not, Tcwn Hill must be put in a sanitary condi- tion. (Hear, hear.) They would not get rid of the matter by removing the pig market. He would advise them to turn their attention to that part of the town, and to allow the poor pigs to remain where they had been so long. - -

Co un cil lor WALLINGTON protested emphaticall v against the charge brought against the committee by Councillor Sutton, that they had been changeable. He did not think it proper that a market like the pig market should be in the centre of the town. He thought it would be better on the Fair Ground, where there was ample space for the'pig market and the shows if they came. Alaerman WEBSTER maintained that it would be better if the matter received some further consideration, and would support the amendment. Councillor GREENING said he would very much like to see the market removed from its present position if a better

div.head: MISCELLINEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLINEOUS.
Street Improvement and Lighting, and Finance Commit- tee proceedings were confirmed— without comment.
SANITARY COMMITTEE: THE REMOVAL OF NIGHT SOIL. Alderman BURGESS moved, and Councillor BARKER se- conded, the adoption of the minutes.

Councillor FIiANCOMB, referring to a resolution that the removal of pails solely in the night time was impracticable, said he.was very glad that the matter had been breught for- ward, but he did not think at the present time the commit- tee were in a position to remove the pails in the night time. As soon as they got over the difficulty at Longford they would be in a position to remove the vans entirely from the streets during the day time, and if they could remove the vans in a town the size of Birmingham he did not see why they could not do the same in Warrington. Councillor DIXON asked if he was to understand that no vans were to be seen in Birmingham during the day. He was there the other day and met two or three, .but if the statement was correct he was afraid his eyesight had got very defective. (Laughter.) Councillor FRANCOMB said be had been to Birmingham twice, and each time he had been to the sanitary work in the night time purposely to see how things were worked. He believed it was an understood thing there that the vans turned out at night. Councillor BURGESS gbserved that he took the trouble to make enquiries as to what was done at Birmingham, and was informed by letter that the ordinary nightsoil was removed in the night time, but the street dust was removed in the day time, and that would probably explain the differ- ence in the statements. He hoped before long the com- mittee would see their way to do the work in the night time.

Alderman BURGESS said the resolution was a unanimous one in reply to a communication from the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority, and it was a true statement of the case. In Warrington it was utterly impracticable to remove in the night time the contents of the pails. When he was at Bir- mingham he asked if they removed the pails in the night time, and the answer was, "So far as we can we do, but what we cannot remove in the night time we have to do in tho day time. But there is this addition: It costs us a very great deal more to do what we are doing than if we were removing in the day time entirely." The committee would take cars that people of properly constituted mind had nothing to be offended at—(hear, hear,)—but he was not prepared to ask the ratepayers to pay a very largely increased charge for the removal of the nightsoil merely to meet the sentimental views of people, which were so utterly imprac- ticable.
The minutes were pls3ed. THE CONDITION OF THE GAS 'AMPS.
Alderman HOLMES proposed, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Gas Corn- mittee.
Councillor DIXON a4ain drew attention to the want of a gas lamp at the top of Parker-street, and said he would be glad if the Chairman of the Committee would see that the lamps were kept clean.

Alderman Ho Lugs, in reply, said the lamps were attended to regularly by a staff of men who were employed to go round the town every day to clean them. Any complaint would be attended to at once, but no complaint had been made prior to this by Councillor Dixon. The minutes were passed.

div.head: PROPOSED TRAMWAYS.-MR. LONGDIN'S SERVICES
div.p: THE PROPOSED TRAMWAYS.-MR. LONGDIN'S SERVICES

The MAYon, in moving the adoption of the General Pur- poses Committce's minutes, said they had had several appli- cations—he thought B—for permission to supply the town with electricity, but they would come before the committee aid be dealt with. Ile referred to the recommendation that the application of Mr. C. S. Pain for permission to lay tram- ways be entertained subject to the details of the work pro- posed t,-) be done being approved by the committee, and sathfactory arrangements being made for power to purchase, and remarked that the matter was under consideration.

Councillor MACKIE seconded, and expressed -pfea‘s-U; that there was a prospect of having tramways in Warrington. Councillor WHITTLE alluded to the recommendation that £175 be paid for extra surveying—.£1.50 to Mr. Longdin and £25 tO his assistants. Haitad always understood that Mr. Longdin MB expected to devote the whole of his time to the duties of his offiu, and did not see how they could pay him for extra services.

Councillor PLATT said he would like to be assured that satisfactory arrangements had been made whereby the Council would have the power to purchase the tramways. He also suggested that the Application for permission to supply the electric light should be refused, and arrange- ments made for keeping the supply in the hands of the Cor- poration. Councillor FRANCOMB thought the chairman should explain what that £l5O was to be given to Mr. Longdin. (Hear, hear.) He believed Mr. Longdin to be one of the most hard-working servants in the town, but at the same time the ratepayers would be more satisfied if they knew what he had actually done for them. Alderman BURGESS sympathised with the observations in reference to the £l5O to be givon to Mr. Longdin. He did not know upon what ground it was justified. Mr. Longdin had not been very many years iu the service of the Corpo- ration, and he had risen in price much more rapidly than any other gentleman that he had known in his long expe- rience of the Corporation. He thought the matter required explanation.

Alderman HARRISON believed if Alderman Burgess were to contrast bills for paving materials with what they were before Mr. Longdin's time, he would he surprised at the im- mense saving that had been effected through Mr. Longdin's instrumentality alone. He believed that every penny Mr. Longdin g)t from them he richly deserved, and he did not think they bad a more indefatigable servant. The services proposed to be paid for were services rendered outside the hours, which he had devoted to the discharge of his public duties, and he believed Mr. Longdin had sat up night after night, for two years, doing work which would have cost the Council three times the amount of money they proposed to give, if it had been done by anyone else. Alderman MEWL'S thought Mr. Longdin richly deserved the money. Councillor BURGESS called attention to the important) recommendation in regard to tramways. He agreed that there should be trarnways, but he thought the Council ought to consider carefully before they adopted a scheme which would take tramways along Sankey, Bridge, Horsemarket, and Buttermarket streets. The streets are very narrow, and he was quite certain tramways could not be put down there without impeding the traffic very considerably. He would be glad to hear some explanation in reference to the matter. Councillor BROADBENT thought the Council might be assured that the work by Mr. Longdin had been very well done, and that if it had been done by any other surveyor it would have cost them very much more money. Alderman HOL3IES stated that only six members were present at the coinmittee meeting at which the recommenda- tion was agreed to, and he thought it had been done very irregularly, as it certainly ought not to have been done with- out notice to the members. Alderman BUBGIESS believed these gratuities ought to be put an end to. Mr. Longdin was appointed at a salary of £250, and in four years his salary had been advanced twice, and was now £4OO. He believed that already two or three gratuities of considerable amounts had been presented to Mr. Lone-din, and now the Council were asked to contribute another £l5O. Councillor WALLINGTON thought this a large amount, aLd that they ought to be careful how they gave gratuities. Alderman HARRISON remarked that what stimulated the committee to.reCornmend the gratuity was that it formed no portion of Mr. Longdin's work to fill up this ordnance map,

div.head: LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS. UNETED GATHERING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS. UNETED GATHERING AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday, the first united gathering of the members of the Warrington lodges of the Loyal Order of Shepherds (Ashton Unity) took place in the DIM Hall, Batk-street. The members, with their wives and sweethearts numbering about 300, sat down to an excellent knife and fork tea, catered by Mrs. Butterworth, Ram's Head Hotel, Horse- market-street. After the tea a meeting was held, over which Bro. Win. Stirrup, P.P.C.S., presided. He was supported by Bro. Edward Mayson, Chief Shepherd, (Burscough Bridge); Bro. James Farron (Ashton-under-Lyne), Cor. Sec. ; Bro. Abel H. Mather, Pro. Cor. Sec.; Bro. James Delocze, P.P.C.S; Bro. John B. Archibald (Ashton-under- Lyne), P.P.C.S., editor of the Order's magazine; Bro. L. Gillooly, P.P.C.S; Bro. C. Burton, P.M.; Bro. Alban Stirrup, P.P.C.S.; Bro. L. Weir, P.P.C.S.; Dr. Cannell, &c. The feature of the evening was the presentation to Bro. Farron, chief secretary of the society for 15 years, of a handsome illuminated address, richly framed in English gilt. - _ _

The CORRESPONDING SECRETARY (Bro. Abel H. Mather) intimated that he had received apologies for non-attendance from Mr. McMinnies, M.P., Sir G. Greenall, Colonel Green- all,7Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. Joseph Davies, Captain Litton, and Bro. John Ward, P.C.S. He was glad to inform them that he had received from some of the gentlemen handsome subscriptions in aid of their funds. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN then proceeded with the toast list, and after the loyal toasts had been given, and received with acclamation, he proposed that of "The bishops and clergy of all denominations," to which Bro. EDWD. MlTsoti suitably responded.

The toast of the "Warrington district" followed, and Bro. ABEL H. MATHER, who responded, said on occasions like that the secretary was expected to read to them the annual -balance sheet ; but this year the District Committee, in order to oblige a large number of members who could not attend their lodges to hear the annual balance sheet read, had deemed it advisable to get it printed for presentation to the members. He would, therefore, confine himself to a few of the principal items in the report of 1881, which were as follows :—The receipts for sick and funeral funds were £2,060 7s. 7d.; received for contributions and entrance fees, £Bl2 19s. 4P.; bank interest, £49 3a. 11d. The amount of money expended for medical aid was £ll9 lei. 3d., for sick- ness £4BO 55., and for deaths or funerals £l2O, leaving a balance in favour of the sick and funeral fund in December Ist, 1881. of £2,242 15s. 84., which wai a gain upon the year of £193 lie. 24. The total number of members up to December 31, 1881, was 986. They had a fund in their district which he thought rather strange in connection with a society like theirs—the Juveniles' Educational Fund. The fund was particularly for the benefit of those families from whom the "bread winner" had been taken away. The fund was established on April sth, 1879, and was supported by a levy of 24 per year upon each member in the district. Since its establishment they had paid for school fees £7 5s sd, and he had a balance in favour of the fund of £l9 3s 54. They were at the present time'payin,g the fees of nine chil- dren, who were being educated at the Heath-side, the Catholic, and Wycliffe scools. He sincerely hoped the fund would prosper—in fact, it was the duty of all present for the sake of their country and themselves to look after the edu- cation of the rising generation. (Applause.) Bro. PARR, Pro. CS., also responded, and, referring to the increase of members, said that the Warrington district had lately opened a new lodge, now numbering 40 members, which promised to be very prosperous. The CHAIRMAN gave the toast "The Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds, which was enthusiastically re- ceived.
Bro. EDWARD MATSON responded, and pointed out the benefits of such societies as theirs.

Bro.JamEs FAnnoN ( Ashton-unler-Lyne) also responded. He observed that the Order of Shepherds comprised about 70,000 members and nearly 30,000 wfves and widows. It had extended to all the principal towns in England, Scot- land, Ireland, and America, was gradually growing in esteem, and was doing a vast amount of good. Seventy-thousand members meant something like t 70,000 a year of an inCome ; and between £30,000 and £40,000 a year was paid for sick and funeral money, leaving out large incidentals given in the shape of keep to the unfortunate; and also a large amount of money spent in gifts to brethren passing from one town to another, looking for employment. In addition to these sums there were many private gifts by lodges and districts to men who had met with accidents, or who had become in- firm with age; or who were suffering from some afiliction which disabled them from following their occupation. They would therefore perceive that the Order in itself was one that commended itself to their judgment, aid, and respect. It was known to all of them that societies existed throughout the length and breadth of this country. There were secieties of every kind where there were trades and working people. The affiliated societies themselves were very extensive. Taking these societies alone they now numbered 4 millions, of members, with funds approaching 121- millions of pounds. He thought he would not be far wrong if he said that their accumulated funds at the present time were very little short of 13 millions of pounds. He would like them to understand that those affiliated societies were composed mainly of the operative classes, and from them men had arisen who had laid the foundation and raised the superstructure to such a grand degree that it now commanded the esteem and careful consideration of the most opulent of the country. It was that vast amount of money, in addition to the vast amount of influence exercised by those societies, which had caused the Government to take cognizance of their condii.ion. Like a wise parent, the Government had acted wisely, in his judgment, in protect- ing that large amount of money, and by taking care that the funds were appropriated for the right purpose. Legis- lation had so far engaged to protect their funds that now he who defrauded the workingman, or he who misappropriated the funds, was immediately taken hold of and punished by the law, which was not the case before. There might be some present not connected with that society who might ask what was the advantage to be obtained from the society. The advantage Ivas that 70,000 saw it. A man became a member, and after he had been enrolled G or 12 months he became entitled to claim upon all the funds according to the rules. For 2s. per month a man received 10s. a week if sick for six months. Was not that a grand help to a man who had been laid up with affliction for the whole six months? 10s. a week, with some other little help, he posi- tively declared under the able management of some of their housewives, without whom they could do but little, would keep the wolf from the door the whole of the time. (Ap- plause.) It was a well known fact that scarcely a member of an affiliated society ever sought parish relief; and if all the poor people would join friendly societies, burial boards might be banished for ever. (Loud applause.) The Chairman next called upon Brother JAMES DELoozs, who made the presentation to Brother Farron. He said he could assure Brother Farron that so impressed were the members with the advice given to them by him on the oc- casion of his visit to their annual tea party last year that he felt they would not be doing their duty unless they pre- sented to him some token of respect. Though they had not had the opportunity of seeing Brother Farron often, they had had the pleasure of seeing and knowing the way in which he had through life discharged the various important duties of his office, and they trusted that he might be spared many years to come, to work for the good of the Order. (Applause.) The address reads as toilets : "To Tames Farron, Esq.—Esteemed sir and brother,—On this occasion of your Second visit amongst us, we, the members of the Olive Branch Lodge, Warrington District, Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds, Ashton Unity, cannot, allow the oppor- tunity to pass without expressing our great respect for you as a brother and a Christian, and our appreciation of the valuable services you have rendered to the Order for a period of half a century, fifteen years of which you have -with great credit filled the honourable position of chief secre- tary. There are many brethren In this district who have personally had frequent opportunities of witnessing the able and impartial manner in which you discharge the various duties of your office. The kindness and geneali!y you d,splay towards all w:th wh nu you come in contact has c&usel your name to be beloved wherever Shepherdy exists. We earnestly pray the Almighty may long spare you to your worthy wife and family, and that y u may continue to render that valuable assistanc • to our noble Order which you have always so freely and so faithfully given We remain, dear sir, yours fraternally, William Stirrup (chairman), James Del .ose (secretary), Edward Bdwardson, Charles Burton, William Edwards, Joseph Adams, and William Gallaghan (committee). Warrington, September 3-th, 1882."

He begged Bro. Farron to accept the address, not for its intrinsic value, but as a mark of the respect in which he was held by each member of the Lodge. Brother FARRON,in acknowledging the presentation, spoke under emotion. He said he did not anticipate such kind- ness. He came to Warrington out of good will, out of high respect to the rnemers of the Warrington district, and strong regard for the welfare of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds. When he cime last year he came with the same feeling that prompted him that day. The warm affection and high respect exhibited by the members of the Warrington district, made the visit a very agreeable one to him. He very willingly accepted the present, because he believed it was the expression of kindly feeling, and had it been worth £l,OOO Ito could not have received it with a warmer expression of gratitude and respect to the brethren. He assured them that memento would have a prominent place in his home, and would be handed down to his family when he was no more. (Ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN then proposed the "Widows, Orphans, and Juvenile society."
Bro. JAMES DELOOAE, in responding, said the contribution to the widows and orphans' fund was only 7d per quarter per member, with an entrance fee. It comprised at present about

75 members, with a balance of £9O in hand. The Juvenile Burial Society was composed of about 11,000 members, with £290 to its credit, having paid during the present year £ll4 alone in death claims, as against £75 during the last year. Both funds were going on satisfactorily. "Success to the Magazine " was proposed by the CHAIR- MAN, and responded to by the EDITOR, Bro. JOHN B. ARCHI- BALD, ; and after Dr. CANNELL had briefly res- ponded for " the medical profession," Bro. L. WEIR proposed that the best thanks of the meet- ing be given to Colonel Greenall, and the officers of the North Lancashire Rifle Voluntaers, for kindly lending them the use of the Drill Hall.—The motion was carried with acclamation.
The meeting afterwards closed, and the room was cleared for dancing, which was indulged in until about 11 o'clock to the strains of the Volunteer band, under the leadership of Sergeant Newns.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting on Wednesday, Mr. G.aßlack- burst presided, and there were present :—The Rev. G. F. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Houghton, Brown, Greening, Greenall, Longshaw, Bonnell, Burn, Darbyshire, Taylor, Woolfall, Garnett, leilshall, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

div.head: ADDITIONS TO THE NEW SCHOOLS.
div.p: ADDITIONS TO THE NEW SCHOOLS.

The minutes of the Building Committee stated that the analysis of water by Dr. Campbell Brown was read and certified by him and approved. The architect submitted a plan of committee reception room and lavatory attached, and It was recommended that same be approved and submitted to the Local Government Board for approval. The com- mittee having considered the several tenders submitted to them, and circumstances connected with the tender of Mr. Napier, making it undesirable toaccept same,recommended the accept- ance of Mr. Porter's tender of £1,897, and the payment of 63 per yard for extra concrete foundations. The committee further recommended that a covenant be made in the agree- ment with the contractor that, in respect of all extras and additions to the work set forth in the plans, and in respect of all deductions therefrom, payment or a reduction be made in respect of such extras, or deductions according to measure- ment and valuation by the architects. The tender of Jas. Newton for carting brickbats and cinders to Padgate was accepted.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Major CARTWRIGHT again maintained that more homes !would still be required. —The CRAIR3IAN gave Major Cartwright credit for being the only person who had not been deceived as to the cost of the schools.—Mr. DABBYSHIRE stated that the country Guardians drove to the schools, and they would have to erect a small stable and shed, and he was sure there would have to be a pigstye. (L tughter). The schools would not be complete without these additions, and he hoped they would have enough money to erect them without borrowing more.—Mr. BROWS said they had not yet made provision for storing straw for mattresses.—The CHAIIMAN : I thought you were doing away with straw mattresses.—Mr. Bgowx : You won't have to do.—The minutes were passed.

THE WASHING DIFFICULTY SETTLED. Mr. BROWN moved the adoption of the minutes of the Schools Committee, and in doing so said he thought it only fair to Mrs. Mackey to refer to a minute which had appeared in the papers abOut the washing. The impression from that minute appeared to be that Mrs. Mackey had not done the washing at all. That, however, was not the case. Mrs. Mackey had done the washing required for the schools, such as sheets, ese., and it had been well done. The only matter which the committee had had to complain of had been the locality where the washing had been done. The com- mittee and officers at the schools had not wanted the washing done at the Barracks, neither had they wanted Mrs. Mackey on the premises. (Hear, hear).—Mr. LONGSHAW seconded the motion.—The ChERIC then read the following entry which appeared ma the House Committee's book:— Mrs. Mackey appeared before the. committee and com- plained of the misrepresentation that was made at the last Board meeting, and reported in the newspapers, that she had refused to do the washing for the Barracks schools. She utterly denies that it is the case, and that ever since she was instructed to see that it was done, it has been done. She also complains that she has not been asked to appear before the Board to explain the whole matter."—Major CART- WRIGHT, in proposing the confirmation of the minutes, re- marked that Mrs. Mackey considered she had had an injus- tic done to her by the report, and the gentlemen whose names were attached to the minute considered so too. They did so simply for the reason that she never had refused to do the washing. Ever since the Board gave instructions for the work to be done the linen had been attended to. The principal cause of complaint was that instead of Mrs. Mackey doing the work as ordered by the Board she had done it down at the 2arracks. Well, she complained that the Board wanted her to do impossibilities ; and she had satisfied the House Committee she could not do the work under the circumstances. There were complaints that the blankets had not been washed, but those blankets had not been sent to the House before that morning, and no doubt now they would be washed in duo course.—The CHAIRMAN here read the following letter from Mrs. Mackey :—" Gentlemen,—l was-greatly surprised when reading the report of your proceedings in the paper of te- day, concerning the Barracks' washing. It conveys the impression that the work has not been done, which is incor- rect. I should like an opportunity of explaining that every article which has been sent to Me I have had washed regu- larly, and handed over clean. When I was unable to do it at the Workhouse I went to the Barracks and did it there, and, in fact, at the time the matter was reported to you the clean sheets were on the beds. In conclusion, I beg to say the weekly washing lists will prove the truthfulness of my statement. I regret that I should be subjected to such mis- representation."—The CHAIRMAN (to the Clerk): Will you tell us what the complaint was?—The CLERIC explained that although the Board had said the particular washing sent to the Workhouse should be done there, the matron, with tube, utensils, arrt persons for washing, proceeded to do that which the Be trd said she should not do, and which the Local Goverr.nent Board said they were justified in sly- ing.—Mr. (; itERNING then moved, and Mr. BONNELL seconded tlat Mrs. Mackey be called into the room.—Mr. BONNELL asked how long the machinery had been out of order, and whether it had now been put in order. He thought it hardly fair that they should condemn Mrs. Mackey until that question had been answered.—Major CA RTWRIGHT stated that the Board had delayed obtaining estimates for the repair of the machinery, and Mr. Stephen Moss, who had had the work in hand only completed it on Friday last. —Mr. BONNELL thought the House Committee were to blame in the matter.—The CHAIRMAN never could accept Mrs. Mackey's explanation inasmuch as she could go to the schools, take women evith her, and stay the whole of the day washing, and surely if she could do that at the Barracks she could do it at the House.—Mr. LONGSHAW, in the couse of a few observations, said they had had the washing question before them so often, the public would think the Guardians were only a lot of old washerwomen. (Laughter.)—Mr. DARBYSHIRE said Mrs. Mackey had persistently refused to obey the orders of the Board since June, and if she continued to disobey the orders of the Board they eught to suspend her. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. GREENING denied that any blame rested with the House Committee, and said the committee had been anxious to get the washing done, but when Mrs. Mack, y told them she could not do the work they were bound o believe her. (Hear, hear.)—Mrs. Mackey was then called in, and the CHAIRMAN, addressing her, said there had been instructions given in regard to the washing, and it did not appear that they had keen carried out. Mrs. Mackey said something in •her letter aboat some changes in reference to the work. He did not think any changes had been made about the work. It was a well known fact she had done it; but what the Board complained of was that they had ordered work to be done at the house which she persisted in doing at the Barracks. It appeared to the Guardians that if she could do the work at the Barracks she could do it at the Workhouse.—The MATRON said she did the washing at the Workhouse as long as she possibly could, and when she found it impossible to do it there she went down to the Barracks and did it.—The CHAIRMAN: •But you see they have no convenience at all at the Barracks for washing. It is only a temporary place. You have all the convenience here, and if your machinery was broken *down, could you not with the staff have done it at the house ?—The MATRON: No, sir; I could not.—The CHAIRMAN : Why? —The MATRON replied that what machinery she had was not sufficient to do the washing required for the house. If she had not taken the women she employed to the Barracks they would have interfered with her washing, because there was no room for them at the house, and she had been put to great inconvenience to do the washing for the inmates of the house. She occupied the washhouse from Monday morning until Saturday afternoon, and was not able to do all the washing she had.—Mr. BONNELL: Could you have done the washing if you had had the machinery in good working order ?—The MATRON: Not until I had completed my own blankets. The CHAIRMAN said the Matron had not done what the Board had ordered her to do. The MATRON said she had always done her duty, and had done more extra duty than any other officer connected with the Board.—The CHAIRMAN said that really was not the question. The question was whether she had obeyed the lawful orders of the Board.—The MATRON said she did not consider she had disobeyed any order of the Board.—Mr. DARBYSIIIRE main- tained that there was plenty of room at the Workhouse to do the washing, but the fact was the matron did not want to do it there.—The MATRON remarked that she had never said she did not want to do it. and rather than the children should suffer from the want of clean linen she had gone to the Barracks to wash it. There had been no determination on her part not to do the washing at the house, because it was an utter impossibility to do it.—After further discussion, the MATRON said that if the Board avould allow her to con- tinue to wash at the Barracks a fortnight longer she would be able to do the work at the house afterwards, and on the motion of Mr. BONNELL, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the explanation of Mrs. Mackey was accepted, and the subject dropped.—This was all the business of interest.

THE NEWTON (RUGBY) FOOTBALL CLUB.—The annual meeting of the members of the Newton FoAball.Club has been held at the Millstone Inn, Newton. The officers for the ensuing season were appointed as follows :—President, A. C. McCorquodale, Eq.; vice-president, T. Stone. Esq. ; captain Ist team, George Lane; vice-captain, T. Massey; captain 2nd team, J. Rimmer ; Messrs. J. Appleton, C. Arnott, R. Barclay, J. Boardman, T. Braddock, A. J. Croughton, S. J. Hewitt, W. Lane, G. McCormick, ani G. Wood, were appointed as committee; Mr. T. Appleton hon. treasurer, and Mr. T. Fairclougli hon. secretary.
