div.head: LIBERAL SOIREE AT WIDNES.
div.p: LIBERAL SOIREE AT WIDNES.
MEErING IN THE VOLUNTEER HALL.

On Monday evening a soiree and public meeting, in con- nection with Widnes Liberal Association, was held. Tea was provided in Lacey-street school-room, and was"partaken of by several hundred people. Subsequently a meeting was bold in the Veltanteer Hall. There was a large audience, which included a number of ladies, and the proceedings passed off with conscderable eclat. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the chairman of the Association, presided, and he was supported on the platform by the Rev. Charles Beard, of Liverpool; Messrs. F. H. Gossage, E. Carey, R. Shaw, Holbrook Gaskell, jun., ef Taylor, J. Tallon, P. Tallon, and H. B. shores (secretery). The CHAIRMAN called upon Mr. Shores, the secretary of the association. te read the following communication : "Woolton Wood, lid October, 1852. My dear Carey,-1 am sorry I cannot be with you this evening. I returned home on Sattoday, and do not feel equal to attend a public meeting in the evening jest now. I am not well. Please make my excuses, and present my good wishes and cordial greeting to our Liberal friends at Widnes, and believe me, ever yours faithfully, HOLBROOK GISKELL." Mr. Powell, the secretary of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Associa- tion, telegraphed as follows :—" Sorry cannot be with you this evening. Hope you will pass strong resolutions in favour of procedure rules, and in support of great Liberal leader." (Hear, heir.) The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheering, then addressed the meeting. The time which they had selected for the meeting was, he thought, a very opportune one, as they had to celebrate the triumphs and success of the Government in Egypt, and also to do what they could to aid the Government in passing the procedure rules in the autumn session of Parliament. Whatever view might be taken of the necessity of the war in Egypt, he thought all Liberal's would be of opinion that the manner in whieh the cam- paign had been carried out refi cted great credit upon the present Government as administrators. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) It showed, at any rate, that in the administrative department, they far excelled the Tories. (Hoar, hear, and laughter.) Now, the Tories, their immediate opponents in this district, had for a lone time been quiescent. It was a considerable time since they held a public reeeting. As far as he could recollect what was said on the occasion, Major Cross descanted upon "Fair Trade," and other speakers spoke of the blunders of the Government, and of their peace at any price policy, alleging that the Government was unable to sustain the glory of the Empire. The Fair Trade clues- tion did not seem to meet with that response which the Tories evidently expected; but the accusation of the dis- graceful conduct of the Government, and the peace-at-any- price policy, which the Tories throughout the country as- cribed to the Government, because they withdrew from the unjust wars which had been entered into by their pre- decessors, had evidently been withdrawn, or, at any rate, the Tories had spoken very little about it since the success of the campaign in Egypt. The Central Tory Organisation, however, had begun to move, thinking the time had now come when they should resume all their attacks on the Government. Lord Salisbury's fiasco might perhaps give Sir Stafford Northcote a greater chance as a leader of the Tory Party, but he (the chairman) drought if they could accept the utterances of a member of the Hones of Peers—Lord Car- narvon—they might conclude that our hereditary legislators remain, what they ever had remained, unable to judge of the signs of the times. Lord Carnarvon was certainly not one of the most stupid of what was called the stupid party, which he represented, and he informed an audience, com- posed, it was said,—he did not know with what truth—of workingmen, who were a most intelligent audience—(hear, hear)—that the Tory party rere supported by three-fourths of the literary power and four-fifths of the intellectual power of the country. Before anyone made a statement of that kind he ought certainly to have considered the question; he ought to have told whether that extraordinary prepon- derance of ability in the Tory party had only taken place since Lord Beaconsfield, then Mr. Disraeli, spoke of having educated the party. (A. laugh.) Bet, however, that might be, if what Lord Carnarvon said was true, it was astonishing hog that extraordinary amount of ability had been wasted'. Alnheir literary ability as far as he (the chairman) could see, had been exercised in the abuse of Mr. Gladstone, and the effect of that abuse continued daily and weekly, had been to make the glorious leader of the Liberal party more popular than ever. (Hear, hear.) Then if they looked to the results of the writing, and the intellectual ability with which the Tories treated political subjects, they most "find that pretty nearly everything which they prophe- sied had been falsified by the result. They had told us that the policy of the Liberal party, particularly as regarded Ire- land, was one of spoliation and confiscation, and yet the Tories in that House where they had a large majority had been compelled to pass measures which the Liberal Govern- ment had passed. He might say that Lord Cameroon seemed to belong, like a former leader of the Tory party, to what Lord Derby said was the pre-scientific age. When we reasoned in science we judged by results, and if the re- sults of the exercise of the powers of the Tory party were so puerile as they appeared to be then we must conclude that the ability aad power claimed by Lord Cirnaryon was wanting. But it was also extraordinary that if they had such a large amount of literary power, their papers, at any rate in the northern division of this country, did not seem to be more' prosperous. The charges of bad conduct against the Liberal party, and that it was the party of confiscation and spoliation, had been silenced by the manner in which the Government had carried on the cam- paign in Egypt. Although we might coma to the conclusion that the Tory party was the stupid party, and they were told by an eminent German poet that With stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain," still the Liberals knew from past experience that if they were only true to themselves they would be able to conquer in spite of the stupidity of the Tory party. If they only supported the Government in the procedure rules, which they -were about to bring forward in the autumn session of Parliament, they would have as a result legislation on the subject of county government, extension of the franchise in the counties, and complete reform of the land laws, which would tend to the contentment and prosperity of the nation. (Cheers.) Mr. ROBERT &raw' president of die Runcorn Liberal As3ociation, moved the following resolution: "That this meeting expresses its hearty satisfaction with the success- ful and speedy termination of the war in Egypt, and records its full confidence in the pledges given by Her Majesty's Government, that in the settlement of the questions in- volved they will have regard to the security and develop- ment of the liberties and self-government of the Egyptian people—(hear, hear)—the safety of our communication with India by means of the Suez Canal, and the maietenance of those interests which, in common with all the states of Ewope, this country has in the establishment of peace, order, and prosperity in Egypt; and this meeting earnestly trusts that Her Majesty's Government will, during the coming autumn session, he enabled to pass such rules of procedure for the House of Commons as will restore the efficiency of the House as an instrument of legislation." (Hear, bear, and applause). If he remembered anything of the Liberal party, remarked Mr. Shaw, and if he remembered anything of Liberal professions, he thought that Liberals, of all people in the world, ought to be satisfied at the conclusion of the war. (Hear, hear, and cheers). He firmly believed that there were at times necessities which could not be put aside, but he thought that when war was forced upon them, it should be something so conclusive as to take with them the whole of the people of the country, who were able to examine the question and feel that it was a war which was reasonable and just from the Liberal standpoint. About the war which had taken place and ended he would say this, that if the Liberal party had bad a clean board to commence with he would not have voted for the resolution which he had read; but he felt satisfied that the Tories would join in voting for that resolution because the founda- tion of the war was laid by the late Government. When they took from three to four millions of the hard earned money of the people of this country, and invested it in the Suez Canal, they laid the seeds of the war which had just token place. ( Hear, hear. ) He did not think the country would ever gain anything by ! the money which was sunk into the Canal, because of this : England was the greatest user of the Canal, and whether she owned a cent in it or not her way was safe. Five- eights of the money received from the Canal in tolls was paid by this country. Therefore, whoever owned the Canal, whoever bad money invested there, there wasa way for Eng- land, because of the enormous amount of money that we were constantly paying for the traffic that we sent through it. Another thing was that England and France agreed in sOlllO shape or other to put the present Khedive on the throne of Egypt, and having done so they could not allow Turkey or anyone else to remove him. Looking at this question with what had been done by the late Government, he theught they might congratulate themselves that they were out of the Egyptian difficulty for the present, and he trusted the present Government would make such arrangements as would effectually prevent that great destroyer of the peace of Europe—Turkey--from again in- terfering in Egypt. (Hear, hear, and applause). When one came to look back upon what the people of this country bad had to suffer and pay for Turkey—when they remem- bered the Crimean war and the Russia-Turkish war just over—the millions of money, and the millions of lives sac- rificed through Turkey, be thought it was time the Powers of Europe should prevent her from again meddling and causing them to shed blood and spend treasure on her. (Hear, hear, and cheers). He had confidence that the pre- . sent Government would do something in this respect in the anal settlement. Coming to the second part of the resolu- tion—the closure rules—the speaker, referring to the state- ment that they were un-English, said the present rules were the most un-English rules in existence. At the present time 10 or 20 men could prevent, and did prevent, 600 from dis- charging the business of the country. He wished to know if that was Ene,lish ; if it was what any sober man could -defend? He knew .of no inetitution in the country besides the House of Commons where less than half its number cc uld govern. A majority of one in L'verpool Town Council could make six aldermen in a day —a majority of one could pass any business in any as- sembly in the world, as far as he knew of, except the House of Commons. Well, he wished to know whether the work- ingmen of this country were willing to allow all the good which they hoped would be done by this Government, or OTIS following to be stopped by a few men. (" No.") He did not think so. He explained that the new procedure rules gave the House of Commons the power of saving by a majority when a debate should be closed: the rules meant that a majority of the House should do the business, but the

Tories wanted something else, and he would tell them what It was they wanted. They say, "Don't let us have the House of Commons like any other sensible assembly. (Laughter.) Don't let 301 govern 299, but let us vote like this, that it shall take two-thirds of the members to do it; then we shall get on well." If this proposition was adopted the business of the legislation could not be carried on at all. Whether there was a Liberal Government or a Tory Govern- ment in power—he did not care which—let a majority be able to decide what business should be done, because if it was bad business the country would soon be alive to it. How long did it take to give a workingman a vote? Years [upon years the question had been fought, and why? Be- cause of that old ruety machinery, which should have been altered long ago. And for every improvement that was required for the comfort and happiness of the people of this country they would still have to go on agitating year after year, except they altered, and remedied in some measure the House of Commons. He hoped the meeting would unanimously vote for this resolution, which was the most English resolution that had ever been submitted to a meet- ing. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Mr. F. H. GOSSIGE seconded the resolution, the first part of which, he said, was to a great extent a foregone conclu- sion. The war had been fought so manfully and successfully ; and in a shorter time no n ation could have carried the war through to such a conclusion. With regard to the second part of the resolution, he thought they one and all should heartily sup- port Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—and the Liberal Government. If they wanted any proof of the power of Mr. Gladstone and the gentlemen forming his Government they had it demon- strated pretty nearly to perfection in the war just concluded. That the rules of procedure would ba passed by the House in the autumn session, he had no doubt, and the country would make greater progress under such management than we did at present. (Applause.) The Rev.ICHARLEs BEARD, on rising, was warmly cheered. Referring to the recent war, the rev, gentleman said, as Liberals, they all hated war and warlike expenditure; they were heartily glad when the battle flags were furled and peace again proclaimed throughout the nation. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) But at the same time when war was a stern necessity, and he believed it was sometimes, it was impossible not to feel some satisfaction at the thought that it was now successfully demonstrated, not only to Europe, but to their political opponents at home, that if a Liberal Government thought it necessary to strike, and just to strike, they could strike swiftly and strongly and , surely; and there was no mistake about the success of their endeavours. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) It was not merely that this expedition was most carefully prepared with a very unusual amount of forethought vigour; that it was sent out to Egypt under the command of skilled generals; that all arrangements were made with the utmost possible perfec- tion; and that the new army arrangements of the Liberal party, which it had been said over and over again would prove a but broken road in the hour of peril, had been suc- cessful. Not only these, but all Europe was amazed at the admirable astuteness and good temper of Lord Dufferin's diplomacy in Constantinople. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) Turkey would give anything that was possible to quarrel with us, but dare not at the present moment. Prince Bis- mark, the arbiter of continental politics, and Europe at large, asked nothing more from England than that she should complete the work she had begun. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Why was it that Europe was so content? Because Europa knew that when Mr. Gladstone stated publicly that England had no selfish interests to serve in Egypt, that she desires only a free way for ships and soldiers, that she de- sired the prosperity and happiness of the Egyptian people, they knew they were dealing with a man who was speaking the simple truth—(cheers)—a man who would suffer sooner than not stand to his engagements. They were quite sure that Turkey would have no island stolen from her on the present occasion— (laughter)—that no English diplomatists would have any secret treaties in their pockets—(cheers)--but that every- thing would be plain, straightforward, and above board. (Cheers.) He knew that many who called themselves Liberals had been dissatisfied with the war. One or two circumstances, however, seemed to show that we had been justified in what we had done. They must recollect that Arabi Pasha distinctly belonged to the military party, and he did not hesitate to say that in England, Egypt, or any- where else he distrusted military parties, who, under the pretence a national independence and organisation, made an appeal to force. In the next place he had the profoundest distrust in the capacity of Mahommedan States to sustain a peaceful and settled civilization. We were now at the beginning of the thirteen hundredth year of Mahommed- anism, and he challenged anyone to pro.luce an instance throughout the wholeof that time in which Mahommedanism had produced a civilised, peaceful, and prosperous State. (Applause.) Grave responsibilities with regard to India lay on England's shoulders, and as an Imperial people hav- ing Imperial duties to fulful we must be faithful to our imperial position, and with a full determination to do justice,must, when the necessity was laid upon us, tArike and spare not. Mr. Beard then referred to the cloture, observ- ing that the adoption of a two-thirds majority would, by allowing Tory obstruction, prevent the passing of measures which the Liberal party and with it the great mass of the nation imperatively demanded. (Cheers.) Speaking of the condition of Ireland, Mr. Beard said the sentiment of true Liberals must be one of the utmost satisfaction and delight, when they recognised the fact that under the legislation of the last two sessions, Ireland was becoming more and more content, and he thought one of the strongest signs of better things was that on the part of the people there was no longer a disposition to hide from the vengeance of the law the murderers who had committed so many shocking out- rages against human life and property. Altogether they were beginning to feel that it was possible to look forward to a happier and brighter time in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Great wrongs had been committed in that country—(hear, hear)—and it was pleasing to think that it was by the agency of the law, by the agency of properl constituted land courts, that these wrongs were being re- vealed and remedied. He had great confidence in the good feeling of his fellow subjects in Ireland, and also in the fact that they would cease to feel some of their imaginary wrongs when their pockets and stomachs were well filled—(hear, hear)—when they were permitted to enjoy the fruits of their labour, and when they received the benefit of what they placed upon the land, without the shape of rack and cut. They would then realise that after all they had thousands of friends in England, of whose existence they were before unaware. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried with enthusiasm.

Mr. CAREY, in moving a resolution urging all Liberals who had claimed votes to attend the revision court, spoke of the importance of registration and the necessity of a strict party discipline. Mr. HOLBROOK GASKELL, jun., seconded the resolution. Mazzini, he believed, made use of the words, "We do not ask to be well governed; we wish to govern ourselves well." In this country, fortunately, we governed ourselves. The resolution was carried. The CHAIRMAN moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Beard for his most admirable and eloquent address. The motion was seconded by Mr. Jocose 'I.ALLoic, and carried.
Mr. BEARD replied; and a-similar compliment was pad to, the Chairman on the motion of Mr. MARTIN TAYLOR. seconded by Mr. PIERCE TALLON. The meeting then separated.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.

THE WOMAN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. A woman named Mary EliZl Brown was brought up at the Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, before Messrs. Hol- brook Gaskell, junr., and John Brock, charged with attemp- ting to commit suicide by cutting her throat with a carving knife on the 14th August. Mr. Husband appeared on behalf of the prisoner.—Jane Lonsdale deposed: lam a domestic servant for Mr. Davies at the Stanley AVMs. I remember the 14th August. I was working in the house on that day. I saw the prisoner walking about. About ten o'clock at night Mr. Davies got his supper in the bar, and while he was ; getting it the prisoner served the customers. About five minutes afterwards the prisoner went upstairs to her own bedroom. I was upstairs, I had gone before her. She trild me to go to hed and I went into my bedroom. Ten minutes afterwards, in consequence of hearing a noise, I went into the prisoner's bedroom with a light, and I found her in the bed undressed bleeding from the throat, and she was covered with blood. She could not speak. I saw the cut throat the following day. I did not see any instrument and don't know how the wound was made. She has been confined to her bed up to a week ago, and she left the house yesterday.—By Mr. Husband: I have been at the place nine months and have noticed her acting queerly, not like a sensible woman. I know she had brain fever a little time back. She was acting queerly the day the wound was caused—By Inspector Barnett: I have acted under the prisoner's instructions since I have been there, but she has not been able of late to give me instructions.—Dr. O'Keeffe said :—On the 14th of August, about a quarter to eleven at night, I was called to the Stanley Arms, a public-house in Lugsdale-road, Widnes. When I got there the prisoner was in bed. I noticed the upper portion of her chest and chemise covered with blood. I examined her and found a transverse wound on the throat ' and neck from four to five inches in length. It was bleeding copiously, and the air from the lungs was coming rapidly through it, so strong that it would blow out a candle, The windpipe was almost cut through. She was completely unconscious, and almost in a dying state, and she would have been dead in two or three minutes if a doctor had not been called in. I stitched up the windpipe and wound and dressed them, and have attended her almost daily ever since until a week ago. She is in a very weak state still, and needs to take care of herself, but is out of danger so far as the wound is concerned. The wound must have been caused by some sharp instrument. I searched the prisoner's bedroom, and my assistant found an ordinary carving knife which was besmeared with blood on the bed. A great deal of force must have been used to inflict the wound, as the edge of the knife was not very sharp. The prisoner has since expressed her regret to me that she ever committed the act —By Mr. Husband: I attended the prisoner when she had brain fever in January and February. I have been called in several times, and have noticed that the prisoner has been peculiar at times since. I have been called in and found her suffering from aberration of mind, attributable to her former illness.—By Inspector Barnett: She was an ex- citab!e woman, and after the fits of excitement passed she was in a perfectly rational state.—lnspector Barnett said: I am inspector of police at Widnes. About 20 to 11 at night on the 14th August last, I was passing down Lugsdale-road, Widnes, and from what was said to me I went to the Stanley Arms and found the prisoner up in her bedroom, undressed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 7, 1882.

She was laid on her back. Her throat was cut and bleeding very much, and she was in an unconscious state. The doctor arrived shortly afterwards and dressed the wound. I pro- duce the carving knife found by Dr. O'Keefe's assistant on the bed in my presence. It was covered with blood and wet. This morning I received the prisoner in custody from Sergt. McGregor, who found her at the railway station in company , with Davies, making their way to Birmingham, and I charged her with attempting to commit suicide. She replied, "I don't remember it at all."— Dr.O'Keeffe explained that the prisoner was going away on Wednesday to recruit her healtli as per his instructions, in order to enable her better to go through the ordeal of the trial. He called at the police station to mention the state of the woman's mind to the inspector of police, but he was unfortunately away from home. The prisoner was not going away to evade justice. He was afraid that if she was immediately brought to trial her mind might again become detnented.—Mr. Husband, for the defence, contended that the witnesses had distinctly proved that the prisoner was not sane at the time of the attempted suicide. The law stated that no conviction could take place unless it was proved to their worships' satisfaction that the act was com- mitted wilfully when a person was in a sound state of mind, and there was no doubt whatever from the evidence but what the woman was suffering from temporary insanity.— Inspector Barnett asked that the prisoner be sent to the Assizes.—The Bench, however, discharged the prisoner, on her promising never again to attempt so rash an act.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. 1 The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, when there were present Mr. Marsh (chairman), the Revs. T. Finegan, and J. Barnacle, and Messrs. Dobell, Hu'me, Eatock, Birchall, Syder, Newsome, Tyrer, Jackson, Saddler, Buckley, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Kenwright, Meadows, Gilbody, and W. Longton. WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT. The WonKuorsE MASTER reported that there were 447 inmates in the Workhouse, as compared with 452 last week, and 454 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 127 boys and girls in the Kirkdale schools, three having been sent during the fortnight. The number of deaths dur- ing that period was five.

AN UNTRAINED RELIEVING OFFICER. The CLERK stated that an application for a boy haying been made by Mr. P. J. Courtenay, of Walton, he made enquiries from the West Derby Guardians as to whether he was a fit person to have charge of a boy. The Clerk to those Guardians replied, en- closed a report by one of their relieving officers, Charles Smith, which stated that be had made enquiries respecting Courtenay and found that he kept a shop in the green-grocery, fish, and earthenware line, and that the boy would be required to attend to the shop, run errands, and look after a pony. The report also stated that Courtenay and his wife "are both Irish and Catholics, but a miserable- !orAing pair they are," and concluded by stating that he (the relieving officer) did not consider the parsons fit per- sons to look after any children bat their own.—Fathet FINEGAN asked who the relieving officer was who wrote that letter.—The CLERK said it was not one of the Board's officers.—Father FINEGAN said he thought the officer had gone a very long ray indeed out of his way. He believed he was the only Irishman present, and he certainly thought that officer had gone out of his way saying the people were Irish, and he protested against such a thing, as the question of nationality was not before the Board.—Mr. TYRER scarcely thoughr, from the wording of the letter, that anything offensive had been meant.—Father FINEGAN said ho decidedly objected to a report like that. —Mr. TYRER said that there was a resolution of the Board to the effect that no Catholic boy should be put in charge of any but Catholics, and it was necessary to know the person's rcligion.—Father FINEGAN: It was not necessary to say they are Irish because they are Catholics— many Irish belonged to other churches. He thought it was done to prejudice the case. In their enquires they did not ask whether people were Irish, English, or Scotch. If the letter had not already been answered, he should have pro- posed a reply.—The CLERK said he would be seeing their clerk the day after, and he would speak to him abouL, train- ing their officers bdter.—The subject then dropped.

to cultivate their artistic faculties, and their love of the beautiful. Art might perhaps be defined to be the por- trayal of the beautiful in nature and for the portrayal of the beautiful in nature we required the eye to see and the hand to portray. He would go farther than this and assert that it was only the artist—he who had had large practice in artistic matters—who really had the eye to see. He did not believe that any person without artistic faculty really ever made proper use of his eyes; and, therefore, on that very utilitarian point of view,he would argue that they ought to cultivate art as well as science, in order that they might cultivate their faculty of seeing and also their faculty of portraying what they saw. In Widnes their main business was with applied science, which, though perhaps not on so high a level as pure science, was still of the greatest importance to the people. The labours of Wheatstone, Farady, Grove, and Spottiswood made certain things possible, which Siemens, Edison, Swan, and other men had made actual. Speaking of chemistry, Mr. Carey said there was no appliances for the study of applied science of which they would make such goad use as the new Laboratory, for whicll they were mainly indebted to Mr. Gossage. (Applause.) He had had the pleasure of knowing Mr. Gossage for more than 20 years, and he well knew how generous he was; and he rejoiced, and they also, that he had the ability and the means to be as generous as his heart dictated. He was sure they would all join with him (Mr. Carey) in thanking Mr. Gossage most heartily for what he had done in the Laboratory, and united with their best wishes for hi,s future prosperity and happiness. (Ap- plause. Mr. HOLBROOK GASKELL, jun., seconded the motion, remarking that Mr. Gossage was interested in the spread of education. The glasses had been remarkably *--essful, and there was great credit due not only to the teachers, but the students also for that success, because it had been achieved in spite of some disadvantages. (Hear, hear.) Dr. HURTER suppo7ted the motion in art appropriate speech. The vote was ea ried by acclamation. Mr. GOSSAGE, in reply, thanked those present most heartily for the vote which they had accorded to him. He had given Widnes the Laboratory simply for the reason that he had long seen young men who had very little education, and who had not the means to educate them- selvee, striving to educate themselves and become usdul members of society, yet lacking the opportunity. Mr. Carey had explained the use of the Laboratory to the inhabitants of Widnes; it now remained to be seen whether he had done right in presenting it to Widnes. With such a teacher as Mr. Watts and others, who would make use of the Laboratory as directors, the earnest pupils who would assemble there would have an opportunity of becoming great and good men of science, and would deserve the suc- cess for which they had worked, even if they are not able to attain it. (Applause.) He and his partner had both got sons, and theyboth hoped that they would come to Widnes to work—(applause)—hut when they came they would not find that there had been no one before them wishful to for- ward the educational interests of the people. That was another incentive to support education ia Widnes, and one of the reasons he had for forwarding the school in every way he could. As one of the trustees of Farnworth Grammar School, he trusted that they would in a short time be able to take in those students from the Board schools who had attained as high a position as they could, and for small remuneration to allow them to continue their studies to tit them for almost any position in life that they might have to take—(applause)—and so further the cause of higher education of which Widnes was so much in need. He again thanked them most heartily for the vote they had passed and only hoped that the Library would obtain the success that he wished it. (Applause.) Mr. HUNTER proposed a vote of thanks to the committee in suitable terms. Mr. SHOWAN seconded the motion. Mr. MoitutsoN suitably replied on behalf of the Com- mittee.
On the proposition of the Rev. G. BOND, seconded by Mr. CROSSLEY, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the proceedings concluded.

div.head: TUE AGTION AGAINST THE GLYCERINE WORKS.
div.p: TUE AGTION AGAINST THE GLYCERINE WORKS.
THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS DEFEATED. _

On Monday morning, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, the case of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners against M. Victor Clolus, who was charged that he did en the 20th July and on divers other days, after the passing of the Public Health Act, 1875, unlawfully establish and carry on a certain noxious or offensive trade, via., the trade of a glycerine manufacturer, without having obtained the consent in writ- ing of the Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority, and that he carried on such as aforesaid for 40 days. The magistrates on the Bench were the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. William Bankes.—Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, again repre- sented the defendant, and Mr. Linaker appeared for the Com- missioners.

The case had been adjourned for the production of Dr. McDougall, who stepped into the box. Mr. Fletcher: Have you any explanation to make to the Bench for your non-appearance orr the last occasion ? Dr. McDougall : I have no explanation to make. He added that he was a member of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, and he was present at the meeting which was held in January, at which an application was nude by the defendant for permission to establish these works. He remembered Mr. Handley moving a resolution, which he seconded, but he could not exactly tell what were the terms of the resolution. The resolution he believed was iu the minute book.—Mr. Fletcher: I am bound to ask this question. Have you not stated that the minute is a record of of the proceedings? Witness: No. If you ask me whether in my opinion M. Victor Clolus was badly treated, I tell you I think so.—Was not the proposition that consenc be given? I cannot exactly say. My memory doesn't carry me back so far.—Have you not had some conversation with the defendant's agent in this action? M. De La Rue called upon me the other morning, and I repeated to him the substancs of what you have heard to-day. Dr. McDougall further said the resolution was passed upon a re- port presented by an engineer from St. Helens.—Mr. Fletcher pointed out that the resolution was passed before the report was presented, and said Dr. McDougall's memory was totally unreliable.

Mr. .J. W. Clough, reporter, said he attended the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners and prepared a re- port of the proceedings from his notes for the information of the Runcorn public. He had a distinct recollection of what took place, as he was somewhat astonished that the Board should so quietly pass an unqualified resolution of consent, after the complaints that had been made.—By Mr. Linaker : He had not the shorthand notes with him. Mr. Fletcher said if their Worships wished he could call Dr. Bagnall, who did not agree with the evidence of the medical officen

Dr. Bagnall said he had been in practice in Runcorn over three years. In his opinion the increase of disease in the district could not be attributed to the Glycerine Works. In 1880 there was more diarrhan than in the present year. The deaths frora marasimus entered on his returns, meant that a child had been born in a weakly condition. It would never gain strength ; never become fit for anything; and even- tually die. The works had no more to do with the deaths than he had. He did not know of any death arising from the nuisance from the works. The death rate was, in his opinion, entirely due to diarrhca, scarlatina, and measles; the symptoms of which diseases were not attributable to these works.—By Mr. Linaker : His patients had said there were bad smells. The smells from the Glycerine Works were very offensive, but he would rather have them than chlorine. —By Mr. Fletcher: There were other worgs in the neigh- bourhood which emitted offensive smells.

At the reqo3st of Mr. Fletcher the minute book; Mr. Abbot's report on the works ; and the memorial to the Com- missioners, asking them to take proceeding under the 111th section, were put in as evidence. Mr. Linaker admitted that the application to the Com- missioners asked them to take proceedings under the 114th section. The Rev. Ed. A P. Campbell: Nevertheless you proceed under the 112th. Our decision is this : That the resolution of the Board entered on the books and signed by the chair- man of the Board, as in this instance, constitutes absolute consent, and must bc considered a consent in writing within the meaning of the clause. Therefore we dismiss the sum- mons.

Mr. Fletcher asked that the costs of the proceedings he paid by the Commissioners. He made this applieation because be thought their worships would be of opinion, after judgment they had just delivered, that the Commis- sioners had not dealt fairly with M. Clolus, who had been put to considerable expense in defending these proceedings. which clearly should never hive been taken. The feeling of the constitueats of the Board was clearly against them. Mr. Linaker asked the Bench to grant the Commissioners a case, and said he thought the Bench ought only to grant costs on one day's hearing. The Chairman said the Bench would grant a case, and as the hearing on the last occasion was adjourned entirely on Mr. Fletcher's own responsibility, he thought one day's costs would be sufficient.
Mr. Fletcher: I only thought that Dr. McDougall would have felt disposed to pay the extra costs that were incurred. We have no power to compel him, but there is such a thing as conscience money. ,

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS, Mr. John Ashton, the vice-chairman, presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton workhouse on Tuesday. There wer3 also presmt the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. C. Rigby, Knowles, Davies. Mclntyre, Andrews, Hall, Jackson, Darbyshire, Whitlow, Pickering, Norman, G. S. Hazlehurst, J. Smith, E. A. Wallington, J. Weir, Fisher, W. Handley, Whittaker, J. Mounfield, J. Higbfield, H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said the Finance Committee recommended the payment of £lOO on account to Mr. Stel- fox, the contractor for the hospital works, which with £l,BOO previously paid made a total of £.1,900 towards £2,460, which was the amount of the contract.

MASTER'S REPORT. Mr. JoNgs, the master, reported that there were 90 adults not able-bodied in the workhouse, as compared with 85 in the corresponding week last year. The adults able-bodied numbered 10, being the same number as last year, while there were 190 children as compared with 169 the previous year. There had been 23 vagrants relieved during the week. Thirty-one boys and 30 girls were attending school, and 13 girls were receiving industrial training. There were 13 imbeciles in the house. THE REPTtESENTATIoN QUESTION: GUARDIANS 'INSULTED." Mr. W WHITLOW called attention to the order issued by the Local Government Board for the amalgamation Of Daresbury to Kekewick and tockhain to Norton for , election purposes, and said he saw no reason for the Local Government Board to meddle in the matter.—The DEPUTY' CLERK: They have the power to do it.—Mr. WHITLow We might as well stop at home.—The CLERK: They have the power and they will use it.—Mr. WHITLOW said he had seen one Guardian whe said he would never attend another Guardians' meeting on account of the Local Government Board's action. He (Mr. Whitlow) considered it was a great insult to the Guardians.—The Rev. J. Lommoon in- quired if the Local Government Board had based their action upon the population or rateable value of the townships, or upon both. He should ceitainly ask the Local Government Board their reason for their action.-The CLERK read the letter from the Local Government Board, previously published, from which it appeared that their action was based upon the rateable value, awl also the population.—Rev. J. LocKvrour. said Bartington was very much below the places selected as regarded population, and he should like to know why these particular places were pressed upon. the Guardians. He knew the ratepayers felt it very much indeed.—The CLERK re- marked that as representative of the Aston estate he su Tested that Bartington should be added to Dutton; but the Board repudiated the matter.—The DEPUTY-CLERK said the Guardian for Kekewick had only attended the Board on four occasions since 1878.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said be should enter his protest against the Local Government Board's action after the Guardians coming to a unanimous resolution on the subject.—Mr.WHlTLow said the Guardians affected by the proposed change did not think so much about the a.nalgamation as of the treatment of the. Board after passing the resolution. They felt disgusted with the matter.—The discussion then ceased.

div.head: CONTRACTS.
div.p: CONTRACTS.

Contracts were accepted- -as iAows :—Drapery, Mr. F. Fairhurst, Runcorn; flour and oatmeal, Mr. James Cowap, Preston-o'-th'-Hill ; groceries, Mr. Samuel Collier, Runcorn; drugs, arc., Messrs. Smith and Co, Runcorn; meat, Mr. Dobson, Warrington; clothing, Mr. Oldbury, Runcorn; shoes, Pocock Brothers, Loudon; coffins, Mr. Lightfoot, Aston.

REVISION COURT AT GRAPPENHALL.—Mr. W. L. Ffoulkes, revising barrister, held a court at the Barry Arms, Grappenhall, on Saturday, to revise the lists of voters in the townships of Altrincham, Bowdon, Dunham Massey, Hale, Rostherne, and Tinverley. The Liberals were repre- sented by Mr. A. E. Paterson, and the Conservatives by Mr. Lance Bentley. The business, however, was of a formal character.

div.head: COST OF THE NEW CHAPEL.
div.p: THE COST OF THE NEW CHAPEL.

Mr. ME.ipows said that it had often been stated that the new chapel should not cost over £l,OOO, but now he under- stood that the sum had been exceeded. Some time ago there had been a furnishing committee formed, and that committee was to buy a few articles for the chapel, understood to cost only a few pounds, but at the Finance Committee the day before, an account of .£74 was submitted for several books, hassocks, crosses, and candlesticks. He should like to know if that committee ever ordered those things, as it was never intended they should go to such an amount. He thought it was very wrong that the ratepayers should be called on to pay the amount which ought rather to be defrayed by sub- scription.—Mr. BARNACLE said he believed the purchase of those articles had been left to Father Henry, it being believed that he would purchase nothing more than what was reason- able, but as a member of the Finance Committee he (Mr. Barnacle) had been surprised by the largeness of the sum. He sugfrested that the Clerk should get a return of the ex- penses incurred both for the Catholic department and that of the Church of England.—Mr. HALL'said the account had been paid, and he could not see what the Board could do in the matter.—A GUARDIAN: What has been purchased is the property of the Guardians • Father Henry has not got it for himself.—Mr. Nitwsomis also thought it would be better to let the matter drop.—The matter then dropped. THE GUARDIANS AND TUE PRESCOT GAS COMPANY.

Mr. NEWSOME called attention to the great cost of light- ing the Workhouse. He found that daring the last three years the cost of gas at the Workhouse had been £175 5s 4d, and that of water £154 is sd. The cost of the gas supplied by the Prescot Gas Company was enormously high, being 5s 4d per thousand. He should ask that a committee of practical men should be appointed to con- sider a scheme for manufacturing their own gas.—The CHAIRMAN said it would require a great deal of calculation to estimate whether it would be cheaper to manufacture their own or to continue to get it from the gas company.— Father FINEGAN also thought the price of the gas was ex- cessive. At Widnes he said they had gas at 3s. 61 per thousand, although the Widnes company had had to lay pipes over a very wide area. The matter certainly required investigation, and he was glad Mr. Newsome had brought it forward.—The matter was ultimately, on the motion of Mr. NEWSOME, seconded by Mr. MEADOWS, referred to the Building Committee—This concluded the business of pub- lic interest.

div.head: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLA SSES.
div.p: WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLA SSES.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting for the distribution of prizes to the successful students of these classes w.l.s held in the Volunteer Hall, on Wednesday evening. Great interest ap- pearel to be manifested in the occasion, and the large hall was filled with an intelligent audience. Mr. J. L. Muspratt, chairman of the Committee, presided, and was supported on the platform by Rev. George Bond, vicar of Farnworth, Rev, J. Wright-Williams, Dr. Hurter, Messrs. E Carey, F. H. Gossage, J. H. Crossley, Holbrook Gaskell, junr., Henry Showan, and J. Morrison (secretary). Mr. MORRISON read the following report During this session the entries to the classes numberel 171, and 120 of these presented themselves to the Government examinations in May. The results are as follow :

No. No. Par Examined. Passed. Centaga. freehand Drawing 24 ... 3 ... IA Machine Constructiun Building Construction Mathematics Inorganic Chemistry 37 ... 24 ... 65 Acoustics, Light lc Heat 14 ... 11 ... 79 Alkali Manufacture

The result of the At class is very disappointing, but the Com- mittee do sot be,ieve that this is due to want of ability on the part of the students. . . The Committee ate glad to report a great improvement in the chemistry class, 85 per cent having passed, as compvel with 44 per cent the previous year. In the technologicil class, alkali manufacture, al the students were successfui at the examination, and Mr. Arthur W. Parkinson obtained .• prize of £3 and bronze medal—(applause)—and Mr. Pamuel Evans a prize of £2 and bronze medal. (Applause.) The number of students who persevered in their studies. and came up for examination at the end of the session is highly gratifying to the Committee. In 1880, 57 per cent of those entered came up for examination ; 1831, 71 per coot; and 1882, 75 per cent. The la ter is the highest result we have had since the formation of the classes.' . . The average attendance at examinations for all the classes in the United Kingdom is about 55 per cent as compared with our 78 per cent. . . . Owing to the munificence of Mr. Gossage the committee are very pleased to be in a position to announce that this session they will be able to provide a chemical laboratory. (Applause ) Mr. Carlile has built a new scenes and art school, which the c immittee have leased for several years , the laboratory is being fitted up in tile most complete manner, and there will be accommodation in it for 32 students. Mr. Ogg very kindly prepared the necessary plans and specifications for the labora- t iry. The total cost of providing this laboratory 13 about £2.0, and Mr. Gos.age, although he had only promised £l5O, has informed the committee that they can debit him with the whole of the expense. (Applause.) Widnes owes much to Mr. Gossage, and the committee venture to predict that this will not be the least useful of the many benefits he has conferred uoon the town (Applause.) A financial statement was given, which showed that the amount of fees and Government grant received was £ll6 163 6d, and the amount of subscriptions £llB 103. The amount of expenditure was £2ll 106 Li, leaving a balance of £47 13s 5d in the bank. The CHAIRMAN, before presentingothe prizes, said the classes were commenced with very great hopes, which they found very good, but even in the short number of years they had been at work they had found that one year the students decreased, and next year had again increased. The classes were started in 1875, and the committee had now made bold to venture upon leasing a schooi for the teaching of art as well as science. That school, of course, was increased by the munificence of his friend, Mr. Gossage. It showed that the classes had really become an institution in the town, and one which must be regarded with pride by all those who were connected with them. When the library was formed, the suggestion was made that it should be a thorough one for the town, but it only existed in a modified form, which might posiibly be developed into something larger. Last year lectures had been given by a number of gentlemen on various kinds of science, alkali manufacture more particularly, and he did not see why in science classes these subjects should not be further deve- loped ; or why some lectures on art in its best form should not be delivered. They wanted every friend that they had, and he thought there were many in Widnes as well aa out- side, to help them to getthe gentlemen to give tholectures. Everybody in Widnes ought to help the Committee in mak- ing the schools a success by urging people to attend, because the more pupils they had and the more they would be able to enlarge the classes, and make them something of a stan- dard even in this district of South-West Lancashire. (Ap- plause.) Only the other day it was found that a large borough near Liverpool, which lately obtained its corpora- tion, was without a scieace and art school, which gave all the more credit to Widnes for what it had done. Even Bootle was following what he might call the example of Widnes, and they might hope that before long Widnes would take a front rank for science and art education. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN then distributed the prizes to the success- ful students, who were applauded as they approached the platform. A list of the prizes has already been published in The Examiner. Mr. E. CAREY sad this year, in the 9th of the existence of the classes, they were entering upon a new era. For the first time they had a building devoted and adapted to their particular purpose, and so far as their power would permit, the committee intended to cultivate both art and science. It might appear rather strange that they in Widnes should care to cultivate art. They were certainly given to the production of the beautiful in Widnes— (laughter)—and there was nothing particularlypretty about i the place, nor were they engaged n manufacturing anything that was pretty to look at. They were engaged in practical affairs, and in the manufacture of certain very useful articles. On that account be thought they were the more called upon

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
THE STATE OF EGYPT.
The Viking is emkarking the sick at Ramleh Hospital. There are eighty cases of typhoid fever. Diarrhce tis also prevalent.

A detachment of the B3rkshire Regiment stationed at Tantah has returned to Alexandria owing to sickness. The Tantah Christians have petitioned for protection, but the Egyptian Government deem it unnecessary.

'The Duke of Teck has left for Englanã in the Assyrian Monarch. A squadron of the Ist Life-guards is embarking in the Assyrian Monarch. and the Viking is embarking the sick. The worst cases are improving, and sickness on the whole decreases.

A tourist river steamer has arrived at Alexandria with 90 sick, and another with 60 on board is momentarily expected. The comfort of the invalids was well attended to, and the experiment of bringing them in these steamers is regarded as a success. Aboukir is occupied by artillerymen, and Damietta by the Malta Fencibles.
THE FUTURE GOVERNMENT OF THE COUNTRY.

Sir Auckland Colvin, now on his way to Egypt, is in- structed not to resume at present his duties as British Comptroller General. Baker Pacha is preparing a scheme which includes both the organisation_ of the Egyptian army and the organisation of a Gendarmerie. The outlines of this schemei- which is declared to be of a comprehensive character, will shortly be ready, the de- tails being left for a later period. The Egyptian Govern- ment has not up to the present asked England to permit recruiting for a gendarmerie in India, but it is considered probable that the request, if made, would be granted.

Mr. Ralli, M.P., has been asked by the Bridport Lioeral Association to contest the borough at the next election. Information was received at Chatham yesterday that none of the Royal Marines were to remain in Egypt with the army of occupation, and that the men would shortly return, home.

At Portadown, early yesterday morning, a blacksmith named Fox, while walking home, fell over a railway bridge, the railing of %I hich, for some unexplained reason,, he had climbed. He fell from the height of 25 feet, and was in- st mtaneously killed. Lord Rosebery, who was announced at the recent National Tichborne Conference to be a sympathiser with the Claimant ,has replied to a letter asking him to support a memorial to the Home Secretary for Orton' s release that it was impossible he should support the movement. The miners' strike in South Staffordshire and East Worcester districts terminated yeeterday. The secretary of the federation of miners for the Midland Counties had an. interview yesterday with the chairman of the coal trade, who agreed to grant an advance of ten per cent., which the men have accepted. The Central News says we have authority for stating that the London Echo will not after all change hands, Mr. Edwards, M.P., having paid Mr. Storey, who purchased the paper a few weeks ago, £5,000 and expenses in considera- tion of the contract to purchase the paper being cancelled. by mutual consent. _

-Seven deaths from scarlet fever have been registered at Accrington this week, as compared with six last week and nine the week previous. Some of the deaths are of persons who have 1.).?.en suffering for several weeks. The new cases are diminishing in number. A shocking accident occurred at Kersley on Thursday night. A man named Richard Williams, aged 27, a native of Cornwall, was being lowered into the main sewer exca- vation, thirty feet deep, when he relaxed his hold of the rope, and fell to the bottom, being killed on the spot. The chairman of the South Staffordshire coal trade yesterday informed the miners' secretary that coal would be advanced one shilling per ton from Monday next, and wages would rise fourpence and twopence, or 10 per cent. This will probably put an end to the strike. A special cable message received from Maros (Sp tin), dated Thursday evening, states that the large iron steamer General Court, bound. from Cardiff to Barcelona, with a full cargo of coals, has founderesl off Cape Finiaterre, and lies in 36 feet of water. No mention is made as to the fate of the crew.

lrA mass meeting of miners was hPld at West Bromwich yesterday, when it was announced that Mr. Fisher Smith had given his award in favour of a ten per cent. advance. The meeting unanimously resolved that work be resumed on Monday nest. This decision affects 15,000 miners, and has been accepted by about 12,000.

The Central News Claremorris correspondent telegraphs: —" A bailiff, while returning to this town yesterday morn- ing with a cow he. had seized upon, was attacked by the owner of the cow, a woman, who, with a pitchfork in hand, followed him for three miles, and eventually rescued the cow after inflicting some injuries on the bailiff. The police are investigating the case.' it is proposed to apply to Parliament next Session for an extension of the municipal boundary of Burnley. On Friday afternoon the agents of Sir Ughtred Kay Shuttle- worth, Bert., with the Mayor and Town Clerk and several members of the Burnley Corporation, went round the proposed new boundaries, to which it is believed no ob- jection will be raised by the landowners. The lad Higgins, who was given into the etre of his father by the Oldhani magistrates on Thursday, has ab- sconded. His father was bound in £2O for the lad's ap- pearance on Monday. It will be remembered that the boy had told an extraordinary story of an adventure in South America. and a journey from New York to Liver- pool, but which was found to be untrue. THE CHURCH CONGRESS. The congress resumed its sitting yesterday morning, but only one meeting was held, it having been arranged that "Devotional Life" should form the subject. The Bishop of Lichfield presided, and the drill hall was crowded.

div.head: DE.IIH FROM CHLOROFORM.
div.p: DE.IIH FROM CHLOROFORM.

An inquest was held at Bolton, yesterday, on the body of Michael Cronin, aged 33, salesman, who had die& whilst undergoing an operation at the Infirmary. He had sus- tained a fracture of the outer bone of the leg and Aislocation, and on Thursday Dr. McDonald was dministering three drachms of chloroform on lint, prior to reducing the dislo- cation, when the deceased suddenly struggled to get up, and fell back dead. He had been previously examined, and showed no signs of heart disease. The jury exonerated the Infirmary officials.

div.head: ROBBING ALMS BOXES.
div.p: ROBBING ALMS BOXES.

At the London City C )tirt yesterday morning, Joseph Tebett pleaded guilty to robbing the alms boxes of Keble College and St. Aloysius's Church, and was setenced to three mouths' impriaourceut for each off ince, The Mayor said

these were by no means the first offences of the kind tha prisoner had committed and been punished for, and highly complimented the police, as had it not been for their energy the prisoner would have escaped.

KICKING A WOMAN. A brutal kicking case was heard at Accrington yesterday morning. On Monday, a single young woman, named Walding, was walking in the fields with Cbristepher McGee, with whom she co-habited, when McGee kicked her in the lower part of the body with a pair of clogs, doing her serious injury, the woman having been laid up ever since. McGee was committed to prison for three months, with hard labour.

THE MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF A SIGNALMAN. An inquest was held yesterday morning at Timperley, on the body of John Hunt, signalman, who was found in a pit at Timperley Hall on Wednesday When last seen on Sunday the deceased was perfectly sober. From the appearance of the pit side deceased seems to have walked or fallen in, as his body was almost covered with weeds. The coroner said the deceased might have been thrown or tumbled into the pit. A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned. The pit was only 3ft. deep.

THE DUKE OF ALBANI'S VISIT TO GLASGOW. The Duke of Albaay has telegraphed to the Lord Provost of Glasgow that he accepts the honour of the freedom of the city of Glasgow, leaving the arrangements to Sir Archibald Campbell, of Blythewood, whose guests the Duke and Duchess are to be. It was decided yesterday that the free- dom of the city b 3 presented on Saturday the 14th October at noon, His Royal Highness opening the Art Needlework Exhibition at three.

BURNED TO DEATH. Yesterday afternoon an inquest was held by Mr. 'bet- son, at Chorley, on the body of Elizabeth Nelson, a girl who was burned to death. Deceased was left in bed with her sister whilst her mother went to a shop for provisions. On her return the girl was in flames, and was shockingly burned. She said she had been playing with lighted paper and her clothes ignited. She died the same day. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

CHESTER IMPROVEMENT BILL. A poll of the citizens of Chester has been taken on the Improvement Bill, which was intended to provide for the abolition of Dee Bridge tolls and the extension of the borough boundaries. The counting of the voting papers was commenced on Wednesday. The result which was an- nounced yesterday morning was: against the bill 3,303; 3,194; majority against the bill 113.

MANCHESTER CORN, THURSDAY.—M—essrs. Wm. Warburton and Yo. report as follows :—There has been a steady consump- tive demand for the leading articles since last market day at about the price then curt ent. Large supplies of wheat and flour have again c)me to hand at Liverpool, but impirts of other produce have been exceptionally small. There was a numeroui attendance at this day's market, an a fair inquiry. Best samples of new English wheat brought full prices. Foreign red was Id to 2d per cental higher. White steady. Flour sold slowly without change. Oats were again difficult to quit, though offered at lower prices. Beans sold slowly at late rates. Peas were id to 2d per cental lower. Maize was taken for consump- tion at Id to 2d per cental under the currencies of Thursday last.

_ LIVERPOOL PRODUCE, FRIDAY. The sugar market is quiet, but steady. Molasses unaltered Rum, coffee, cocoa, and rice show no new feature. Rustle and logwood steady. Cutch firm. Gambier as last. Nitrate of soda slow. Lard, 645. Palm oil quiet Fair demand for tallow. Olive and seed oils unchanged. Resin as last. Turpentine, 37s 6d. Petroleum. 7kd to 71d. Cotton: Steady market, especially for American. Jute very dull. Tallow, bracked, 54s spot. Oils: Rape, 31s 6d; linseed, 22s 6d to 22s 9d. Turpentine. 365. Petroleum, 61d to 6d spot, 7d in November and December. CLYDE CRUSHED SUGAR, FRIDAY. —Fine sugars in good demand at steady prices: other qualities slow and in buyer's favour.—The official report states: Moderate business done; prices unchanged. LIVERPOOL .PROVISIONS, FRIDAY.—Beef dull at a reduction. Pork irm but not active. Only a moderate demand far bacon. Hams slow at the quotations. Shoulders inaative. Lard firmer. line cheetls brings full rates. Butter steadier. LONDON Paovisiox, FRIDAY —Butter moderate; busine.s in foreign descriptions at about late rates. Friesland 116 s to 1245. Kiel and Danish 118 s to 136 s ; Normandy 104 s to 1265; Jersey 90s to 104: ; American and Irish unaltered. Bacon, light t :mac erate weights 77s to 82s; heavy and oversize 76s to 80s. Hams unchanged. Lard remains quiet. Cheese: Finest new American 56s to*sBs.

The market for wheat 1)1- came more active, and sales were effected to a good extent closing quotations showing an advance of Id to 2d on Taesday's rates. Beans and peas steady at previous values. Indian c ,rn about 2d dearer generally, and in fair request. Weather fine since Tuesday. WAKEFIELD CORK, FRIDAY.—There is more demand for wheat this morning, and last week's prices are readily main- tained, Indian sorts having recovered the undue depression of the last few weeks. There is a good enquiry for all useful English barley, but foreign does not meet with much attention Maize and oats steady. Beans in buyers' favour. Weather bright and fine.

T. HELENS SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. The DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZ FS AND CERTIFICATES to the successful candidates at these classes in the last examina- tions will take place at the TOWN HALL on FRIDAY, OCTOBER 6th. CLARKE ASPINALL, Esq., J.P., has kindly promised to distribute the prizes and to deliver an ADDRESS. The chair will be occupied by HIS WORSHIP THE MAYOR (R. Pilkingthn, Esq., J.P.). Doors open at 7-30; chair to be taken at 8-0. Tickets of admission free. The Session commenced on Monday. September 25th. Classes will be held in Acoustics, Light and Heat, Inorganic Chemistry, Machine Construction and Drawing, Mathematics, Physiography, Animal Physiology, Freehand Drawing, Model Drawing, Plane Geometry, and Perspective. Terms :-3s. 6d. per subject, for those who sit for examination; 10s. 6d. extra for those who do not. Government and Local Prizes are offered for competition. Tickets, Syllabuses, and other particulars may be obtained from the Master, or from C. CIILSHA.W, Hon. Secretary, 23, New Market-place.

CIOWLEY'S MIDDLE SCHOOL.—These Schools will be OPENED for tuition on MONDAY the 9th OCTOBER NEXT. M. E. J. SIMPSON, M.A., Trinity College, Cambridge, Head- master of Hinckley Grammar Sohool, has been appointed Head Master of the boy's school, and Miss Kate Jurgenson, L.L.A., S. Andrews, late assistant mistress at Norwich High School, Head Mistress of the girls' school. Tuitron fees: boys, £8 per annum; girls, £7 per annum ; entrance fee, Ll. To enable the governors to determine the number of assistant masters and mistresses required, intendinu pupPs are requested tl apply for admission tO the schools without delay. Applications for ad- mission must be made on forms to be obtained from me, the undersigned. No boy or girl under 8 years admittel. The ex- amination for admission will be held at the schools on Thurs- day, the sth day of October next, the following being the standard. Reading simple narrative, writing text hand, sums in the first rules of arithmetic with the multiplication table. THOMAS BREWIS, Clerk to the Governors. Town Hall, St. He!ens, 10th August, 1882.

TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Parchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be s3lected from the best makers for ecanomy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, wig lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882.
